articles.body:
Effective Date: December 1, 2026
This Notice at Collection and Privacy Policy (“Privacy Notice”) describes how Backblaze, Inc. (“Backblaze,” the “Company,” “we,” “our,” or “us”) collects, uses, discloses, processes, and retains personal information (“Information Practices”). This Privacy Notice explains the privacy rights available to you under applicable privacy laws and how you can exercise those rights. We respect your privacy and are committed to providing a transparent notice of our privacy practices.
Backblaze is headquartered in the United States and is a data storage company that provides two primary services. The first, Computer Backup, offers unlimited cloud backup solutions for individuals and organizations using Mac or PC devices, including laptops and desktops. The second, B2 Cloud Storage, provides scalable cloud storage solutions designed to meet the needs of individuals and organizations.
This Privacy Notice explains how Backblaze collects, uses, and shares your personal information when Backblaze acts as a data controller, meaning Backblaze determines the purposes and methods of processing your personal information unless otherwise specified in a separate agreement or required by applicable law. Click here to learn more about the controller-processor distinction.
This Privacy Notice applies when you visit our website (www.Backblaze.com), use the Backblaze App, and all features, applications, social media channels, browser plugins, content, downloads, and other online services that we make available or that link to this Privacy Notice (together, the “Platform”). It also applies to personal information we collect directly from you when you interact with us, including when you communicate with us through emails, phone calls, texts, or other channels; use our products, services, and applications; engage in commercial transactions with us; or register for and participate in webinars, events, programs, marketing, and promotional activities. In addition, this Privacy Notice covers information we collect offline and information collected indirectly through third parties, including our partners, in the course of our business.
The terms used in the Privacy Notice have the same or similar meaning as those terms under applicable privacy laws, or the closest approximation of such terms.
We recognize that privacy and data protection requirements vary across jurisdictions, and we are committed to meeting our obligations under each applicable legal framework. Accordingly, this Privacy Notice sets forth our privacy practices on an organization-wide basis, and jurisdiction-specific components, obligations, and rights that may apply to individuals in particular states, regions or countries are described in specific sections below. In the event of any conflict between the general provisions of this Privacy Notice and a jurisdiction-specific section, the jurisdiction-specific section shall control to the extent of such conflict.
We encourage you to read this Privacy Notice in its entirety, including the jurisdiction-specific sections that may be relevant to you based on your location or residency, so that you understand the full scope of our data processing activities and the rights available to you under applicable law.
The following notice identifies the categories of personal information to be collected from you and the purposes for which the personal information will be used, including whether that information is sold or shared for the purposes of cross-context behavioral advertising (e.g., targeted advertising).
Most U.S. state comprehensive privacy laws apply only to personal information processed about individuals acting in an individual or household context and exclude personal information processed about individuals acting in a commercial or employment context. Where applicable state law excludes such information from the scope of consumer rights, those rights are not available through this Privacy Notice for that information. The California Consumer Privacy Act (“CCPA”) differs in that it extends certain rights to California employees and job applicants. If you are a Backblaze employee or job applicant, please refer to our separate Employee Privacy Notice here for information about how we collect, use, and protect your personal information in that context.
Note: We do not collect Biometric Information, Inferences and Profile Data, Professional or Employment-Related Information, or Education Information in the consumer context.
    
Note: We do not collect other sensitive personal information under applicable state laws.
The period of time for which we retain personal information depends on the purposes for which we collect and use it. We will delete or de-identify personal information when it is no longer needed to fulfill the purposes listed for each category, unless a longer retention period is required or permitted to: (a) comply with applicable laws, including tax, accounting, and recordkeeping laws; (b) establish, exercise, or defend legal claims; (c) prevent fraud and ensure the security of our services; or (d) fulfill another legitimate business purpose permitted by applicable state law. Where technical or operational limitations prevent complete deletion or de-identification, we will take reasonable measures to prevent further processing.
Our use of tracking technologies may be considered a “sale” or “sharing” of personal information with third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising (e.g., targeted advertising) under applicable state law. You can opt out of such tracking by clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link in the footer of our website, which will allow you to access our cookie and tracking preference center and select or modify your preferences. Please note that this mechanism provides opt-out rights under applicable state privacy laws. You may also opt out by enabling a recognized opt-out preference signal, such as the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”), on your browser or device. See “Making Requests to Opt-Out; Opt-Out Preference Signals and Universal Opt-Out Mechanisms” below for additional details.
The purpose of this Privacy Policy is to provide you with a comprehensive description of our online and offline practices regarding our Information Practices. You have certain rights to control the use of your personal information. This privacy policy describes your rights as it relates to our Information Practices as to your personal information and how you can exercise those rights.
The following table includes disclosures for the preceding 12 months of: categories of personal information we have collected about consumers, the categories we have disclosed for a business purpose, and categories of third parties with whom we shared the personal information during that period.
Unless otherwise allowed by applicable state law, we will only collect certain types of sensitive personal information with your consent. We will only collect, process, or disclose sensitive personal data where it is strictly necessary to provide or maintain a specific product or service you have requested, and we will not sell sensitive personal data. We do not use or disclose the below sensitive personal information for purposes other than those business purposes specifically enumerated under applicable state law.
In the previous 12 months, we did not collect any other sensitive personal information under applicable state laws.
For each category of personal information identified above, we also disclose such personal information to the following categories of third parties:
Mobile information. We do not share mobile information with third parties or affiliates for marketing or promotional purposes. Text messaging originator opt-in data and consent are excluded from all categories of information we disclose and will not be shared with any third parties, excluding aggregators and providers of the Text Message services.
De-identified and aggregated information. We may disclose aggregated information about our users and de-identified data or information that does not identify an individual, without restriction.
Where we maintain de-identified data (data that cannot reasonably be used to infer information about, or otherwise be linked to, an identified or identifiable individual), we commit to the following: (1) we take reasonable measures to ensure the data cannot be associated with an individual; (2) we publicly commit to maintaining and using the data in de-identified form and will not attempt to re-identify the data, except for the purpose of determining whether our de-identification processes comply with applicable law; and (3) we contractually obligate any recipients of the de-identified data to comply with all applicable requirements regarding de-identified data. Data used for usage analytics and business intelligence may be anonymized or aggregated so that resulting insights do not constitute Personal Information.
Sources of Personal Information. The categories of personal information identified above were collected from the following categories of sources: you directly; your devices when you interact with our websites, platforms, and applications; service providers acting on our behalf; third parties such as data aggregators, social media companies, and publicly available sources; your employer or organization in connection with business customer relationships; and business partners, such as event or conference organizers.
AI Processing Disclosure: We may employ artificial intelligence (AI) technologies to support and enhance our operations; any such processing is conducted in compliance with applicable laws and governed by data processing agreements.
We have sold or shared with third parties for cross-context behavioral advertising (e.g., targeted advertising) the following categories of personal information to advertising networks and analytics providers in the preceding 12 months: Identifiers; Internet or Other Similar Network Activity; Commercial Information; Geolocation Data. We do not sell or share sensitive personal information.
You have the right to direct us to stop selling or sharing your personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising (the “Right to Opt-Out”). You may exercise this right by: (1) Clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link to manage your preferences; or (2) Submitting your request through an Opt-Out Preference Signal/Universal Opt-Out Mechanism, such as the Global Privacy Control (“GPC”), as described further below.
We do not have actual knowledge that we sell the personal information of minors under 18 years of age.
You may opt out of marketing communications at any time:
The Platform may contain links to other websites or applications. Please be aware that we are not responsible for the content or privacy practices of such other websites or applications. We encourage our users to be aware when they leave our Platform and to read the privacy statements of any other website or application that collects personal information.
Right to Know/Access: Certain states provide the right to request our disclosure of any of the following:
Right to Correct: You have the right to request that we correct inaccurate personal information we maintain about you, taking into account the nature of the personal information and the purposes of our processing. We may request documentation from you to help assess accuracy. If we determine the contested information is more likely than not accurate based on the totality of circumstances, we may deny the request and will explain the basis for our decision.
Right to Delete: You have the right to request that we delete personal information we have collected from or about you, subject to certain exceptions permitted by law. If we cannot fully comply with a deletion request, we will explain why and delete the information that is not subject to an exception.
Right to Opt-Out of Sale/Sharing; Targeted Advertising: You may have the right to “opt out” of the “sale” or “sharing” of your personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising, or processing of your personal data for purposes of targeted advertising (as those terms are defined by applicable state law).
Right to Withdraw Consent: Where we have collected or used your personal information based on your consent, you have the right to withdraw your consent at any time.
Right to Appeal: If we deny your request to exercise any of the rights described above, you may have the right to appeal that decision by submitting a request to appeal to us.
Right to Non-Discrimination: We will not discriminate against you for exercising any of your state privacy rights. However, we may still offer you certain financial incentives permitted under applicable state law, such as discounts, rewards, premium features, loyalty accounts, or club card programs that can result in different prices, rates, or quality levels.
Making Requests to Know/Access, Delete, or Correct: You may exercise your rights, as applicable by state law, by submitting a verified consumer request to know information (and to receive your personal information in a portable format), to correct information, or for deletion.
The response to a request to know will provide the personal information we have collected and maintained about you, in a portable format, unless an exception under applicable state law applies. Please note that, depending on the applicable state law, we may not be required to provide personal information to you if you make multiple requests in a certain time period.
You may submit a request by using our Privacy Rights Request Form available here, or by contacting us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com. We will verify your request using the information you provide through the request form or in your communication. If you submit a request that is not through one of the above designated methods or is deficient in some manner unrelated to verification, we will provide you with information on how to submit the request or remedy any deficiencies with your request. We cannot respond to your request or provide you with personal information if we cannot verify your identity or authority to make the request. We will only use personal information provided in a verifiable consumer request to verify the requestor’s identity or authority to make the request.
Once we receive your verifiable consumer request, we will confirm receipt within 10 business days, or as allowed under applicable law, and describe our verification process. We will confirm receipt of your request and respond, consistent with applicable law, if we can verify your identity. Requests for deletion will require separate confirmation that you want your information deleted. We do not knowingly collect information of minors under the age of 18.
Making Requests to Opt-Out; Opt-Out Preference Signals and Universal Opt-Out Mechanisms: Our use of tracking technologies may be considered a sale or sharing for targeted advertising under applicable state law. You may exercise your right to opt out of sale, sharing, or processing for targeted advertising by (1) clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link at the bottom of our website and selecting your preferences, or (2) broadcasting an opt-out preference signal or universal opt-out mechanism (“UOOM”) that we recognize, including the Global Privacy Control (GPC) (on browsers and/or browser extensions that support such a signal). We recognize and process opt-out preference signals and UOOMs as valid opt-out requests as required by applicable state law. If you do not have a Backblaze account or are not logged into your account, your request to opt out will be linked to your browser identifier only and not linked to any account information. Because the signal is browser-specific, you will need to broadcast subsequent signals if you access our website through different devices (e.g., computers, smartphones, or tablets). You may return to the preference center at any time to review or update your cookie and tracking selections by clicking the "Your Privacy Choices" link in the footer of our website.
Withdrawing Consent: Where we have collected or used your personal information based on your consent, you may withdraw your consent at any time. If your request relates to cookies, online tracking, targeted advertising, or similar technologies, you may withdraw or modify your consent by clicking the “Your Privacy Choices” link in the footer of our website and updating your preferences through the Cookie Settings link.
Appealing a Denial of a Request: If we deny or decline to take action on your verified consumer request, you have the right to appeal. To submit an appeal, please email us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com within 90 days of receiving our denial. Within 45 days after receipt of your appeal, we will inform you in writing of the action taken or not taken and provide a written explanation of the reasons for our decision. If we deny your appeal, we will also provide an online mechanism or other method through which you may contact your state Attorney General or applicable regulatory authority to submit a complaint.
California: Only you, or a natural person or a business entity registered with the Secretary of State to conduct business in California that you have authorized to act on your behalf, may make a verifiable consumer request related to your personal information, to opt-out of sale or sharing, or to limit the use or disclosure of your sensitive personal information. If you use an authorized agent, you may provide a power of attorney executed pursuant to California Probate Code sections 4000 to 4465. If a power of attorney that meets those provisions is not submitted, you will be required to provide the authorized agent signed permission to submit a request, verify your identity directly by submitting a verified consumer request according to the procedures in the section “How to Exercise Your Rights,” and directly confirm with us that you provided the authorized agent permission to submit the request. To submit authorized agent documentation, contact us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com.
Other States: If you use an authorized agent, you may provide a power of attorney executed pursuant to applicable state law. If a power of attorney is not submitted, you may be required to provide commercially reasonable identification of your identity and evidence of your authorized agent’s authority to act on your behalf. For example, you may need to provide the authorized agent signed permission to submit a request, verify your identity directly by submitting a verified consumer request according to the procedures in the section “How to Exercise Your Rights,” and directly confirm with us that you provided the authorized agent permission to submit the request, by contacting us at privacyrequest@backblaze.com.
This section of the Privacy Policy applies if you are in the European Economic Area (EEA) or the United Kingdom (U.K.) and supplements the Privacy Policy.
Under the General Data Protection Regulation (“GDPR”) and/or the United Kingdom General Data Protection Regulation (“UK GDPR”), we are required to have a valid legal basis for processing your personal information, and we must inform you of that legal basis. Our legal basis for collecting and using the personal information described above will depend on the specific personal information concerned and the context in which it is collected. Generally, we will collect personal information from you only when you have consented to such collection, when we need the personal information to perform our obligations under a contract with you (for example, when you create an account or use our services), or where the processing is in our legitimate business interests (for example, to detect and prevent fraud and to analyze usage for analytics, modeling, and business intelligence). In some cases, we may also have a legal obligation to collect personal information from you (for example, to verify your identity when accessing your account or services).
Where we rely on legitimate interests, we balance our interests against your interests, rights, and freedoms and apply appropriate safeguards to protect your personal data.
If we ask you to provide personal information to comply with a legal requirement or to enter into a contract with us, we will make this clear at the time we request that personal information. We will also tell you whether providing that personal information is mandatory or not (as well as the possible consequences if you do not provide your personal information). Similarly, if we collect and use your personal information, we will provide you with our legitimate business interests for such collection and use.
If you have questions about or need further information concerning the legal basis for which we collect and use your personal information, please contact us as provided in the Contact for More Information section below.
We use industry-standard methods of securing electronic databases of personal information. However, you should know that no company can fully eliminate security risks associated with personal information. To help protect yourself, please use a strong password, do not use the same password to access your Backblaze account that you use with other accounts or services, and protect your usernames and passwords to help prevent others from accessing your accounts and services.
Your personal information may be transferred to and processed in the United States and other countries where Backblaze and its service providers operate, which may have data protection laws that differ from those in your jurisdiction.
Where required by law, we implement appropriate safeguards for such transfers, including contractual protections and other legally recognized mechanisms. While your information is outside of your country of residence, it is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction in which it is held and may be subject to disclosure to governments, courts, law enforcement, or regulatory agencies pursuant to applicable law.
If you reside within the EEA or in the U.K., you have the following rights under applicable law, which you can exercise at any time:
Please see the Exercising Your Privacy Rights section below to exercise your privacy rights.
We will respond to your request within 30 days of receipt. Where a request is complex, or we have received a large number of requests, we may extend this period by a further two months, as permitted under applicable law. If we extend the response period, we will inform you within 30 days of receiving your request and explain the reason for the delay. We will not charge a fee for responding to your request unless the request is manifestly unfounded or excessive, in which case we may charge a reasonable fee or decline to respond.
If you have an account, you may log in to access, update, or delete your personal information and associated data. If you are unable to access your account, you may contact us using the information provided in the Contact for More Information section below.
In cases where we rely on your consent to process personal information, you can revoke your consent by contacting us. Revoking your consent does not affect the lawfulness of any processing conducted prior to your withdrawal.
You may manage your cookie and tracking preferences through the cookie and tracking preference center, which may be accessed by clicking the Cookie Settings link in the footer of our website or through any other cookie settings mechanism made available on the Platform. Please note that cookie and tracking preferences are generally browser- and device-specific, and data collected before we can identify or authenticate you may not be able to be associated with your account.
Backblaze does not make decisions about you that produce legal effects or similarly significant effects based solely on automated processing, including profiling. In particular, we do not use automated decision-making to make decisions about your eligibility for services, pricing, or access to functionality. This does not prevent us from using personal information for ordinary business purposes, such as analytics, lead management, marketing segmentation, customer relationship management, fraud prevention, security, or service improvement, where such processing does not produce legal or similarly significant effects concerning you.
If you are not satisfied with how we handle your personal information, or with our response to a request you have made, you have the right to lodge a complaint with the relevant data protection authority in your jurisdiction. You may contact the applicable authority by clicking below:
We encourage you to contact us first using the information in the Contact for More Information section below, so that we may address your concerns directly.

You may access or modify your cookie and tracking preferences at any time by clicking the Cookie Settings link in the footer of our website. The exact choices available to you may depend on your location and the laws that apply to you.
Cookies: Cookies are small data files stored on your device when you visit. Cookies allow us to recognize your device during subsequent visits and personalize your experience based on your preferences. They may also provide information to our service providers to help us improve website functionality and usability.
The Platform may use first-party and third-party cookies, as well as other tracking technologies, for advertising and analytics purposes. First-party cookies are set directly by Backblaze and are used to make the Platform function properly, remember your preferences, and support our internal analytics. Third-party cookies are set by our partners and service providers, such as advertising networks and analytics providers, and may be used to track your activity across different websites to deliver targeted advertising and measure performance.
If you consent to the use of cookies by clicking “Accept All Cookies” when you first visit the website, we will collect certain information from you, including Internet Protocol (IP) addresses, browser types, operating systems, page requests, and average time spent on our website. This data helps us understand website activity, monitor performance, and improve the user experience.
You can set your browser to notify you when cookies are received or to block certain types of cookies. However, disabling cookies may limit your ability to access some features of the website. For additional details on how to opt out of the use of cookies, please review our Cookie Notice.
Analytics: We utilize tools like Google Analytics to collect data about website usage, including pages visited, time spent, search terms, and engagement metrics. This information helps us evaluate and enhance the user experience. For example, to opt out of Google Analytics, you can use the Google Analytics Opt-Out Browser Add-On. For more information about how Google uses your data, please visit “How Google uses data when you use our partners' sites or apps.” Please review our Cookie Notice for information on analytics tools used on the website.
Interest-Based Advertising: We work with third parties, such as advertisers, advertising networks, and data exchanges, to deliver tailored content and advertising based on your online activity. These third parties may use their own tracking technologies, including cookies and pixel tags, to collect information about your interactions with our website and other websites. This data helps deliver personalized advertisements for products or services that may interest you.
To opt out of interest-based advertising through cookies or similar technologies on our website, click the Cookie Settings link in the footer of our website and update your preferences in our cookie and tracking preference center. You may also use industry opt-out tools, such as Your Online Choices, where available. Please note that opting out does not mean you will no longer receive ads; instead, advertisements may no longer be tailored to your preferences based on online behavior. Cookie-based opt-outs are generally browser- and device-specific, so you may need to repeat the opt-out process if you use a different browser or device or clear your cookies.
Backblaze complies with the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (EU-U.S. DPF) and the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF, and the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework (Swiss-U.S. DPF) as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce. Backblaze has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (EU-U.S. DPF Principles) with regard to the processing of personal data received from the European Union and the United Kingdom in reliance on the EU-U.S. DPF and the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF. Backblaze has certified to the U.S. Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Swiss-U.S. Data Privacy Framework Principles (Swiss-U.S. DPF Principles) with regard to the processing of personal data received from Switzerland in reliance on the Swiss-U.S. DPF. If there is any conflict between the terms in this privacy policy and the EU-U.S. DPF Principles and/or the Swiss-U.S. DPF Principles, the Principles shall govern. To learn more about the Data Privacy Framework (DPF) program and to view our certification, please visit https://www.dataprivacyframework.gov/.
In compliance with the EU-U.S. DPF and the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF and the Swiss-U.S. DPF, Backblaze commits to refer unresolved complaints concerning our handling of personal data received in reliance on the EU-U.S. DPF and the UK Extension to the EU-U.S. DPF and the Swiss-U.S. DPF to the International Division of the American Arbitration Association (ICDR-AAA), an alternative dispute resolution provider based in the United States.
If you do not receive timely acknowledgment of your DPF Principles-related complaint from us, or if we have not addressed your DPF Principles-related complaint to your satisfaction, please visit https://feature.adr.org/dpf_irm for more information or to file a complaint. The services of ICDR-AAA are provided at no cost to you.

articles.title: Exascale fusion simulation team named finalist for 2026 Gordon Bell Prize
articles.body:
A multi-institutional team leveraged ALCF's Aurora and OLCF's Frontier systems to perform exascale simulations of a liquid-metal fusion breeding blanket, demonstrating new modeling capabilities that could help advance the design of future fusion reactors.
Using two U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) exascale supercomputers devoted to open science, a multi-institutional team has carried out the largest and most detailed simulations to date of a critical component for fusion energy systems. The work has been named a finalist for the Association for Computing Machinery’s prestigious Gordon Bell Prize, which recognizes outstanding achievement in high-performance computing.
The simulations targeted a key part of many proposed fusion reactor designs: the breeding blanket. Located around the plasma in a fusion reactor, breeding blankets are designed to capture energy from fusion reactions, help shield reactor components from damage, and produce tritium, a scarce hydrogen isotope needed as fuel.
The team zeroed in on the water-cooled lead-lithium (WCLL) blanket design for ITER, the international fusion experiment under construction in France. Their simulations captured several processes interacting across the full blanket, including liquid-metal flow under strong magnetic fields, heat transfer, buoyancy, tritium transport and water cooling.
“We’re tackling a very challenging multiphysics, multiscale problem involving fluid systems with very different properties,” said project lead Elia Merzari, a professor of nuclear engineering and mechanical engineering at Pennsylvania State University with a joint appointment at DOE’s Argonne National Laboratory. “This is the first time a blanket has been modeled at this fidelity, including all the physics.”
Meeting that challenge required expertise in both fusion energy science and high-performance computing, along with access to two of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. The project brought together researchers from Argonne, Penn State, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the UK Atomic Energy Authority.
To carry out the massive simulations, the team used Aurora at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility (ALCF) and Frontier at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility (OLCF). Both are exascale supercomputers capable of performing quintillions of calculations per second. The ALCF and OLCF are DOE Office of Science user facilities supported by DOE’s Advanced Scientific Computing Research program.
Fusion blankets are highly complex systems. In a WCLL blanket, liquid lead-lithium flows through breeding zones, where lithium interacts with neutrons to produce tritium. Separate water circuits remove heat. Because the liquid metal is electrically conductive, its flow is strongly affected by the powerful magnetic fields used to confine plasma in a reactor.
Interactions between the liquid metal and the magnetic field can create extremely thin boundary layers — regions where the flow changes sharply over a very short distance. Those tiny features exist within a blanket that spans roughly a meter, creating an enormous difference between the largest and smallest scales in the flow. At the same time, water can move through the system hundreds of times faster than the liquid metal, so the simulation must also account for processes occurring at very different rates. Capturing this wide range of spatial and temporal scales required a high-resolution multiscale model and exascale computing power.
With access to Aurora and Frontier, the team’s calculations used more than 2 billion spectral elements and 2 trillion grid points, making them the largest liquid-metal magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) simulations to date. Spectral elements divide the blanket model into smaller regions that represent its geometry. Grid points are locations within those regions where the model calculates conditions such as velocity and temperature.
“Modeling two trillion grid points is something you can only do with exascale computing,” Merzari said. “The need for that resolution is really driven by the physics. You need very high resolution to capture the thin boundary layers in the flow created by MHD.”
The simulations allowed the researchers to examine how these physical effects influence blanket behavior. One key finding was that MHD suppresses turbulence and reorganize the liquid-metal flow, affecting pressure, temperature and heat transfer. The team also observed that temperature differences in the liquid can drive buoyancy, further altering the flow, especially near the wall facing the plasma. Understanding these complex interactions can help researchers improve fusion blanket designs.
Carrying out simulations at this scale required years of code development and validation. The team used NekRS, an open-source computational fluid dynamics code developed at Argonne, for the high-fidelity multiphysics simulations. NekRS builds on decades of advances in the Nek5000 code, which has supported past Gordon Bell Prize-winning research and demonstrated high performance and scalability for incompressible flow simulations on CPU-based supercomputers. NekRS extends that foundation by adapting and improving algorithms for GPUs. The team also used the open-source OpenMC code to calculate neutron transport, providing data on heating, tritium production and water activation as inputs to the NekRS simulations.
To prepare for the exascale runs, the researchers expanded NekRS to model MHD effects and optimized the code for simulations of this scale. This effort was led by Yu-Hsiang Lan, a doctoral student at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. He worked closely with two mentors and longtime NekRS developers, Paul Fischer of University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and Argonne, and Misun Min of Argonne.
“My role was to develop the solver that brings MHD into NekRS and validate it against similar problems in the literature to make sure everything was working correctly before we pushed it to larger scales,” Lan said.
Lan also implemented a capability known as global mesh refinement in NekRS. This allowed the team to start with a lower-resolution model and progressively add detail rather than building the largest model from the outset.
“In terms of workflow, this was a lifesaver,” Merzari said. “It really helped us get this work done in a fraction of the time.”
NekRS’s ability to run on different types of GPUs allowed the team to perform and scale the simulations on both Frontier and Aurora. Large-scale supercomputers are made up of thousands of interconnected computers, called nodes, that work together to perform complex calculations. The team ran simulations on more than 9,000 nodes on each system, using nearly the full capacity of both machines. They also demonstrated strong scaling on both systems, showing that increasing the number of nodes continued to reduce simulation time.
Frontier served as a primary platform for code development, testing and validation. The system also supported in-situ visualization using the open-source Ascent software. This capability allowed researchers to capture simulation data at high frequency as the calculations ran, enabling them to study transient flow behavior in greater detail and generate high-quality movies of the evolving flow.
The researchers turned to Aurora for their largest simulation, leveraging its substantial memory capacity to run the complete multiphysics model, including MHD, at a resolution of 2 trillion grid points.
High-fidelity simulations provide a valuable complement to fusion experiments, allowing researchers to study and predict how fusion systems behave under extreme conditions.
“These types of experiments are very hard and also very expensive,” Lan said. “Simulation is an important tool for design and can help reduce the cost of actual experiments.”
The detailed data from these simulations can also help researchers develop and test new approaches to fusion engineering. One longer-term goal is to use simulations of different designs and operating conditions to develop faster models that require less computing power.
“Now that we’ve shown this is doable, people can use the results or the code as a tool to validate a low-fidelity model,” Lan said. “Then the low-fidelity model eventually can be used for things like AI design optimization or digital twins.”
Lan is already contributing to a separate Argonne-led project that is building on this work, using data from the blanket simulations to develop simplified system-analysis tools for fusion applications.
More broadly, the team’s exascale simulations mark another step forward for fusion modeling. Their scale and level of detail provide new insights that can help accelerate the path to practical fusion energy.
“There is such interesting physics in simulations at this scale and so much we can learn as we continue working to develop better fusion energy technologies,” Merzari said.
This research is detailed in the paper “Exascale Multiphysics Simulations for Liquid Metal Fusion Blankets,” which will be presented Nov. 17 as part of the ACM Gordon Bell Finalists Presentations session at SC26. In addition to Elia Merzari and Yu-Hsiang Lan, the paper's authors are Misun Min, Haomin Yuan, Patrick Shriwise, Stefan Kerkemeier, Kristopher Rowe and Ramesh Balakrishnan of Argonne National Laboratory; Paul Fischer of Argonne and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign; Tri Nguyen, Maximiliano Dalinger and Luiz Aldeia Machado of Penn State University; Ananias Tomboulides of Aristotle University; and Andrew Davis, Aleksander Dubas and Rupert Eardley-Brunt of the UK Atomic Energy Authority.
The team received computing time on Aurora and Frontier through DOE’s Innovative and Novel Computational Impact on Theory and Experiment (INCITE) program, which is supported by the Office of Advanced Scientific Computing Research. Development of Nek5000 and NekRS was supported by ASCR’s Applied Mathematics program and DOE’s Nuclear Energy Advanced Modeling and Simulation program.
Argonne National Laboratory seeks solutions to pressing national problems in science and technology by conducting leading-edge basic and applied research in virtually every scientific discipline. Argonne is managed by UChicago Argonne, LLC for the U.S. Department of Energy’s Office of Science.
UT-Battelle LLC manages ORNL for DOE’s Office of Science, the single largest supporter of basic research in the physical sciences in the United States. The Office of Science is working to address some of the most pressing challenges of our time. For more information, please visit https://energy.gov/science.

                 draft-ietf-plants-merkle-tree-certs-08
Abstract
   This document describes Merkle Tree certificates, a new form of X.509
   certificates which integrate public logging of the certificate, in
   the style of Certificate Transparency.  The integrated design reduces
   logging overhead in the face of both shorter-lived certificates and
   large post-quantum signature algorithms, while still achieving
   comparable security properties to existing X.509 constructions and
   Certificate Transparency.  Merkle Tree certificates additionally
   admit an optional size optimization that avoids signatures
   altogether, at the cost of only applying to up-to-date relying
   parties and older certificates.

1.  Introduction
   In Public Key Infrastructures (PKIs) that use Certificate
   Transparency (CT) [RFC6962] for a public logging requirement, an
   authenticating party must present Signed Certificate Timestamps
   (SCTs) alongside certificates.  CT policies often require two or more
   SCTs per certificate [APPLE-CT] [CHROME-CT], each of which carries a
   signature.  These signatures are in addition to those in the
   certificate chain itself.
   Current signature schemes can use as few as 32 bytes per key and 64
   bytes per signature [RFC8032], but post-quantum replacements are much
   larger.  For example, ML-DSA-44 [FIPS204] uses 1,312 bytes per public
   key and 2,420 bytes per signature.  ML-DSA-65 uses 1,952 bytes per
   public key and 3,309 bytes per signature.  Even with a directly-
   trusted intermediate (Section 9.5 of
   [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids]), two SCTs and a leaf certificate
   signature add 7,260 bytes of authentication overhead with ML-DSA-44
   and 9,927 bytes with ML-DSA-65.
   This increased overhead additionally impacts CT logs themselves.
   Most of a log's costs scale with the total storage size of the log.
   Each log entry contains both a public key, and a signature from the
   CA.  With larger public keys and signatures, the size of each log
   entry will grow.
   Additionally, as PKIs transition to shorter-lived certificates
   [CABF-153] [CABF-SC081], the rate at which entries are added to the
   log will increase.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                   [Page 5]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   This document introduces Merkle Tree Certificates (MTCs), a new form
   of X.509 certificate that integrates logging with certificate
   issuance.  Each CA maintains logs of everything it issues, signing
   views of its logs to assert it has issued the contents.  The CA
   signature is combined with cosignatures from other parties who verify
   correct operation and optionally mirror the logs.  These signatures,
   together with an inclusion proof for an individual entry, constitute
   a certificate.
   This achieves the following:
   *  Log entries do not scale with public key and signature sizes.
      Entries replace public keys with hashes and do not contain
      signatures, while preserving non-repudiability (Section 12.4).
   *  Long-expired entries can be revoked from relying parties in bulk
      (see Section 7.5).  This allows logging and monitoring
      infrastructure to scale by retention policies, not the lifetime of
      the log, even as certificate lifetimes decrease.
   *  After a processing delay, authenticating parties can obtain a
      second "landmark-relative" certificate for the same log entry.
      This second certificate is an optional size optimization that
      avoids the need for any signatures, assuming an up-to-date client
      that has some predistributed log information.
   Section 3 gives an overview of the system.  Section 4 describes a
   Merkle Tree primitive used by this system.  Section 5.2 describes the
   log structure.  Finally, Section 6 and Section 7 describe how to
   construct and consume a Merkle Tree certificate.
2.  Conventions and Definitions
   The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT",
   "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and
   "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in
   BCP 14 [RFC2119] [RFC8174] when, and only when, they appear in all
   capitals, as shown here.
   This document additionally uses the TLS presentation language defined
   in Section 3 of [RFC9846], as well as the notation defined in
   Section 2.1.1 of [RFC9162].  It extends the numeric types defined in
   Section 3.3 of [RFC9846] with a big-endian, 48-bit integer:
   uint8 uint48[6];
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                   [Page 6]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   U+ followed by four hexadecimal characters denotes a Unicode
   codepoint, to be encoded in UTF-8 [RFC3629]. 0x followed by two
   hexadecimal characters denotes a byte value in the 0-255 range.
   The _decimal representation_ of a non-negative integer is its base-
   ten representation, written with the ASCII digits 0 through 9 (U+0030
   through U+0039).  Zero is written as the single digit 0, and no other
   value is written with a leading 0.
   [start, end), where start <= end, denotes the half-open interval
   containing integers x such that start <= x < end.
   Given a non-negative integer n,
   *  LSB(n) refers to the least-significant bit of n's binary
      representation.  Equivalently, it is the remainder when n is
      divided by 2.
   *  BIT_WIDTH(n) refers to the smallest number of bits needed to
      represent n.  BIT_WIDTH(0) is zero.
   *  POPCOUNT(n) refers to the number of set bits in n's binary
      representation.
   *  BIT_CEIL(n) refers to the smallest power of 2 that is greater or
      equal to n.
   To _left-shift_ a non-negative integer n is to shift each bit in its
   binary representation to one upper position.  Equivalently, it is n
   times 2.  Given non-negative integers a and b, a << b refers to a
   left-shifted b times.
   To _right-shift_ a non-negative integer n is to shift each bit in its
   binary representation to one lower position, discarding the least-
   significant bit.  Equivalently, it is the floor of n divided by 2.
   Given non-negative integers a and b, a >> b refers to a right-shifted
   b times.
   Given two non-negative integers a and b, a & b refers to the non-
   negative integer such that each bit position is set if the
   corresponding bit is set in both a and b, and unset otherwise.  This
   is commonly referred to as the bitwise AND operator.
2.1.  Terminology and Roles
   This document discusses the following roles:
   Authenticating party:  The party that authenticates itself in the
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                   [Page 7]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
      protocol.  In TLS, this is the side sending the Certificate and
      CertificateVerify message.
   Certification authority (CA):  The service that issues certificates
      to the authenticating party, after performing some validation
      process on the certificate contents.
   Relying party:  The party to whom the authenticating party presents
      its identity.  In TLS, this is the side receiving the Certificate
      and CertificateVerify message.
   Monitor:  Parties who watch logs for certificates of interest,
      analogous to the role in Section 8.2 of [RFC9162].
   Issuance log:  A log, maintained by the CA, containing certification
      statements issued by that CA.  A CA operates some number of
      issuance logs, which together contain all statements issued by
      that CA.
   Cosigner:  A service that signs views of an issuance log, to assert
      correct operation and other properties about the entries.
   Additionally, there are several terms used throughout this document
   to describe this proposal.  This section provides an overview.  They
   will be further defined and discussed in detail throughout the
   document.
   Checkpoint:  A description of the complete state of the log at some
      time.
   Entry:  An individual element of the log, describing information
      which the CA has validated and certified.
   Subtree:  A smaller Merkle Tree over a portion of the log, defined by
      an interior node of some snapshot of the log.  Subtrees can be
      efficiently shown to be consistent with the whole log.
   Inclusion proof:  A sequence of hashes that efficiently proves some
      entry is contained in some checkpoint or subtree.
   Consistency proof:  A sequence of hashes that efficiently proves a
      checkpoint or subtree is contained within another checkpoint.
   Cosignature:  A signature from either the CA or other cosigner, over
      some checkpoint or subtree.
   Landmark:  One of a sequence of tree sizes, infrequently chosen and

Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
      used to calculate landmark subtrees for predistribution to relying
      parties.
   Landmark subtree:  One of the two (possibly empty) subtrees
      determined by an interval between two landmarks.  Predistributed
      and used as the basis for landmark-relative certificates.
   Standalone certificate:  A certificate containing an inclusion proof
      to some subtree, and several cosignatures over that subtree.
   Landmark-relative certificate:  An optimized certificate containing
      an inclusion proof to a landmark subtree.  The landmark subtree is
      assumed to be known to the relying party, rather than
      authenticated by cosignatures.
   Directly-signed certificate:  A certificate issued using the
      existing, non-MTC construction, where the TBSCertificate is passed
      directly to the private key's signing operation.
3.  Overview
   In Certificate Transparency, a CA first certifies information by
   signing it, then submits the resulting certificate (or
   precertificate) to logs for logging.  Merkle Tree Certificates invert
   this process: the CA certifies information by logging it, then
   submits the log to cosigners to verify log operation.  A certificate
   is assembled from the result and proves the information is in the
   CA's log.

4.  Subtrees
   This section extends the Merkle Tree definition in Section 2.1 of
   [RFC9162] by defining a _subtree_ of a Merkle Tree.  A subtree is
   itself a Merkle Tree, built over an interval of entries from the
   original tree.  Section 4.1 defines a subtree formally, including the
   constraints on those intervals.
   As with Merkle Trees, a subtree inclusion proof, defined in
   Section 4.3, can prove an entry is contained in some subtree.
   Subtrees, and thus their inclusion proofs, are smaller than those of
   the original tree, so this document uses subtree inclusion proofs as
   a certificate size optimization.
   Not all intervals can form subtrees.  Subtrees are limited to
   intervals that can be efficiently proven consistent with the original
   tree, using subtree consistency proofs defined in Section 4.4.
   However, every interval of a Merkle Tree can be efficiently covered
   by two subtrees.  Section 4.5 describes how to determine these
   subtrees.
   Appendix C.1 and Appendix C.2 provide test vectors for the algorithms
   defined in this section.
4.1.  Definition of a Subtree
   Given an ordered list of n inputs, D_n = {d[0], d[1], ..., d[n-1]},
   Section 2.1.1 of [RFC9162] defines the Merkle Tree via the Merkle
   Tree Hash MTH(D_n).
   A _subtree_ of this Merkle Tree is itself a Merkle Tree, defined by
   MTH(D[start:end]). start and end are integers such that:
   *  0 <= start <= end <= n
   *  start is a multiple of BIT_CEIL(end - start)
   The second condition ensures that MTH(D[start:end]), built over
   D[start:end] as an independent list, is sufficiently aligned with the
   original Merkle Tree to support subtree consistency proofs.  See
   Appendix B.2 for more details.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 13]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   In implementations using fixed-width integers, BIT_CEIL(end - start)
   above may exceed end and potentially overflow.  For example, if start
   is zero and end is 2^63+1, BIT_CEIL(end - start) is 2^64.  The
   following is an example C++ implementation that handles this
   condition.
   bool is_valid_subtree(uint64_t start, uint64_t end) {
     if (start > end) {
       return false;
     }
     uint64_t size = end - start;
     if (size > (uint64_t{1} << 63)) {
       return start == 0;  // bit_ceil below will overflow.
     }
     return (start & (std::bit_ceil(size) - 1)) == 0;
   }
   For all x, [0, x) is a valid subtree (0 is a multiple of everything),
   and [x, x) is a valid subtree (BIT_CEIL(0) is 1).
   The _size_ of the subtree is end - start.
   In the context of a single Merkle Tree, this document denotes subtree
   MTH(D[start:end]) by half-open interval [start, end).  It contains
   the entries whose indices are in that half-open interval.
   As a Merkle Tree grows, its subtrees remain unchanged.  That is, if
   end <= m <= n, the subtree [start, end) of MTH(D[0:m]) and the
   subtree [start, end) of MTH(D_n) are both valid and identical.

4.3.  Subtree Inclusion Proofs
   Subtrees are Merkle Trees, so entries can be proven to be contained
   in the subtree.  A subtree inclusion proof for entry index of the
   subtree [start, end) is a Merkle inclusion proof, as defined in
   Section 2.1.3.1 of [RFC9162], where m is index - start and the tree
   inputs are D[start:end].
   Subtree inclusion proofs contain a sequence of nodes that are
   sufficient to reconstruct the subtree hash, MTH(D[start:end]), out of
   the hash for entry index, MTH({d[index]}), thus demonstrating that
   the subtree hash contains the entry's hash.
   A subtree inclusion proof for a subtree of size n contains at most
   ceil(log2(n)) hashes, or BIT_WIDTH(n - 1) hashes.

4.3.2.  Evaluating a Subtree Inclusion Proof
   Given a subtree inclusion proof, inclusion_proof, for entry index,
   with hash entry_hash, of a subtree [start, end), the subtree
   inclusion proof can be _evaluated_ to compute the expected subtree
   hash:
   1.  Check that [start, end) is a valid subtree (Section 4.1), and
       that start <= index < end.  If either does not hold, fail proof
       evaluation.
   2.  Set fn to index - start and sn to end - start - 1.
   3.  Set r to entry_hash.
   4.  For each value p in the inclusion_proof array:
       1.  If sn is 0, then stop the iteration and fail proof
           evaluation.
       2.  If LSB(fn) is set, or if fn is equal to sn, then:
           1.  Set r to HASH(0x01 || p || r).
           2.  Until LSB(fn) is set, right-shift fn and sn equally.
           Otherwise:
           1.  Set r to HASH(0x01 || r || p).
       3.  Finally, right-shift both fn and sn one time.
   5.  If sn is not zero, fail proof evaluation.
   6.  Return r as the expected subtree hash.
   This is the same as the procedure in Section 2.1.3.2 of [RFC9162],
   where leaf_index is index - start, tree_size is end - start, and r is
   returned instead of compared with root_hash.
   Appendix B.3 explains this procedure in more detail.
4.3.3.  Verifying a Subtree Inclusion Proof
   Given a subtree inclusion proof, inclusion_proof, for entry index,
   with hash entry_hash, of a subtree [start, end) with hash
   subtree_hash, the subtree inclusion proof can be _verified_ to verify
   the described entry is contained in the subtree:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 18]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   1.  Let expected_subtree_hash be the result of evaluating the
       inclusion proof as described Section 4.3.2.  If evaluation fails,
       fail the proof verification.
   2.  If subtree_hash is equal to expected_subtree_hash, the entry is
       contained in the subtree.  Otherwise, fail the proof
       verification.
4.4.  Subtree Consistency Proofs
   A subtree [start, end) can be efficiently proven to be consistent
   with the full Merkle Tree.  That is, given MTH(D[start:end]) and
   MTH(D_n), the proof demonstrates that the input D[start:end] to the
   subtree hash was equal to the corresponding elements of the input D_n
   to the Merkle Tree hash.
   Subtree consistency proofs contain sufficient nodes to reconstruct
   both the subtree hash, MTH(D[start:end]), and the original tree hash,
   MTH(D_n), in such a way that every input to the subtree hash was also
   incorporated into the original tree hash.
4.4.1.  Generating a Subtree Consistency Proof
   The subtree consistency proof, SUBTREE_PROOF(start, end, D_n) is
   defined similarly to Section 2.1.4.1 of [RFC9162].
   If start = end, the consistency proof is empty:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(start, start, D_n) = {}
   Otherwise, start < end and SUBTREE_PROOF is defined by a helper
   function:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(start, end, D_n) =
       SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D_n, true)
   The boolean parameter tracks whether the first hash in the proof will
   be omitted by the base case.  The first hash is omitted when it's
   equal to the original subtree hash MTH(D[start:end]), since the
   verifier will already know that hash.  That happens when the original
   subtree's root is a node in the Merkle Tree constructed from D_n, or
   equivalently, when the original subtree is full or has end = n.
   If start = 0 and end = n, the subtree is the root (base case):
   SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, n, D_n, true) = {}
   SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, n, D_n, false) = {MTH(D_n)}
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 19]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   Otherwise, n > 1.  Let k be the largest power of two smaller than n.
   The consistency proof is defined recursively as:
   *  If end <= k, the subtree is on the left of k.  The proof proves
      consistency with the left child and includes the right child:
      SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D_n, b) =
          SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D[0:k], b) : MTH(D[k:n])
   *  If k <= start, the subtree is on the right of k.  The proof proves
      consistency with the right child and includes the left child.
      SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start, end, D_n, b) =
          SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(start - k, end - k, D[k:n], b) : MTH(D[0:k])
   *  Otherwise, start < k < end, which implies start = 0.  The proof
      proves consistency with the right child and includes the left
      child.
      SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, end, D_n, b) =
          SUBTREE_SUBPROOF(0, end - k, D[k:n], false) : MTH(D[0:k])
   When start is zero, this computes a Merkle consistency proof:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(0, end, D_n) = PROOF(end, D_n)
   When end = start + 1, this computes a Merkle inclusion proof:
   SUBTREE_PROOF(start, start + 1, D_n) = PATH(start, D_n)
   Appendix B.4 explains the structure of a subtree consistency proof in
   more detail.

4.4.3.  Verifying a Subtree Consistency Proof
   The following procedure can be used to verify a subtree consistency
   proof.
   Given a Merkle Tree over n elements, a subtree defined by [start,
   end), a consistency proof proof, a subtree hash node_hash, and a root
   hash root_hash:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 22]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   1.  Check that [start, end) is a valid subtree (Section 4.1), and
       that end <= n.  If either does not hold, fail proof verification.
       These checks imply 0 <= start <= end <= n.
   2.  If start equals end, check the following conditions:
       *  proof is an empty array.
       *  node_hash is equal to HASH(), the hash of the empty string.
       If either condition does not hold, stop and fail the proof
       verification.  If both hold, stop and accept the proof.
   3.  Set fn to start, sn to end - 1, and tn to n - 1.
   4.  If sn is tn, then:
       1.  Until fn is sn, right-shift fn, sn, and tn equally.
   5.  Otherwise:
       1.  Until fn is sn or LSB(sn) is not set, right-shift fn, sn, and
           tn equally.
   6.  If fn is sn, set fr and sr to node_hash.
   7.  Otherwise:
       1.  If proof is an empty array, stop and fail verification.
       2.  Remove the first value of the proof array and set fr and sr
           to the removed value.
   8.  For each value c in the proof array:
       1.  If tn is 0, then stop the iteration and fail the proof
           verification.
       2.  If LSB(sn) is set, or if sn is equal to tn, then:
           1.  If fn < sn, set fr to HASH(0x01 || c || fr).
           2.  Set sr to HASH(0x01 || c || sr).
           3.  Until LSB(sn) is set, right-shift fn, sn, and tn equally.
       3.  Otherwise:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 23]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
           1.  Set sr to HASH(0x01 || sr || c).
       4.  Right-shift fn, sn, and tn once more.
   9.  Compare tn to 0, fr to node_hash, and sr to root_hash.  If any
       are not equal, fail the proof verification.  If all are equal,
       accept the proof.
   Appendix B.5 explains this procedure in more detail.
4.5.  Efficiently Covering Arbitrary Intervals
   This document uses subtrees to sign over arbitrary intervals, [start,
   end), of a Merkle Tree.  However, not all intervals are valid
   subtrees.  While a protocol could build a smaller Merkle Tree,
   MTH(D[start:end]), and compute inclusion proofs of any element, this
   smaller Merkle Tree cannot, in general, be efficiently proven
   consistent with the overall Merkle Tree.
   Enlarging the interval to a valid subtree would mitigate this.

   larger than [start, end).  For example, Figure 9 shows the smallest

4.5.1.  Selecting Two Subtrees
   Given any interval, [start, end), this section defines a procedure
   for selecting two subtrees, left and right, such that:
   *  left and right are valid subtrees, so it is possible to compute
      subtree consistency proofs.
   *  The disjoint union of left, followed by right, contains [start,
      end).  That is, left.start <= start <= left.end = right.start <=
      end <= right.end.
   *  While left may contain extra elements before start, right does not
      contain any extra elements.  That is, end = right.end.
   *  Each subtree's size is at most BIT_CEIL(end - start).
   The pair of subtree hashes for left and right can support inclusion
   proofs for any element of [start, end).  The largest such inclusion
   proof is no bigger than the largest inclusion proof in
   MTH(D[start:end]).  Unlike MTH(D[start:end]), these subtree hashes
   can be shown consistent with the overall Merkle Tree using subtree
   consistency proofs.
   The subtrees are selected as follows:
   1.  If end - start is less than or equal to 1, return the subtrees
       [start, end) and [end, end).
   2.  Otherwise:
       1.  Let last be end - 1, the last index in [start, end).
       2.  Let split be the bit index of the most significant bit where
           start and last differ.  Bits are numbered from the least
           significant bit, starting at zero. split is the height at
           which start and last's paths in the tree diverge.
       3.  Let mid be last with the least significant split bits set to
           zero. mid is the leftmost leaf node in the above divergence
           point's right branch.
       4.  Within the least significant split bits of start, let b be
           the bit index of the most significant bit with value zero, if
           any:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 25]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
           1.  If there is such a bit, let left_split be b + 1.
           2.  Otherwise, let left_split be zero.
           left_split is the height of the lowest common ancestor of the
           nodes in [start, mid).
       5.  Let left_start be start with the least significant left_split
           bits set to zero. left_start is the above lowest common
           ancestor's leftmost leaf node.
       6.  Return the subtrees [left_start, mid) and [mid, end).
   Intuitively, this procedure considers the tree MTH(D[0:end]) and
   finds the lowest common ancestor of the elements in [start, end).  It
   splits the interval by that ancestor's left and right children and
   returns the lowest common ancestor of each half.
   The following Python code implements this procedure:
   def find_subtrees(start, end):
       """ Returns a pair of subtrees that efficiently cover
       [start, end). """
       assert start <= end
       if end - start <= 1:
           return (start, end), (end, end)
       last = end - 1
       # Find where start and last's tree paths diverge. The two
       # subtrees will be on either side of the split.
       split = (start ^ last).bit_length() - 1
       mask = (1 << split) - 1
       mid = last & ~mask
       # Maximize the left endpoint. This is just before start's
       # path leaves the right edge of its new subtree.
       left_split = (~start & mask).bit_length()
       left_start = start & ~((1 << left_split) - 1)
       return (left_start, mid), (mid, end)

5.  Certification Authorities
   A CA consists of the following components:
   *  A CA ID (Section 5.1), which uniquely identifies the CA.
   *  A collision-resistant cryptographic hash function, used by the
      CA's issuance logs.  SHA-256 [SHS] is RECOMMENDED.  Throughout
      this document, this hash function is referred to as HASH, and the
      size of its output in bytes is referred to as HASH_SIZE.
   *  A series of issuance logs (Section 5.2), which contain all
      statements the CA has certified.  One issuance log is designated
      as the current log.
   *  A CA cosigner (Section 5.4), which signs subtrees of issuance logs
      to certify their contents.
   *  Optionally, a landmark sequence per log (Section 6.4.1), to
      support optimized landmark-relative certificates.
   Section 5.5 defines an X.509 certificate representation of a CA.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 27]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
5.1.  Certification Authority Identifiers
   Each Merkle Tree Certificate CA has a _CA ID_ to identify it.  This
   CA ID is a trust anchor ID [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].
   Once allocated, the ID's entire object identifier (OID) arc is
   reserved by this protocol.  Given a CA ID whose OID representation is
   caID, this document allocates the following OIDs:
   *  For each positive integer N, the OID {caID logs(0) N} represents
      the issuance log N (Section 5.2).
   *  For each positive integer N and L, the OID {caID landmarks(1) N L}
      represents landmark L (Section 6.4.1) of issuance log N.  These
      OIDs may be used as trust anchor IDs, as described in Section 8.2.
      These OIDs are used when it is necessary to identify an individual
      landmark, e.g. as in the recovery mechanism described in
      Section 5.6 of [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].
   *  For each positive integer N and L, the OID {caID landmarkGroups(2)
      N L} represents a trust anchor group (Section 6 of
      [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids]) containing landmark L of log N
      and earlier landmarks of that log, as defined in Section 8.2.1.
      These OIDs may be used to advertise a series of landmarks at once.
   Future extensions to this protocol MAY define further allocations by
   adding to the registry defined in Section 13.2.3.
   The CA's ID determine's the CA's PKIX distinguished name using the
   construction described in Section 4.1 of
   [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].
5.2.  Issuance Logs
   A CA operates a series of issuance logs, each identified by a
   positive integer _log number_. Log numbers are numbered consecutively
   from 1 to at most 65535 (2^16-1).
   Each issuance log has a _log ID_, which is a trust anchor ID
   constructed by concatenating the following OID components:
   *  The CA ID (Section 5.1)
   *  The constant 0
   *  The log number of the log
   A log ID specifies both the CA and the log number in a single ID.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 28]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   Each issuance log describes an append-only sequence of at most 2^48-1
   _entries_ (Section 5.2.1).  Each entry is identified by an integer
   _index_, assigned consecutively starting from zero.  Each entry is an
   assertion that the CA has certified.  The entries in the issuance log
   are represented as a Merkle Tree, described in Section 2.1 of
   [RFC9162].
   Unlike [RFC6962] and [RFC9162], an issuance log does not have a
   public submission interface.  The log only contains entries which the
   log operator, i.e. the CA, chose to add.  As entries are added, the
   Merkle Tree is updated to be computed over the new sequence.
   A snapshot of the log is known as a _checkpoint_. A checkpoint is
   identified by its _tree size_, that is the number of elements
   committed to the log at the time.  Its contents can be described by
   the Merkle Tree Hash (Section 2.1.1 of [RFC9162]) of entries zero
   through tree_size - 1.
   At any point in time, one of the CA's issuance logs is its _current_
   log.  Initially, this is log 1.  A CA MUST NOT append to any log that
   is not the current log.  Logs before the current log may have
   historical entries.  Logs after the current log MUST be empty.  A CA
   MAY increment its current log number as part of recovering from
   certain operational failures.  See Section 12.2.1 for further
   discussion.
5.2.1.  Log Entries
   Each entry in the log is an MTCLogEntry, defined with the TLS
   presentation syntax below.  An MTCLogEntry describes certificate
   information that the CA has validated and certified.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 29]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   struct {} Empty;
   enum { (2^16-1) } MTCLogEntryExtensionType;
   struct {
       MTCLogEntryExtensionType extension_type;
       opaque extension_data<0..2^16-1>;
   } MTCLogEntryExtension;
   enum {
       null_entry(0), tbs_cert_entry(1), (2^16-1)
   } MTCLogEntryType;

       MTCLogEntryExtension extensions<0..2^16-1>;

5.2.2.  Publishing Logs
   This protocol aims to enable monitors to detect misissued
   certificates by observing the issuance log.  See Section 12.2.
   This document does not prescribe a particular method of observing the
   issuance log.  The access protocols do not affect certificate
   interoperability, and different applications could have different
   needs.  For example, a PKI that authenticates public services might
   publicly serve issuance logs, while a PKI that authenticates a single
   organization's intranet services might keep the log private to the
   organization.  Relying parties SHOULD define log serving
   requirements, including the allowed protocols and expected
   availability, as part of their policies on which CAs to support.  See
   also Section 10.3.
   If a serving protocol supports serving only a portion of the log,
   relying party policies SHOULD include requirements on which portions
   to serve.
   For example, [MTC-TLOG] defines a profile for Merkle Tree
   Certificates that uses [TLOG-TILES].

5.3.  Cosigners
   This section defines a log _cosigner_. A cosigner follows some
   append-only view of the log and signs subtrees (Section 4) consistent
   with that view.  The signatures generated by a cosigner are known as
   _cosignatures_. All subtrees signed by a cosigner MUST be consistent
   with each other.  The cosigner may be external to the log, in which
   case it might ensure consistency by checking consistency proofs.  The
   cosigner may be operated together with the log, in which case it can
   trust its log state.
   A cosignature MAY implicitly make additional statements about a
   subtree, determined by the cosigner's role.  This document defines
   one concrete cosigner role, a CA cosigner (Section 5.4), to
   authenticate the log and certify entries.  Other documents and
   specific deployments MAY define other cosigner roles, to perform
   different functions in a PKI.  For example, [TLOG-WITNESS] defines a
   cosigner that only checks the log is append-only, and [TLOG-MIRROR]
   defines a cosigner that mirrors a log.
   Each cosigner has a public key and a _cosigner ID_, which uniquely
   identifies the cosigner.  The cosigner ID is a trust anchor ID
   [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids].  By identifying the cosigner, the
   cosigner ID specifies the public key, signature algorithm, and any
   additional statements made by the cosigner's signatures.  If a single
   operator performs multiple cosigner roles in an ecosystem, each role
   MUST use a distinct cosigner ID and SHOULD use a distinct key.
   Following the principle of key separation [KeyReuse], cosigner keys
   SHOULD NOT be used for purposes outside this document.  Additional
   uses MAY be defined but MUST NOT overlap with the signature format
   defined in Section 5.3.1.  See Section 12.8 for additional
   discussion.
   A single cosigner, with a single cosigner ID and public key, MAY
   generate cosignatures for multiple logs.  In this case, signed
   subtrees only need to be consistent with others for the same log.
5.3.1.  Signature Format
   A cosigner computes a _subtree signature_ for a subtree in a log by
   signing a CosignedSubtree, defined below using the TLS presentation
   language (Section 3 of [RFC9846]):

       uint8 label[12] = "subtree/v1\n\0";
       opaque cosigner_name<1..2^8-1>;

   signature construction in [TLOG-COSIGNATURE], but it supports
   signature algorithms other than ML-DSA-44 and tree hashes other than

   string subtree/v1, followed by a newline (U+000A), followed by a zero
   byte (U+0000).

   the issuance log's ID (Section 5.1), respectively.  They contain the
   concatenation of:
   *  The 16-byte ASCII string oid/1.3.6.1.4.1.
   *  The trust anchor ID's ASCII representation (Section 4 of
      [I-D.ietf-tls-trust-anchor-ids])

   *  The four-byte ASCII string oid/
   *  The trust anchor ID as a full OID, in dotted decimal notation
   For example, the trust anchor ID 32473.1 would be encoded as the
   ASCII string oid/1.3.6.1.4.1.32473.1.
   OID components in a trust anchor ID can be arbitrarily large.

   signature generation or verification if an OID component is out of

   subtree_hash MUST be the subtree's hash value in the cosigner's view
   of the log.  See Section 4.1.
   If timestamp is non-zero, it MUST be the time that the signature was
   produced.  This time is represented as seconds since the Epoch, as
   defined in Section 4.19 of Volume 1 of [POSIX].  Additionally, if
   timestamp is non-zero, the following MUST be true:
   *  start MUST be zero.
   *  end MUST be the size of the largest consistent tree that the
      cosigner has observed for the log.
   timestamp MAY be zero, in which case no additional constraints are
   placed on start or end (beyond being a valid subtree), and no
   statement is made about the signing time or largest observed tree.
5.3.2.  Signature Semantics
   Before signing a subtree of some log, the cosigner MUST ensure that
   subtree_hash is consistent with its view of the log.  Different
   cosigner roles will obtain this assurance differently.  For example:
   *  A cosigner MAY maintain a full copy of the log, e.g. if it's the
      log operator.  The cosigner can then compute subtree_hash from
      this copy.
   *  A cosigner MAY maintain the hash of the largest consistent tree
      observed by the log.  The cosigner can then check subtree_hash
      with a subtree consistency proof (Section 4.4).
   *  A cosigner MAY maintain any other representation of the log which
      allows it to verify the consistency of the log.
   In all cases, the cosigner MUST ensure that, as it updates its view
   of the log, the old and new views are consistent.
   When a cosigner signs a subtree, it is held separately responsible
   _both_ for the subtree being consistent with its other signatures,
   _and_ for the cosigner-specific additional statements.  That is, if a
   cosigner signs an inconsistent subtree, it is held responsible for
   its additional statements on all entries in the inconsistent subtree,
   even if some other signed subtree exists that asserts different
   entries.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 35]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
