12.5.  Extensibility
   MTCLogEntry (Section 5.2.1) contains several extension points:
   *  New X.509 extensions can be added to TBSCertificateLogEntry.
   *  New MTCLogEntryType values define new formats for the entry
      contents.
   *  New MTCLogEntryExtensionType values define new entry extension
      fields.
   X.509 extensions apply to Merkle Tree Certificates without any
   modifications.  The two entry-level extension points are new to this
   protocol.  Older CAs, cosigners, relying parties, and monitors may
   encounter unrecognized entries:
   Different cosigner roles interact with extensions differently.  Some
   roles, e.g. [TLOG-MIRROR] and [TLOG-WITNESS], do not interpret entry
   contents.  Unrecognized extensions do not impact these roles.  Other
   roles, such as CA cosigners, have semantics that depend on the entry
   contents.  If a cosigner role interprets log entry contents, it MUST
   define how it interacts with unrecognized types and extensions.
   Section 5.4 forbids a CA from logging or signing entries that it does
   not recognize.  A CA cannot faithfully claim to certify information
   if it does not understand it.  This is analogous to how a correctly-
   operated X.509 CA can never sign an unrecognized X.509 extension.
   Unrecognized entry types do not impact older relying parties.  In
   Section 7.2, the relying party constructs the MTCLogEntry that it
   expects.  The unrecognized entry will have a different type value, so
   the proof will never succeed, assuming the underlying hash function
   remains collision-resistant.
   However, unrecognized entry extensions will be ignored by relying
   parties, analogously to a non-critical X.509 extension.  Entry
   extensions thus SHOULD be defined so that this is safe.
   If a monitor observes an entry with unknown type or entry extension,
   it may not be able to determine if it is of interest.  For example,
   it may be unable to tell whether it covers some relevant DNS name.
   Until the monitor is updated to reflect the current state of the PKI,
   the monitor may be unable to detect all misissued certificates.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 71]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   This situation is analogous to the addition of a new X.509 extension.
   When relying parties add support for log entry types or new X.509
   extensions, they SHOULD coordinate with monitors to ensure the
   transparency ecosystem is able to monitor the new formats.
12.6.  Certificate Malleability
   An ASN.1 structure like X.509's Certificate is an abstract data type
   that is independent of its serialization.  There are multiple
   encoding rules for ASN.1.  Commonly, protocols use DER [X.690], such
   as Section 4.5.1 of [RFC9846].  This aligns with Section 4.1.1.3 of
   [RFC5280], which says X.509 signatures are computed over the DER-
   encoded TBSCertificate.  After signature verification, applications
   can assume the DER-encoded TBSCertificate is not malleable.
   When the signature verification process in Section 7.2 first
   transforms the TBSCertificate into a TBSCertificateLogEntry, it
   preserves this non-malleability.  There is a unique valid DER
   encoding for every abstract TBSCertificate structure, so malleability
   of the DER-encoded TBSCertificate reduces to malleability of the
   TBSCertificate value:
   *  The version, issuer, validity, subject, issuerUniqueID,
      subjectUniqueID, and extensions fields are copied from the
      TBSCertificate to the TBSCertificateLogEntry unmodified, so they
      are directly authenticated by the inclusion proof.
   *  serialNumber is omitted from TBSCertificateLogEntry, but its value
      determines the inclusion proof index, which authenticates it.
   *  The redundant signature field in TBSCertificate is omitted from
      TBSCertificateLogEntry, but Section 7.2 checks for an exact value,
      so no other values are possible.
   *  subjectPublicKeyInfo is hashed as subjectPublicKeyInfoHash in
      TBSCertificateLogEntry.  Provided the underlying hash function is
      collision-resistant, no other values are possible for a given log
      entry.
   X.509 implementations often implement Section 4.1.1.3 of [RFC5280] by
   equivalently retaining the original received DER encoding, rather
   than recomputing the canonical DER encoding TBSCertificate.  This
   optimization is compatible with the assumptions above.
   Some non-conforming X.509 implementations use a BER [X.690] parser
   instead of DER, and then apply this optimization to the received BER
   encoding.  BER encoding is not unique, so this does not produce the
   same result.  In such implementations, the BER-encoded TBSCertificate
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 72]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   becomes also non-malleable, and applications may rely on this.  To
   preserve this property in Merkle Tree Certificates, such non-
   conforming implementations MUST do the following when implementing
   Section 7.2:
   *  Reparse the initial identifier (the SEQUENCE tag) and length
      octets of the TBSCertificate structure with a conforming DER
      parser and fail verification if invalid.
   *  When copying the version, issuer, validity, subject,
      issuerUniqueID, subjectUniqueID, and extensions fields, either
      copy over the observed BER encodings, or reparse each field with a
      conforming DER parser and fail verification if invalid.
   *  Reparse the serialNumber field with a conforming DER parser and
      fail verification if invalid.
   *  Reparse the signature field with a conforming DER parser and fail
      verification if invalid.  Equivalently, check for an exact
      equality with the expected, DER-encoded value.
   *  When hashing subjectPublicKeyInfo, either hash the observed BER
      encoding, or reparse the structure with a conforming DER parser
      and fail verification if invalid.
   These additional checks are redundant in X.509 implementations that
   use a conforming DER parser.
   Section 5.2.1 requires that the TBSCertificateLogEntry in an
   MTCLogEntry be DER-encoded, so applying a stricter parser will be
   compatible with conforming CAs.  While these existing non-conforming
   implementations may be unable to switch to a DER parser due to
   compatibility concerns, Merkle Tree Certificates are new, so there is
   no existing deployment of malformed BER-encoded
   TBSCertificateLogEntry structures.
   The above only ensures the TBSCertificate portion is non-malleable.
   In Merkle Tree Certificates, similar to an ECDSA X.509 signature, the
   signature value is malleable.  Multiple MTCProof structures may prove
   a single TBSCertificate structure.  Additionally, in all X.509-based
   protocols, a BER-based parser for the outer, unsigned Certificate
   structure will admit malleability in those portions of the encoding.
   Applications that derive a unique identifier from the Certificate
   MUST instead use the TBSCertificate, or some portion of it, for
   Merkle Tree Certificates.

12.7.  Revocation
   This document does not define a new certificate-level revocation
   mechanism.  Existing mechanisms like CRLs and OCSP apply unchanged to
   Merkle Tree certificates.  The sequential serial numbers assigned by
   issuance logs may enable future improvements to revocation, but such
   work is out of scope for this document.
12.8.  Signature Domain Separation
   The signature format defined in Section 5.3.1 includes a fixed label
   prefix to ensure domain separation.  Provided other uses of the same
   key use a non-overlapping prefix, signatures in one context cannot be
   substituted for those in another.
   Section 5.4 permits a CA cosigner key to be used to sign CRLs and
   OCSP responses.  These signatures do not include a domain separation
   prefix.  Instead, X.509 relies on an undocumented assumption that the
   TBSCertificate, TBSCertList, and OCSP ResponseData structures do not
   overlap at the level of individual ASN.1 fields.
   These ASN.1 structures all begin with a SEQUENCE tag, which is
   encoded in DER as 0x30 or the ASCII digit "0".  The domain separation
   label used in Section 5.3.1, subtree/v1\n\0, does not begin with "0",
   so their inputs do not overlap.  More generally, this label is not a
   prefix of any DER or BER encoding.
   Domain separation analysis based on the structures themselves is
   fragile, particularly when individual ASN.1 fields must be analyzed.
   This document depends on a structure-level analysis for CRLs and OCSP
   responses due to how these legacy protocols were defined.  Future
   uses of the key SHOULD use a more robust mechanism, namely a fixed
   label prefix or a context string parameter if the signature scheme
   supports it.
12.9.  Subordinate Certification Authorities
   Merkle Tree Certificates' transparency properties only apply to
   certificates directly issued by the CA, not certification paths.  The
   CA might issue a certificate that describes an unconstrained,
   subordinate, non-MTC CA.  Certificates issued by the subordinate CA
   would not be visible in the MTC CA's issuance log and thus may not be
   visible to monitors.  However, the subordinate CA certificate that
   enables this bypass will still be visible in the issuance logs.
   Although the scope is larger, this scenario is similar to an
   unauthorized end-entity certificate and can be handled analogously:
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 74]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   Relying parties with transparency requirements SHOULD define policy
   requirements on trusted CAs that prevent these bypasses, with any
   violation treated as an unauthorized certificate.  For example, a
   relying party might require that all subordinate CAs have name
   constraints (Section 4.2.1.10 of [RFC5280]) or forbid subordinate CAs
   entirely.  In addition to holding CAs responsible for meeting these
   policies, relying parties SHOULD programmatically enforce these
   policies as part of certification path validation.
   Monitors SHOULD monitor for adherence to applicable policies as part
   of monitoring for unauthorized certificates.  For example, a monitor
   that looks for entries covering example.com SHOULD look for either a
   subject alternative name (Section 4.2.1.6 of [RFC5280]) of
   example.com or a basic constraints (Section 4.2.1.9 of [RFC5280])
   extension with the cA boolean set to true.
   It is not sufficient to constrain the MTC CA with a path length
   constraint (Section 4.2.1.9 of [RFC5280]) of zero.  Self-issued
   certificates do not contribute to path length constraints, so such an
   MTC CA might still issue CA certificates with the same name as
   itself.

Appendix B.  Merkle Tree Structure
   This non-normative section describes how the Merkle Tree structure
   relates to the binary representations of indices.  It is included to
   help implementers understand the procedures described in Section 4.

Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
B.1.  Binary Representations
   Within a Merkle Tree whose size is a power of two, the binary
   representation of a leaf's index gives the path to that leaf.  The
   leaf is a left child if the least-significant bit is unset and a
   right child if it is set.  The next bit indicates the direction of
   the parent node, and so on.  Figure 11 demonstrates this in a Merkle
   Tree of size 8:
          +----------------+
          |     [0, 8)     |        level 3
          +----------------+
           /              \
      +--------+      +--------+
      | [0, 4) |      | [4, 8) |    level 2
      +--------+      +--------+
       /      \        /      \
   +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+
   |[0,2)| |[2,4)| |[4,6)| |[6,8)|  level 1
   +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ +-----+
     / \     / \     / \     / \
   +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+
   |0| |1| |2| |3| |4| |5| |6| |7|  level 0
   +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+ +-+
                Figure 11: An example Merkle Tree of size 8
   The binary representation of 4 is 0b100.  It is the left (0) child of
   [4, 6), which is the left (0) child of [4, 8), which is the right (1)
   child of [0, 8).
   Each level in the tree corresponds to a bit position and can be
   correspondingly numbered, with 0 indicating the least-significant bit
   and the leaf level, and so on.  In this numbering, a node's level can
   be determined as follows: if the node is a root of subtree [start,
   end), the node's level is BIT_WIDTH(end - start - 1).
   Comparing two indices determines the relationship between two paths.
   The highest differing bit gives the level at which paths from root to
   leaf diverge.  For example, the bit representations of 4 and 6 are
   0b100 and 0b110, respectively.  The highest differing bit is bit 1.
   Bits 2 and up are the same between the two indices.  This indicates
   that the paths from the root to leaves 4 and 6 diverge when going
   from level 2 to level 1.
   This can be generalized to arbitrary-sized Merkle Trees.  Figure 12

   The numerical constraints on start and end in Section 4.1 restrict
   subtrees to ensure that they are properly aligned with the original
   tree as to permit subtree consistency proofs.  A Merkle Tree built
   over [start, end) has size end - start, and is constructed as if
   start were the first element of the sequence at index zero.  To be
   aligned, start must be the leftmost leaf of the lowest common
   ancestor of start and end - 1 in the original tree:
   *  Numerically, this means the least significant BIT_WIDTH(end -
      start - 1) bits of start must be zero.  Equivalently, start must
      be divisible by BIT_CEIL(end - start).
   *  In the tree, this means subtrees are constructed by taking any
      node in the tree, setting start to the leftmost leaf under the
      node, and end to one past any other leaf under the node.

   necessarily in the larger Merkle Tree, as shown in Figure 5.  In
   general:
   *  Subtrees whose sizes are a power of two are called _full
      subtrees_. A full subtree's root node will always be in the
      original tree.
   *  Subtrees whose sizes are not a power of two are called _partial
      subtrees_. A partial subtree's root node will be in the original
      tree of size n, if and only if n = end.  Otherwise, non-leaf nodes
      along the partial subtree's right edge will not be part of the
      original tree.
   The difference between full and partial subtrees does not impact
   their usage, but they can help in understanding the proof
   constructions below.
B.3.  Inclusion Proof Evaluation
   The procedure in Section 4.3.2 builds up a subtree hash in r by
   starting from entry_hash and iteratively hashing elements of
   inclusion_proof on the left or right.  That means this procedure,
   when successful, must return _some_ hash that contains entry_hash.
   Treating [start, end) as a Merkle Tree of size end - start, the
   procedure hashes based on the path to index.  Within this smaller
   Merkle Tree, it has index fn = index - start (first number), and the
   last element has index sn = end - start - 1 (second number).
   Step 4 iterates through inclusion_proof and the paths to fn and sn in
   parallel.  As the procedure right-shifts fn and sn and looks at the
   least-significant bit, it moves up the two paths, toward the root.
   When sn is zero, the procedure has reached the top of the tree.  The
   procedure checks that the two iterations complete together.
   Iterating from level 0 up, fn and sn will initially be different.
   While they are different, step 4.2 hashes on the left or right based
   on the binary representation, as discussed in Appendix B.1.
   Once fn = sn, the remainder of the path is on the right edge.  At
   that point, the condition in step 4.2 is always true.  It only
   incorporates proof entries on the left, once per set bit.  Unset bits
   are skipped.
   Inclusion proofs can also be evaluated by considering these two
   stages separately.  The first stage consumes l1 = BIT_WIDTH(fn XOR
   sn) proof entries.  The second stage consumes l2 = POPCOUNT(fn >> l1)
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 89]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   proof entries.  A valid inclusion proof must then have l1 + l2
   entries.  The first l1 entries are hashed based on fn's least
   significant bits, and the remaining l2 entries are hashed on the
   left.
B.4.  Consistency Proof Structure
   A subtree consistency proof for [start, end) and the tree of n
   elements is similar to an inclusion proof for element end - 1.  If
   one starts from end - 1's hash, incorporating the whole inclusion
   proof should reconstruct root_hash and incorporating a subset of the
   inclusion proof should reconstruct node_hash.  Thus end - 1's hash
   and this inclusion proof can prove consistency.  A subtree
   consistency proof in this document applies two optimizations over
   this construction:
   1.  Instead of starting at level 0 with end - 1, the proof can start
       at a higher level.  Any ancestor of end - 1 shared by both the
       subtree and the overall tree is a valid starting node to
       reconstruct node_hash and root_hash.  Use the highest level with
       a common ancestor.  This truncates the inclusion proof.
   2.  If this starting node is the entire subtree, omit its hash from
       the consistency proof.  The verifier is assumed to already know
       node_hash.
   A Merkle consistency proof, defined in Section 2.1.4 of [RFC9162],
   applies these same optimizations.

B.5.  Consistency Proof Verification
   The procedure in Section 4.4.3 is structured similarly to inclusion
   proof evaluation (Appendix B.3).  It iteratively builds two hashes,
   fr (first root) and sr (second root), which are expected to equal
   node_hash and root_hash, respectively.  Everything hashed into fr is
   also hashed into sr, so success demonstrates that root_hash contains
   node_hash.
Benjamin, et al.           Expires 6 May 2027                  [Page 92]
Internet-Draft          Merkle Tree Certificates           November 2026
   Step 2 initializes fn (first number), sn (second number), and tn
   (third number) to follow, respectively, the paths to start, end - 1
   (the last element of the subtree), and n - 1 (the last element of the
   tree).
   Steps 3 and 4 then skip to the starting node, described in
   Appendix B.4.  The starting node may be:
   *  The entire subtree [start, end) if the subtree root is in the
      tree.  This will occur if end is n (step 3), or if [start, end) is
      a full subtree (exiting step 4 because fn is sn).
   *  Otherwise, the highest full subtree along the right edge of
      [start, end).  This corresponds to the process exiting step 4
      because LSB(sn) is not set.
   Steps 5 and 6 initialize the hashes fr and sr:
   *  In the first case above, fn will equal sn after truncation.  Step
      5 will then initialize the hashes to node_hash because the
      consistency proof does not need to include the starting node.
   *  In the second case above, fn is less than sn.  Step 6 will then
      initialize the hashes to the first value in the consistency proof.
   Step 7 incorporates the remainder of the consistency proof into fr
   and sr:
   *  All hashes are incorporated into sr, with hashing on the left or
      right determined the same as in inclusion proof evaluation.
   *  A subset of the hashes is incorporated into fr.  It skips any hash
      on the right because those contain elements greater than end - 1.
      It also stops incorporating when fn and sn have converged.
   This reconstructs the hashes of the subtree and original tree, which
   are then compared to expected values in step 8.
   In the case when fn is sn in step 5, the condition in step 7.2.1 is
   always false, and fr is always equal to node_hash in step 8.  In this
   case, steps 6 through 8 are equivalent to verifying an inclusion
   proof for the truncated subtree [fn, sn + 1) and truncated tree tn +
   1.

   The following are "accumulated" [Accumulated] test vectors for the
   various subtree algorithms defined in Section 4.
   They are hash values of the outputs of all possible inputs for each
   algorithm, for trees of sizes up to 130.  They can be used to verify

   include a large number of individual test vectors.
   For all the test vectors, a tree D_n of size n is constructed with
   leaf values d[0] = 0x00, d[1] = 0x01, .... The hash function used is

C.1.1.  Subtree Hashes
   For each value of end from 0 to 130, and each value of start from 0
   to end, if [start, end) is a valid subtree, add to the rolling hash
   the ASCII string [START, END) HASH followed by a newline (U+000A),
   where START and END are the decimal representations of start and end,
   respectively, and HASH is the hexadecimal encoding of
   MTH(D[start:end]), according to Section 4.

   b82806ad4265bb151c1119c0f4db437bb4d1a1f887b3a7fba1cd4ebf552e3e81

   import hashlib

articles.title: Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
articles.body:
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which total roughly $900 billion over the coming years.
All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.
You’ll hear us talk about the company’s unique corporate governance structure, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have let Anthropic go public first, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to Decoder on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Hayden Field, The Verge’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, welcome back to Decoder.
Thanks. Great to be here.
I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.
I know.
It’s like a normal thing that happened.
It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.
[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.
Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.
Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”
What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?
I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.
But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.
I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.
So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.
I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?
Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.
Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.
Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.
I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.
Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?
They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw one estimate from Steve Rattner saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.
But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.
I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.
But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.
I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.
I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.
That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.
That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?
I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for passing on costs to consumers. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.
This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.
The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.
They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to moat them in and hope for the best.
What’s interesting there is that consumers are sensitive to price in one way. I think Anthropic’s big business customers, which is where they’ve been historically focused, are sensitive to price in different ways.
If you’re paying Anthropic a lot of money, you might want to be able to switch providers quickly and you might demand data sovereignty and all this stuff that big enterprises are thinking about. Anthropic either has to deliver that, which would kill their moat for their big enterprise customers, or say, “We’re so good, you can’t have that.” I’m not sure that they can say the second one yet.
That’s why they’re marketing this safe, trustworthy AI line so deeply, because it’s the only thing they’ve really got going for them here. When you have an enterprise customer, most of the time you do have to give them data sovereignty. You can’t trade on their data. There’s a lot of stuff that Anthropic could be doing to make more money that they can’t do when someone is paying that much.
I think that’s really why they’re driving home this point of being the safe, trustworthy alternative because that’s the only thing that’s really going to get people to stick around, particularly if they also drive home the cybersecurity tools in an age when everything’s getting hacked all the time.
The other interesting thing is even not with huge enterprises, but with small to medium-sized businesses, I’ve been chatting with a bunch of them and they’ve all been creating their own internal tools to kind of track which tasks they need specifically to use an expensive Anthropic model for and which ones they can port over to maybe an open-source model or a really cheap model.
So a lot of companies like law firms — and people in a lot of different industries that have small to medium-sized businesses — are literally creating their own internal benchmarks about, “Okay, let’s save money as much as we can to just only put 10 percent of our tasks toward the expensive Anthropic model, and then this 40 percent can go to an open-source model and this 50 percent can go to a mid-tier, cheaper model.”
So that’s what’s really interesting to me. People are trying to figure this out on their own and not even sharing those benchmarks publicly because it’s their own way of budgeting.
I actually heard Nadella this week say every company will have its own set of evaluations and they will test the models against them and always use the most efficient one and this will become one of the major things that every company does.
The flip side to that is I’ve heard Anthropic executives say, “Well, you will always want the frontier model because your competitor will always be using the frontier model and if you use a cheaper one, you’ll be left behind.” And that has always seemed somewhere between naive and idealistic to me because I think a lot of companies do cheap things knowing that their competitors will also do cheap things.
I agree completely. Everyone’s being cheap.
Yeah, I think if you can get away with good enough, you’re going to find out exactly where good enough is and you will not assume that your competitor is going to eke out a 5 percent advantage by using a more expensive model. Somewhere on the margin is where all of the costs should be and the market will figure it out.
Exactly.
It just feels like the basics of the business, maybe on IPO day, the pressure isn’t on that, everyone’s just very happy and rich. The next quarter’s earnings are going to be where we start to see this shakeout. Can it keep growing the way it’s growing at the margins it needs to build everything, especially when its own suppliers are now major shareholders?
Totally. And we saw one quarter where they experienced huge growth and then the next quarter wasn’t that much. So yeah, I mean they’re going to have a lot to reckon with.
Let’s talk about the governance issues. Because of Nvidia, corporate governance is the hottest topic in American business. Like you said, OpenAI and Anthropic have some of the most complicated governance structures in history.
If you think that Anthropic’s future is to sell the best intelligence — the most capable, the most cutting-edge frontier, close-to-AGI intelligence possible — you would probably not do a bunch of safety work. You would probably not kill your margins on a bunch of researchers who are telling you to stop or slow down or not release the best model.
Anthropic is deeply committed to doing that. You and I have had conversations before about whether that can withstand the pressures of capitalism and growth. That was hard when they weren’t a public company, but now they are. Talk about Anthropic’s structure and how they’re trying to codify their commitment to safety.
Yeah, that’s a really great question. I just published a piece about this. It’s so interesting to me that Anthropic, despite seeing all the roller-coaster drama that OpenAI went through around the Sam Altman ouster and all of the restructurings that that company has gone through, Anthropic has a similarly unusual structure. And in a way it’s helpful because they’re not beholden, as we said, to shareholder pressure besides if shareholders start selling off their stock or don’t buy more.
But the two kinds of groups of people that have power over what happens at Anthropic are the founders and this group called the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT). Anthropic likes to market this as being like, “Oh, don’t worry about that the founders are doing what’s best for humanity but with no checks. We’ve got this trust above us that can appoint or remove us anytime.” As we’ll see in the movie Artificial, Sam Altman famously says, “Oh, well, the board can fire me whenever.” He says that a million times.
Now, Anthropic is implying the same thing: “Oh, we have this trust above us. They can remove or appoint the majority of board members,” even though it’s actually not all of them, but we’ll get to that in a minute. So this trust is a group of right now four people and none of them have a lot of AI experience. It’s [former Federal Reserve Chairman] Ben Bernanke, a foreign policy analyst named Richard Fontaine, an experimental physicist named Christopher Stubbs, and a former GiveWell executive named Neil Buddy Shah, who is chair of the LTBT.
I spoke to a couple of former Anthropic employees that left not too long ago and one of them said that this trust is kind of handpicked to not rock the boat at Anthropic. The founders appointed them. They’re not going to be appointing someone that’s going to probably disagree with them a lot.
Ironically, the trust doesn’t have the authority to step in on everyday decisions at Anthropic, unlike even the OpenAI nonprofit board that existed. They could say, “Oh look, don’t release this model. It’s too dangerous.” The trust doesn’t have any of those powers. All it can do is appoint or remove certain board members. Even then, they have to give 30 days’ notice to a small committee of the board, which includes Daniela Amodei, the chair of that little committee who is also a founder of Anthropic.
To oversimplify things, out of these seven board seats, the trust gets to pick three, the founders get to pick three, and then the kind of tie-breaking seat, the seventh one, the trust technically appoints, but they have to basically get founder approval to do it. So it’s one of these things that’s so complex, but when you really look at the nitty-gritty of it, the founders have pretty unchecked control here. I think that’s something that’s getting lost in the narrative of, “Oh, this trust is above us. Don’t worry.” Okay, well, they don’t really have much power to check you.
The founder control structure is the wildest thing I have ever read about in years of doing the show and thinking about business. Anthropic has seven founders. They have been issued a single share of stock that holds 50.1 percent of the voting power of the company. That is issued to a company called Founder LLC, and they’re the seven co-owners of Founder LLC.
How on earth does that work? Do they just all get together and then decide how to vote the one share of stock?
Yeah, it’s really interesting and that’s why I was kind of oversimplifying it a minute ago with who gets to choose this tie-breaking seat because it’s technically Founder LLC. It’s just a total mess. But when you really look at the simplified version, it’s that yes, through all of these weird structures and things they’ve done, they basically have pretty unchecked power and that’s the way they want it.
When I was talking to a former employee who recently left, they said it’s not necessarily that the founders have a financial interest in making the most money. In their eyes, it’s more that they have an interest in unchecked control. I think that’s a really important point here.
Some dissenters within the ranks of Anthropic think it’s not about them wanting to get rich, but rather it’s about them wanting that total control, which does track with a lot of their public statements. They say, “You can’t do safety from second place.” They’re all in on speeding up this race, but the problem is when you speed up the AI race, you’re speeding it up for everyone involved.
The safety piece is the really interesting portion of this to me because it’s the thing you would spend money on, absent some huge litigation drama or liability concern, that no other company would spend money on.
So let’s say it’s proven in court that model companies are liable for what people’s agents do. I think then all the model companies would build safety systems. They would have some big incentive to make sure their models are safe. That has not yet happened. We don’t know. There’s a big debate about safety and where the regulation will come from and what will create the incentives.
In the meantime, you’ve got seven founders holding a single share of stock who right now appear to be aligned on investing in safety in various ways inside of Anthropic. What happens if they start to disagree?
Yeah, that’s a great question. I think that the other interesting question here is what happens when you can explain away anything in the name of safety if you’re thinking it’s “for the greater good,” which as we know is a common villain trope in every movie. But it’s also one of Anthropic’s main things on its website. They’re like, “We want to do this for the greater good, for the global good.”
If you’re saying, “Hey, we have to win this race at all costs because we’re the only good guys and anyone else who wins it is going to do worse than us,” are you really the good guy at that point? And can’t you just explain away any single decision, even dropping some safety measures, as saying, “Oh, it’s slowing us down too much. We’re going to lose. We’ve got to win at all costs”? So you drop this or drop that. And then you look in the mirror at the end of the race and you say, “Oh, actually, we’re the exact same as the other company we’re trying to be different from.” I think that’s increasingly happening.
So I mean, right now they’ve said, “Look, we’re really committed to this.” You do have to remember that these people are almost religiously dedicated to this idea of safe AI. A lot of them think that AI systems are potentially conscious. I mean, this is by Anthropic founders’ own statements.
So I think that it’s not like they’re just secretly only trying to make money and just talking about safety and they don’t mean it. I think it’s more something a little more dangerous in that they want complete control because they believe that they have the right plan for AI safety and they will do it better than anyone else.
But as we know, absolute power corrupts absolutely. So a lot of Anthropic employees that I was talking to, former ones, were saying, “Yeah, it does not make sense that this industry is so unregulated. There’s no external regulation. Even if these seven people think they have the best idea for AI safety, okay, then prove it to someone else — that you shouldn’t be the only ones deciding this. Because you’re not elected.” So that’s the consensus among some.
They have a morally binding handshake agreement to allow external auditors, Hayden. It’s going to be fine.
Oh, yeah, with employee-level access.
Also, it’s called “Super Intelligence” now. It’s going to be totally fine. They all went to the White House and they looked deeply into each other’s eyes and said it was going to be fine.
Obviously Anthropic came up with this structure well before the events with Nvidia and Jensen Huang, but I can’t help but put them together in my head. They are happening at the same time. And Nvidia has a very traditional corporate governance structure.
Jensen owned 3 percent of the company, but he had a board of directors. The board of directors determined that he had violated the company’s code of conduct in some way. He resigned. It’s very obvious that he was thoroughly encouraged to resign, but that’s just normal corporate governance. That’s what you learn about in school. A company has a board of directors. Their number one job is to hire and fire the CEO.
That’s very different in Silicon Valley, right? Founder control of companies is a big story everywhere. Mark Zuckerberg famously has control over Meta, even though Meta shareholders repeatedly vote to remove him, which is one of the underemphasized stories in all of American business. Sergey Brin and Larry Page control Google.
Is this more in the, “We need to insulate our founders from the demands of the market and boards of directors” in classic Silicon Valley style? Or is it, “We need to insulate our founders and Dario from the demands of the market so we can stay focused on AGI and safety”? Because it feels like a combination of both.
It’s definitely a combination. I mean, they say it’s the latter. I think in a lot of ways it’s like the former. It’s totally a combination. I’d say it’s about 50/50. I mean, they want control so that they can focus on what they think is best and not lose control to someone that they don’t think knows best. But ironically, as we know, no one group of people should be in control of what is best here. So at least that’s what a lot of my sources say.
So I think that, yeah, I mean, it’s just a combination. Elon Musk famously won’t run a company that he doesn’t have voting control over. So I think it’s just a new Valley thing and it’s pervading here for a couple of different reasons.
There are seven of them. What seven different people do over the course of the next five to 10 years is as unpredictable as anything. What happens if one of them does something illegal or lies to the board or smuggles chips to China or anything? Is there some way to remove one of these founders from this LLC?
Yeah. I mean, allegedly the trust has the power to remove. They haven’t said whether they have the power to remove all of the board or just some, but in some way when you’re looking at the fine print of the S-1, basically if the trust gives 30 days’ notice to essentially Daniela Amodei and her other two people on this subcommittee, then they can suggest removal of a board member. Again, they can waive that 30-day notice if they deem it correct, if Daniela does.
But yeah, there’s a lot of fine print here. Essentially, yes, you can remove someone and there is stuff about that in the S-1 saying if they’ve done something illegal, if they’ve done something really bad, they can be removed, but it’s definitely not easy. It also depends on who it is, I think.
It’s interesting. I keep coming back to this because it is so complicated, it’s so unusual, and it is right next to the Nvidia situation where he materially misrepresented his relationship to the shareholders by having his PR people issue statements saying it was all normal. He had to admit that it wasn’t all normal and he was in fact involved in extramarital affairs and the board fired him.
I felt a little bad for that PR guy who had to put his name on all those statements that ended up being a lie.
I feel nothing. As the audience may know, as Hayden is well aware, we make all the PR people put their names on everything just in case something like this happens. That’s just a little bit of Verge trivia.
Anyhow, right, I mean, that’s just normal governance. Here you have a company where the only check might be the market itself, right?
Yep.
If they can’t sell tokens for more than what they make them for, they’re going to have to report that in the financials and the market might say this company is failing and pull all the money back. That is a very different kind of pressure.
If the only meaningful way that Dario might lose his job is if the company goes bankrupt and then the swirl of things is he’s got to buy chips before OpenAI can buy the chips, he’s got to increase the number of verticals that Anthropic competes in within the enterprise, and he also idealistically has to train the next model and the next model with RSI to get to AGI, it feels like actually the pressure is to go as fast as possible. If I just added that up, I would say I would not slow down ever.
Yeah. That’s why I say you can kind of explain away anything if you’re trying to be first, which they are. And they’ve been very public about that. Regarding the money thing, Ann Lipton, a law professor at the University of Colorado Law School, told me this week that the trust and the founders together are the ones who actually have governance power and that you either trust that they’re going to balance the interest of society appropriately or you don’t.
But either way, the real constraint on whatever impulses they have is going to be the fact that Anthropic needs money. That’s the thing, Anthropic needs money. In a livestream recently, Dario told the CEO of JPMorgan Chase that compute is the “deepest business dilemma” that the company faces. Essentially if you buy too much, you can financially overextend yourself. If you buy too little, then you can’t support inference for customers.
Even more importantly, you can’t do the R&D. You can’t come up with new models. So they’re extremely compute-constrained, even maybe more so than OpenAI because OpenAI was made fun of for a long time for losing a ton of money, but they were investing a lot in compute. Anthropic did not do that as much, and now they’re having to pay the piper.
So it’s an interesting turnaround here. Hopefully for them and their interests, I guess, if they can get the compute they need. But as we know, the supply is a lot lower than the demand. So it’s just going to be interesting to see what they will do to make money and therefore money to buy compute.
It’s funny. A couple of weeks ago I told our colleague, Liz Lopatto, that the Anthropic IPO would be one of the biggest stories of the year. She was laughing at me today, because she says it’s not even the biggest story of the week because of Jensen Huang and Nvidia.
My argument — take it or leave it, and you can judge whether I’m correct — is that they are the same story. That if Nvidia’s financing architecture fails or wobbles because Jensen isn’t there to bully everyone into believing in it, then maybe you do have a glut of chips sitting in data centers without the appropriate permitting or power to light them up and the market for chips will change dramatically.
Maybe a company like CoreWeave does get way more wobbly or some of the already wobbly neoclouds start to get wobbly and the price of compute falls and lets Anthropic compete differently. Maybe a bunch of chips that were allocated to China on the gray market come flooding back to the United States.
That apparently will happen.
Right? So there’s a lot of ways the Nvidia story affects Anthropic’s financials. Has the company said anything about that yet? Is the market reacting to that in any way?
Not yet. They’ve just talked about how important compute is and that it’s going to be a really big issue for them. And Anthropic’s IPO, it has a lot of ties to Nvidia and there’s a lot of complexities here because Nvidia had agreed to buy $10 billion in Anthropic shares via private placement on top of a $10 billion funding promise it made last year.
So they are in bed together, and that’s going to be interesting to see, too. The new CEO of Nvidia has made a lot of claims about diverting chips that were potentially going to China and bringing them back so they’re not doing that anymore.
Now we’re going to see if there’s more supply or not. Also, Jensen personally made some of these deals, especially with large financial institutions to fund the AI infrastructure buildout last August. So he’s wheeling and dealing a lot. And so it’s going to remain to be seen whether the new chief executive has that kind of power to wheel and deal and pressure people into doing stuff like this or not.
This is my last question. Obviously everyone’s just celebrating today. We are probably throwing the most cold water on this by noting that the structure of Anthropic is very odd. What should people be looking for? What are the signs that you’re looking for now that Anthropic is a stock that’s trading? What’s the relationship in your mind between the value of Anthropic stock on any given day and the broader AI story?
I think that stock is a little bit like benchmarks in the AI industry in that sometimes it doesn’t mean what you think it means and also it never means everything. So you always take it with a grain of salt. It’s all vibes based. It’s all hype. So people get scared, they sell, and people hear one good thing or a rumor and they buy. So I think it’s important to look at it and see what’s driving that fear or hype that day or that week. But it’s also really important to see what the company says in these reports and earnings calls.
That’s what I think is the most interesting. Not really the numbers all the time, but instead, what they try to sneak into these reports by saying, “Oh, we sidelined this team,” or, “We discontinued this safety initiative all in the name of being first.”
That’s the type of thing that I think we’re going to see a lot of and that’s what I want to watch for. Because the company that made its bed on safe AI is increasingly looking the same as OpenAI and is going to have a lot of swept-under-the-rug type of updates like that, if my sources are right.
You heard it here first. Former CNBC reporter Hayden Field says, look past the day-to-day swings into the fundamentals of the company. That’s good. Also, the stock market is only vibes. That’s the other thing I heard you say.
Yep. I mean, it’s controversial, but after being a financial reporter, yeah, I mean, there’s a lot of vibes there. It’s a lot of vibes.
Oh, I agree. I think sometimes the only thing they ask me to go on CNBC to say is this is just vibes, and then they usher me off the air very quickly.
Hayden, this is great. We’re obviously going to be talking about this story many times with you in the year to come. Hopefully we can do another straightforward business story and not just a soap opera one.
I’ll be here for both. We’ve got to do them both.
Amazing. Thank you so much, Hayden.
Thanks.
Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!
Decoder with Nilay Patel
A podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.

articles.title: The game of the year is finally here
articles.body:
Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 153, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, thank you for tearing yourself away from GTA to be here, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.)
The game of the year is finally here
Plus, in this week’s Installer: A better YouTube Kids, new ways to get stuff done, the FTX story on Netflix, and more.
This week, I’ve been reading about nuclear radiation and F1 brains and phone scammers, watching about 10 minutes of Madden before bailing, playing a lot of Madden NFL instead, learning my way around Instagram Edits on the Mac, trying the 12-3-30 workout while watching Mission: Impossible movies in half-hour increments, getting my new Apple HomeView up and running (still don’t know why I bought one…), and dreaming up stuff to do with the Flipper One.
I also have for you the game of the year (decade? century?), a couple of great new productivity tools, a Netflix take on the FTX story, and much more. But mostly, it’s GTA week. Let’s do it.
Also, programming note: Installer is off next week. It’s Thanksgiving, there’s food to eat and football to watch. Hope you have a great couple of weeks, and we’ll be so back in December.
(As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What have you been watching / reading / listening to / playing / adding to your holiday lists this week? Tell me everything: installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.)
The Drop
- Grand Theft Auto VI. I mean, this literally could be the whole newsletter. But it appears this game is everything we’ve been waiting for, and I anticipate spending too much of the rest of my life playing it. No regrets.
- The GTA VI soundtrack. I can’t think of many games whose soundtracks have this kind of power: It’s a 34-song compilation, including a bunch of new music from huge artists. I’m going to listen to this while I work, which I assume will make all my writing cooler and more crime-filled.
- The Teenage Engineering EP/BC-1. I’ve been thinking about rebooting my physical media collection, and I can’t think of a better way to start than with this beautiful CD player. Like all Teenage Engineering gear, it is somehow retro and futuristic at the same time, and it’ll slide neatly into a synth setup or just look extremely rad in your living room.
- Alfred 6. A long-awaited update to the launcher and workflow tool so many Mac users love. I see some nice interface changes here but otherwise not a massively different product… but that’s actually probably the right call. Alfred is very good at being Alfred.
- The TRMNL Frame. A 31.5-inch, programmable color E Ink screen that you can hang on your wall. This either immediately excites you, and $1,299 is a small price to pay, or does nothing for you and is way too expensive. I accept both reactions equally. I also want one so badly.
- Tasks in Gemini. A stupid, stupid, stupid name for an otherwise useful product! Gemini now has a lot of the same “do stuff for you” tools that Muse and Dots offer — this time with much better access to your Google data. I’m slowly working through my inbox with this one.
- Who Wants This? Fun new podcast in which two writers and comedians attempt to make sense of current trends, and whether anyone actually… wants this. The first episode is about protein and proteinmaxxing, and I both enjoyed the hang and learned a lot. It also made me feel like everyone has just completely lost their minds.
- The Altruists. We are due for many, many fictionalized versions of the FTX story. I’ve heard and read some mixed things about this new Netflix series, but I dig the idea of trying to play it as both a love story and a scam story. It really is both those things!
- ClockwiseTV. Respect to Hank Green for being one of the few people bold enough to try and compete with YouTube. The pitch here is smart and simple: curated content for kids, on a timer, no ads, no autoplay. This is immediately going on all my iPads.
- “CIA Meeting Cold Open.” Last week’s SNL was really good overall (though maybe I just love John Mulaney?) but the cold open, with the tech billionaires learning how not to fall for a honeypot, absolutely slayed me. The spray bottle on Elon Musk makes me laugh every single time.
You may not know Tom Hovey, but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show. His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.
I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he said, “but never ever AI.”
I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:
The phone: iPhone 17 Pro.
The wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.
The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.
Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.
Six apps for my kids’ primary school is too many apps.
I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!
iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a new country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.
I also asked Tom to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back:
- I listen to a lot of audiobooks while I’m at my desk drawing and also while running, and audiobooks are the only way I can “read” non-fiction as I just fall asleep immediately if I try and actually read them. Some recent audiobooks I’ve enjoyed: The Castle by Jon Ronson; Thirst: Twelve Drinks That Changed My Life by John Robins; Hidden Valley Road by Robert Kolker; London Falling by Patrick Radden Keefe.
- TV shows I’ve recently watched: The Pitt, Widow’s Bay, This Is a Gardening Show, East of Eden, Star City, Pluribus.
- As an illustrator I’m always looking for excellent people making cool things and in a world where AI art is taking over I am seeking more and more analog art so here are some of the coolest creatives I’m currently enjoying: Natalie Andrewson, Sean Morris, Carla Adams, Ellis Parrinder, Azpeger Tat, and Kawafi.
- I have a WhatsApp chat with a bunch of my old illustrator pals which is a bunch of old men gossiping and sending each other Paul McCartney memes.
- Really enjoying the internet’s response to Damian Lewis’s foray into music.
Crowdsourced
Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky.
“Forget GTA VI, the game of the year is Queen’s Domain. It is only $20 instead of $80, made by two people instead of an army. It is all I have been playing this week.” — Mike
“In Meg Elison’s new novel, Foundling Fathers, some creepy tech billionaires clone Washington Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams and try to raise them in an ‘originalist’ setting. The satire is hilarious and all too plausible.” — aAron
“I’m not playing with it yet myself, but the FM-1 from M-Vave seems to be capturing the first wave of post-vibe-coding synthesized nerds, who are all replacing the stock firmware with homebrew. So a cheap Chinese generic keyboard is suddenly really hot hardware even though it’s like $50.” — Anil
“Reading John Scalzi’s The Kaiju Preservation Society and it is simple, honest sci-fi fun. Classic Scalzi.” — 4nd3rs
“Stick on Apple TV got me through the week until GTA VI!” — Justin
“Claude and I went around this week with a tape measure and built a to-the-inch accurate 3D model and floorplan of our house, which inevitably led to making it a Doom map.” — Michael
“I switched to ReadKit on my Mac and iPhone now that it has iCloud-based RSS sync.” — Todd
“Recently found the book The Canceling of the American Mind by Greg Lukianoff and Rikki Schlott at my local library. It is a well-written investigation into the effects of cancel culture on public debate and education. Wherever you fall on the political spectrum, this book will challenge you to think about how we should engage with ‘dangerous’ and ‘offensive’ ideas.” — Josh
“Been watching From since the first three seasons are available on Netflix right now. It’s a good show, has very Lost vibes to it.” — Bobby
Signing off
One of the most underrated strange things about the tech industry is how much The Social Network changed the way people think about Mark Zuckerberg. Yes, the movie takes huge liberties, and yes, every single person involved with the movie was quick to remind us that it was fiction. But for so many people, Jesse Eisenberg’s character just became who Zuck was.
I think Andrew Garfield in Artificial might be about to do the same thing to Sam Altman. The new trailer looks fabulous, all the early buzz about the movie seems to be great, and the movie absolutely could not be more perfectly timed. It’s apparently a pretty brutal look at Altman, OpenAI, and the whole AI movement — I wonder how Garfield and his handsomeness might bend the way the world responds. I cannot wait to see this movie.
See you in two weeks!

articles.title: Experts warn: nearly everyone in AI is susceptible to a honey trap scheme right now
articles.body:
Even as the fall-out for Nvidia over Jensen Huang’s alleged honey-trap scandal is still unfolding, Silicon Valley has yet to reckon with a new reality: many more people among them are at risk.
“Nobody briefs founders on counterintelligence,” Aaron Brown, a former senior CIA officer and current founder of the software company Lumbra, told TechCrunch.
That’s because historically honey traps have been associated with politicians, the military, and national intelligence — the people “behind clearances and a workforce trained to expect an approach,” from spies and other attackers.
But now many of the most valuable secrets “sit inside companies building chips, models, and infrastructure,” Brown says, adding that a spy “wants what the CEO can touch. The roadmap, the export decisions, the customer list, who gets the technology. The CEO is the shortest path to all of it.”
Huang has been accused of falling for just such a honey trap by having an affair with Alice Huang. She’s a former executive of a Singapore neocloud who’s been accused of being a Chinese spy and of smuggling billions of dollars’ worth of restricted Nvidia chips into China.
After the Huang allegations broke, jokes flooded the internet about which tech CEO will be next, but it’s not just CEOs and founders who are at risk. The WSJ reported that OpenAI started warning its employees about outsiders trying to cozy up to them in search of company secrets. Anyone with access to sensitive information — from board members to executive assistants — can be the target of a honey trap.
And typically, the attackers aren’t lovers. Friendship is actually the oldest honey-trap scheme around, Brown said.
Honey traps gain access to their targets as investors, customers, recruiters, and consultancies. Their requests look legitimate on paper and don’t need their targets to fall in love. “They need you to feel comfortable talking,” Brown said. “They last longer because nobody’s looking.”
What’s interesting, too, is the irony. So many tech founders are moving to automate and digitize so much of human life and yet remain vulnerable to the oldest bug around, a person who preys on the human need to be understood by others.
“Why fight through a firewall when you can get close to the person who can open doors, influence decisions, or make requests nobody wants to question?” Perry Carpenter, a criminologist and chief deception strategist at KnowBe4, told TechCrunch.
Once targets realize they have been compromised, the threat can escalate: attackers now have a means of blackmail.
Another irony: AI has made honey-trapping much easier and cheaper. Planning a scheme used to take months or years of research, crafting a persona, knowing the target, and executing a plan. These days, it’s easy to use AI to research a target, generate fake social profiles, fake backgrounds, even fake voice calls.
“AI can help sustain an entire fictional backstory,” Carpenter said. “The technology helps set the stage, but the deception ultimately plays out through human relationships.”
The AI industry “became a national security industry faster than its culture caught up,” Brown said.
“Part of being honey-trapped is not knowing,” he added. “It doesn’t feel like manipulation. It feels genuine, even lucky.”
Carpenter said a good first step is looking for unusual patterns. Note, for instance, “coincidental encounters that happen a little too often,” he said. There are also obvious signs, like persistent curiosity about work and colleagues, or requesting secrecy about meeting up, and pressing for introductions or information.
Bigger red flags include if someone’s requests are getting bigger, pushing the boundaries of what you usually would be uncomfortable doing. “A simple gut check,” Brown said. “Would this person still be around if you lost your job tomorrow?”
It also helps to try and understand when emotions might be influencing a decision. Carpenter suggests putting up a clear boundary between one’s personal and professional life. Within companies, it also helps to “eliminate executive exceptionalism,” he said, the idea that the rules don’t apply to people in power at the company.
Brown added that company culture plays another role, too: Are employees comfortable with raising concerns, challenging unusual requests, and escalating possible threats? “One of the most dangerous security cultures is one where nobody feels comfortable questioning the CEO,” Carpenter said.
“Founders need to take risks, and they need to explore business opportunities,” Brown said. “Paranoia doesn’t help. Recognizing you’re a target does.”

articles.title: Anthropic shares tank after IPO as the Nasdaq erases 2026 gains
articles.body:
The surging stock market of 2026 capsized Friday, wiping out gains for the year in the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite while the broad S&P 500 and the Dow entered correction territory, meaning they have declined 10% from recent peaks.
The dramatic sell-off is raising fresh fears about the viability of the AI investment wave that had powered stocks and economic growth for the first half of the year.
Friday’s declines were led by Anthropic, whose blockbuster IPO just 24 hours earlier now feels like a blip after the stock lost 9%, wiping out hundreds of billions in paper wealth and putting shares just a few dollars above the IPO price.
Nvidia also dragged markets lower, tumbling about 14% following a Reuters report that regulators are looking into accounting irregularities at the chip giant.
With Friday’s losses of 3.7%, the S&P 500’s seven-day losing streak is its worst since the Covid pandemic; the index is now up less than 1% on the year.
The Nasdaq finished the day down 5.3%, and the Dow dropped 1.9%.
The losses also sully one of the most visible bright points of President Donald Trump’s second term. Amid sticky inflation and frozen housing and jobs markets, U.S. equities were the one part of the economy that appeared resilient. The AI investment boom created seemingly insatiable demand for stocks among investors, minting multiple new trillion-dollar companies in the process.
While Friday’s declines were stark, they were not sudden, capping instead a weekslong slide that began in early October as the combination of elevated oil prices, rising interest rates, mounting corporate debt loads, stubborn inflation, supply chain issues and a flagging consumer put increasing pressure on stock prices.
The sell-off picked up steam earlier this month in the wake of Democrats’ midterm victories, which raised fears of a slowdown in the tech sector’s data center buildout. Losses accelerated again last week as the scandal erupted involving former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and advanced chips potentially being diverted to China.
“The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth,” wrote Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners, in a client note. “This has been exacerbated by the Nvidia crisis and the Democratic midterm win, which were a one-two punch for the AI story.”
Alongside the stock sell-off, investors have increased purchases of U.S. Treasury bonds — a sign that investors are seeking more reliable returns amid signs of weakening growth from higher interest rates and a stalling economy in China.
“The pressure is becoming increasingly widespread, and that’s been felt across other asset classes too,” Deutsche Bank managing director Jim Reid wrote in a note to clients Friday.

Kevin Gordon, head of macroeconomic strategy and research at Charles Schwab, told NBC News that markets are feeling particular pressure from an increasingly “hawkish” Federal Reserve that is signaling aggressive rate hikes in the face of unrelenting inflation.
“They’re signaling that they want to be aggressive in raising rates,” Gordon said. Combined with a weeks-long downturn among AI and tech stocks, “we have dual forces hitting the market.”
