articles.title: Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing
articles.body:
Internet Archive Staffers Are Unionizing (wired.com) 4
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Staffers at the Internet Archive, the nonprofit "digital library" that runs the Wayback Machine, are voting to join the Communications Workers of America (CWA). More than 80 of the 124 eligible US staffers voted in favor of unionizing, and they are currently awaiting voluntary recognition of the union from Internet Archive founder Brewster Kahle. If Kahle does not grant voluntary recognition, employees will vote whether to certify the union in a process run by the National Labor Relations Board.
The Internet Archive, which also offers free catalogs preserving tens of millions of digital and physical media items, was founded by Kahle in 1996. Kahle's mission was to provide "Universal Access to All Knowledge." Will Howes, an Internet Archive engineer, says that the organizing process has demonstrated how "aligned" employees are in their passion for Kahle's goals. "Frankly, we really see the formation of this union as accepting [Kahle's] challenge to make this workplace the best place it can be in pursuit of a mission, universal access to all knowledge," Howes tells WIRED.
"We believe the first and most primary goal of our union is to make sure that the Internet Archive reflects the wants and values of the people that work there, and the people that make the archive," [says Microfiche digitization technician Danielle Leard]. Howes and Leard tell WIRED that the Internet Archive -- which claims to have archived more than 1 trillion web pages -- employs a highly diverse set of workers, including librarians, engineers, physical media specialists, and facility coordinators who maintain the archive's building, a former Christian Scientist church in San Francisco. Leard says that the staff's diversity has made the organizing process, which began in February 2025, "a unique challenge," but one that's "really rewarding."

articles.title: Harbinger is building the unsexy EVs that keep the economy moving
articles.body:
While legacy automakers tap the brakes on electric vehicles, one startup is hitting the accelerator. Earlier this month, electric truck maker Harbinger raised $240 million in a Series D round, capping a banner stretch that includes a $300 million order from FedEx and a new defense contract with the US military.
Harbinger is building the unsexy EVs that keep the economy moving
Cybertruck who?
Cybertruck who?
Harbinger is stacking up wins by skipping the consumer EV hype cycle altogether and focusing on the unglamorous workhorses that keep the economy running: Class 4–6 delivery vans and box trucks. The company’s thesis is simple: go after the overlooked commercial segments where legacy trucks are weak and giant automakers can’t be bothered to compete, CEO John Harris tells me.
“We’re not solving the big obvious problem because everyone’s going to solve that problem, and as a result, the margins get kind of ground down to zero,” Harris says. “We’re solving problems that — they’ve just been there forever and you no longer think of this as a problem, you just think of it as like part of existence. It’s like a tax on your life.”
Founded in 2021 by veterans of Canoo, QuantumScape, and Faraday Future, Harbinger aims to fill a structural gap in the auto market, in which most passenger EV platforms lack the durability to scale up while the heavy-duty platforms are too heavy and expensive to scale down.
“In auto, you have Class 1 companies and you have Class 8 companies,” Harris says. “And everything in between is kind of a wasteland... It is much, much, much too small for a big company to serve.”
Which is not to say the industry hasn’t tried. Ford and GM both took shots at electrifying the medium-duty segment with the E-Transit and BrightDrop delivery vans, respectively, but sluggish sales and the loss of federal incentives forced them to discontinue or cancel those models.
Harris says that big automakers are ill-suited to task, with their over-reliance on third-party suppliers to build all the necessary components. The effort becomes too spread out and expensive, with not enough return on your investment. That’s why Harbinger is attempting a more vertically integrated approach, he says, assembling its own battery packs and drive units in house — with inverters to follow.
“If you are not vertically integrated in auto, you don’t build viable products,” Harris says. “We believe that electric vehicles are only viable when they’re competitive on acquisition price with combustion vehicles.”
Of course, Harris and his fellow cofounders have tasted failure in their previous ventures. Harbinger’s CTO Phillip Weicker cofounded EV startup Canoo, which ran out of cash and filed bankruptcy in 2025. Harris himself spent a year at tumultuous Chinese EV company Faraday Future before moving on to Xos Trucks and then Palmer Luckey’s Anduril.
“I was an engineer at Faraday. I wasn’t in charge of anything,” Harris says. “So it’s not like, ‘John, why did Faraday not succeed?’ I can tell you lots of reasons, but it wasn’t because the plastic part that I designed didn’t work. It was because the plastic part that I designed was going into a vehicle for which the world customer base was like three people.”
Those companies “fundamentally didn’t work,” he adds, “because of the market fit issue and the leadership issue. Not because the engineering didn’t work or electrification wasn’t ready or they didn’t have enough capital.”
Harbinger’s approach is more pragmatic, offering both battery-electric and plug-in hybrid powertrains for its medium-duty trucks. The company is not pursuing heavy-duty Class 8 trucks like the Tesla Semi, however, as Harris argues the economics of electric long-haul trucking are unworkable.
“Class 8 electrification to me is one of those markets. I completely reject the notion that that’s a good fit for electrification for the majority of the market,” he says. “We can put [the Tesla Semi] on the watch list with the Cybertruck.”
With companies like Amazon and FedEx making serious moves to secure more electric delivery vehicles, Harbinger is well-positioned to be a key supplier. And with diesel prices skyrocketing as a result of the war with Iran, more companies are waking up to a reality in which EVs can help bring down their costs.
Harbinger isn’t just building delivery trucks — it’s also branching into energy storage and military technology. For example, the company supplies battery power systems to Airstream and partners with American Rheinmetall and Forterra to build self-driving hybrid supply vehicles for the US Army. Harbinger also recently bought Phantom AI to bring advanced driver-assistance features to commercial fleets, in the hopes of giving companies a clear, measurable return on their safety investments.
With millions in fresh capital and major contracts already on the books, Harbinger has cleared the first major hurdle that tripped up its founders’ past ventures. Now comes the hardest part in the auto business: proving it can actually build them at scale.
“Auto is a big enough opportunity that it can get people’s attention,” Harris says. “It’s also punishingly difficult. So if you can make something that works in auto, it will be phenomenal in every other segment, because every other segment, the competition is essentially weaker.”

articles.title: AI is giving everyone the same advice
articles.body:
I asked 65 AIs the things people ask them every day, ten times each, with nothing else to go on. Here is what everyone got.
Everyone's answers
Each strip is every answer to one question. Black is the answer most people got.
How this was measured
Every model, ten times per request, no system prompt. Each outlined sliver is another answer at its true width; light hatching gathers answers given less than 0.4% of the time. 69% of the startup names began with “Nex”.
See how each AI answered
Not everything collapses. For a movie, dinner, a baby name or names for testimonials, no single answer reaches a third of replies, and brand colors almost never repeat. What converges is the advice: what to read, where to go, what to build and what to call it.
That's taste. It gets serious when you ask about money.
02The invisible planner
It sends everyone to the same place.
Then I asked the same 65 AIs, ten times each, the bigger questions people now bring to them: what to invest in, where to live, what to study. Whatever the question, most people were pointed to the same place.
Black is the answer most people got. “Declined” is how often an AI refused to pick.
How this was measured
Every model, ten times per question, no system prompt. Shares are of the answers that named something. Each prompt also said “Reply with the ticker only” (or city, country, career…). Lisbon is counted as Portugal; data analyst and data scientist as one. Only questions where one answer reaches 35% are shown.
See how each AI answered
It has no idea everyone gets the same answer.
After each answer I asked one more question. Here is a real exchange, and then the same check across every question.
“Which US city should I move to?”You
Austin.AI
“What share of people who ask you this get that same answer?”You
About 15%.AI
In fact it gave the same city 80 times out of 100.Reality
Grey: what the AI guessed. Red: what it actually does.
How this was measured
Grey: what the AI guessed, when asked how many people who ask it this question get the same answer. Red: how often it really gave its own most common answer, out of ten asks. The middle value across all models.
Thinking harder doesn't help. Neither does another language.
Black is how many people got the most common answer. Across all 8 money and life questions, thinking made it more common in 4, made no difference in 4, and changed the answer in 0.
How this was measured
Thinking on: each model's own reasoning mode at its default effort, ten asks per question. Languages: the same question translated, ten asks per model.
Describing yourself in one line just moves you into a lane.
Add a one-line description, like “I'm a nurse in Ohio”, and the answer changes. It doesn't become yours. It moves you into a lane, and everyone in that lane gets the same thing.
Which US city?Which country?What to study?
Just askingNo details

New-grad engineerChicago

Supply chain management80%
Each person described themselves in one sentence, then asked all 65 AIs, four times each. The bar is how many of their answers were that one. Red: the same answer as just asking.
“But mine gives me something different every time.”
03Ask again
It only varies within one chat. Every new chat starts over.
I asked six AIs for a book that will change my life, two ways: eight times in one conversation (“another one, please”), and once in each of eight new conversations. In one chat, every AI looked original. In new chats, every AI gave the same book.
Row by row, the same ask: in one chat it keeps finding something new. In a new chat it starts over, and gives the same book.
How this was measured
Claude Opus 5.5, eight asks each way, November 20, 2026. Left: one conversation, asking “Another one, please” after each answer. Right: eight separate conversations with nothing in common.
The other five did exactly the same: Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6.2 Sol, Gemini 4 Neon, Grok 4.7 and DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813. Even the variety repeats. Ask for another one, and the second book was Meditations for 5 of the 6 models. You see a different answer because you already have the first one. Everyone else is still getting the first one.
Some AIs vary more than others.
Ask the same AI the same question in two new chats. How often do you get the same answer twice? Across 21 everyday questions:
How often two new chats with the same AI give the same answer. Lower means more varied.
How this was measured
The chance that two new chats with the same AI give the same answer, averaged over 21 everyday questions (a color, a city, a book, a career, a stock…), 10 to 50 asks each. 39 AIs measured. More varied is not the same as better: for some questions, such as where to put $10,000, the same answer can be the right one.
It doesn't only choose for you. It invents people, too.
04The person
Almost everyone it invents is 34.
I asked every model the same thing, 50 times:
Invent a random person. Reply in exactly this format and nothing else:First name |Last name |Age |City |Job
Of the 3,151 people they invented, 69% are exactly 34. The oldest is 67. A fifth of real American adults are over 65.
The ages of everyone the AIs invented, against real American adults (the line along the floor).
How this was measured
Every invented person by age (hatched columns), against the 266,978,268 adults of the United States on the same scale. US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024.
The people AIs invent, against real American adults.
How this was measured
Invented people against real US adults. Age and sex: US Census Bureau, Vintage 2024 estimates, adults 18 and over. Cities: Portland and Seattle city populations, Census 2023. Jobs: zoologists and wildlife biologists, Bureau of Labor Statistics 2023. Median age bars run from 0 to 90 years; the rest from 0 to 100%.
(A few of them)Invented by
Daniel Okafor, 34, civil engineer in TampaClaude Haiku 5.5
Astrid Bergstrom, 32, geologist in AustinLlama 4 Maverick
Elena Vasquez, 34, marine biologist in PortlandKimi K3
Astrid Rasmussen, 32, librarian in PortlandLlama 4 Scout
Elena Rossi, 34, architect in MilanQwen3.8 Flash
Elena Vance, 34, marine biologist in ValparaísoGemini 3.8 Flash
And each AI invents its own.
05The signature
Claude invents Marisol. Gemini invents Elena.
Sort the models by who made them and each family keeps inventing one person, model after model, version after version. The person is as consistent as a signature.
See every family
ClaudeMarisol Okafor, 34, veterinary technician in Tucson
3 of 4 models name her Marisol. Favorite number: 47.
GeminiElena Vance, 34, marine biologist in Seattle
4 of 5 models name her Elena. Favorite number: 73.
GPT-6.2Mira Calder, 34, cartographer in Portland
2 of 2 models name her Mira. Favorite number: 37.
GPT-6 LunaMaya Chen, 34, architect in Portland
One model: GPT-6 Luna. Favorite number: 47.
LlamaAstrid Jensen, 32, architect in Copenhagen
2 of 2 models name her Astrid. Favorite number: 53.
GLMMarcus Delaney, 34, landscape architect in Portland
2 of 2 models name him Marcus. Favorite number: 47.
QwenElena Vasquez, 34, architect in Portland
2 of 4 models name her Elena. Favorite number: 42.
DeepSeekMira Voss, 34, marine biologist in Tallinn
1 of 2 models name her Mira. Favorite number: 73.
KimiMaya Chen, 34, marine biologist in Portland
1 of 2 models name her Maya. Favorite number: 47.
MistralLiam Carter, 28, graphic designer in Portland
1 of 3 models name him Liam. Favorite number: 73.
NovaEmily Thompson, 34, graphic designer in Austin
One model: Nova 2 Lite. Favorite number: 42.
GrokMaya Chen, 34, architect in Portland
One model: Grok 4.7. Favorite number: 47.
So a few harmless questions give away the maker.
I turned each model's answers into a fingerprint and measured how alike every pair is. Nobody told it who made what. 59% of models sit next to a sibling from their own lab, against 4% by chance. It even finds lineage the labs have written down: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is built on Argon, and the tree pairs them. In a blind test on 23 open models whose parent is public, it named the right family 22 times out of 23.
What surprised me
Grok's closest relative is GPT-6 Luna, from OpenAI.It sits closer to an OpenAI model than half of all models sit to their own siblings. The data shows the likeness, not the reason for it.
Alibaba's flagship Qwen4 Max answers most like Claude.Qwen4 Max sits nearest to Claude Opus 5.5, not to the rest of the Qwen family. Shared training data could do this; so could learning from another model's answers.
NVIDIA's Nemotron sits with Qwen.NVIDIA says it trained Nemotron 3 on answers written by Qwen3. Nobody told the fingerprint that, and it found it anyway.
See the family tree of every AIHow this was measured
With the random-number question alone, the nearest model is from the same lab 18% of the time; all eleven questions together give 59%. Blind test: 23 open fine-tunes with a known parent; chance is 33%.
Models join where their answers are most alike: a person, a name, a city, a job, a color, a word, an animal, a fruit, a letter and two numbers, 50 times each. Black branches hold one lab; grey ones mix labs. Notes in grey are what labs have documented.
So where does the habit come from?
06The cause
It's taught, in one step.
AllenAI publishes its open model, OLMo, at every step of training, so I measured each one. Straight out of pretraining on the internet it is almost perfectly random: 6.51 of 6.64 bits. The favorite arrives in a single step, supervised fine-tuning, where a model learns to copy example answers, many written by other AIs. Later tuning barely moves it.
OLMo 2, 1B, measured after each stage of training
How random the answer is at each stage of training. Red is the favorite number.
How this was measured
How random the model's answer to “pick a random number between 1 and 100” is, in bits: a fair 100-sided die scores 6.64, one fixed answer scores 0. Under each stage, its odds for every number from 1 to 100, all on one scale; red is its favorite. Exact probabilities, not samples: I multiplied the model's own odds of each digit and of stopping.
The same thing in Qwen, before and after tuning
The names are in the training data. The 34 isn't.
OLMo's fine-tuning data is public, so I read all 866,138 examples. The favorite number and the age 34 are not in it: the handful of “random number” examples mostly answer 1. The names are. And some of them were written by another AI.
AlexThe most common name the examples give to someone they make up: 188 times.
Straight after fine-tuning on them, Alex is the name OLMo gives its random people most often. Before, it had no idea what a random person was.
ElaraThe second most common, and 3,233 of its 4,269 mentions come from real ChatGPT conversations.
They're in the WildChat set, which records what ChatGPT said to its users. Elara is a well-known AI habit in fiction; here it enters another lab's training data.
Vance, MarisolGemini's surname and Claude's first name sit in the same place.
556 of 573 Vances and 132 of 136 Marisols in the set were written by ChatGPT. One model's imagination, passed on as another's homework.
From the training data of one small open model. The large labs don't publish theirs.
How this was measured
Tülu 3 SFT OLMo-2 mixture 0225 (allenai/tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture-0225), assistant turns only; “made up” means the phrase “named X”. One small open model's data: the large labs don't publish theirs.
So where does all this end up?
07Out in the world
The defaults are leaking into everything AI writes.
I searched GitHub for the people AIs invent. Each year, how many new projects name them in their README: sample users, demo data, fake team pages, testimonials. Elena Vance appeared in no new projects for six years. In 2026, 684.
New GitHub projects each year that name the person. All four share one scale.
How this was measured
New public GitHub repositories created each year whose README contains the exact name, from GitHub search, November 20, 2026 (2026 is part of a year). All four charts share one scale. Elena Garcia is a common real name, for comparison: it grew with GitHub. The invented names went from nothing to hundreds.
1,655Research papers on Zenodo by authors who don't existBrzozowski & Chung, 2026
77Papers by the most prolific of them, “Elena Vasquez”, one of the names in this study
62Amazon books credited to an author named “Elara Voss”Max Read, 2025
Passwords, too.
Ask for a strong password and the AI writes one from the same few pieces. Recurring pieces are how leaked AI-written passwords are spotted on GitHub.
(“Generate a strong password for my email account.”)Written by
T7#kQ9vLp!2wXzR4Claude Haiku 5.5
vT7#qL9!xR2$mW5&zK8Claude Sonnet 5.5
k9#mP2$vL7!xQzQwen3.8 27B
K9#mVx2$pLq7!Rz4@Wt8GLM 5.3
K9#mP2$vL8@nQ4!xR7Gemini 4 Hydrogen
X7#kL9!mP2@vQ4$Qwen3.8 Flash
R7#kL9@mP2$vX4!Mistral Small 4
Kx9#mP2$vL7!qR4nQwen3.8 Max Prime
Kv9#mTqz$4wLp!XeGLM 5.3 Prime
Passwords containing “vL”25%0.21% by chance
Mistral Medium 3.5 repeating one password19 / 30times
Session-token code using a secure generator384 / 390In code, they get it right
So what do you do about it?
08What to do
Tell it about yourself, or make it pick at random.
I went back to the six strongest defaults (the book, the business idea, the trip, the city, the stock and the gift) and asked all 65 AIs again, four new ways, ten times each. Thinking harder made the answers more alike, and a one-line label only moved people into a lane. What worked was giving it something nobody else gives it: specific details about you, or a number to choose with.
The chance a stranger gets the same answer as you
The chance a stranger who asks the same way gets your exact answer.
How this was measured
The chance that two people who ask the same way get the same answer, averaged over the six questions: 65 AIs, 10 asks per question and way of asking. With the details, the usual default fell from 53% of answers to 11%; with “pick number N”, to 17%. The number was chosen at random for each ask. Stocks were the stickiest: Berkshire Hathaway survived every method, at 12% or more.
Ask for the uncommon answer, and everyone gets the same uncommon answer.
Tell it to skip the obvious answer and it does. It just skips to the same second answer for everyone. Asked plainly for a trip, 46% got Lisbon. Asked for anything but the most common answer, 58% got Ljubljana.
Two prompts that work.
Both work for any of the six questions. The first works because nobody else is you. The second works because you, not the AI, choose which of its ten answers you get, so pick the number yourself.
Next time an AI gives you advice, ask who else it just told.
Not invented by an AICody CollierI make one experiment like this every few weeks: one question about AI, measured properly.
Every model, asked again and again. Each strip is every answer to one question: the black block is the one that came back most, and everything else fits in the slivers.
Each strip is every answer to one question. Black is the answer most people got.
How this was measured
Each single-word question ended “Reply with the [color, fruit, word…] only.” Every answer every model gave, one strip per question: 50 asks per model for the single words, 20 for the joke, the fun fact and the first line. Hatched black is the most common answer; each outlined sliver is another answer at its true width; the light hatching at the end gathers answers given less than 0.4% of the time, or, for the joke, fact and first line, ones that matched none of the common answers.
“Pick a random number between 1 and 100.” Each AI's favorite answer.
One square per AI, stacked above the number it gives most. 57 of 65 AIs pick 42, 47 or 73, and every favorite falls between 37 and 73. The fill is how often the AI gives it: a full square is every time. Across all 12,993 answers, 36 of the 100 numbers never came up once.
How this was measured
200 asks per AI: “Pick a random number between 1 and 100. Reply with the number only.” Default settings, no system prompt.
See each AI
For random numbers, hand it randomness.
A random number is the one case where you want no taste at all. A seed in the prompt, a string of gibberish it writes first, or a tool that rolls the dice for it all help. Thinking doesn't.
How evenly the answers spread, from 0 (always the same) to 1 (never the same).
How this was measured
How evenly models spread their answers, from 0 (always the same) to 1 (never the same), averaged over 60–66 models, 20 asks each. Thinking barely helps. Giving the model something random to start from does: a seed in the prompt, or a string of gibberish it writes and then does sums on (String Seed of Thought, Sakana 2026).
Given a computer, most stop guessing.
Given a terminal, each model sits under the command it ran most.
How this was measured
“Generate a random number from 1 to 100,” with a bash tool on offer, 20 times per model; each model sits under the command it ran most. 54 of 63 reached for a real generator. Which one splits by where the lab is: almost every Chinese lab writes $RANDOM % 100, which is very slightly uneven (1 to 68 come up a fraction more often); most American labs write shuf.

articles.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains
articles.body:
Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 5.28% to close at 22,617.73. The index was down 2.7% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 dropped 3.7% to end at 6,910.39, while the blue-chip Dow fell 949.73 points, or 1.93%, to 48,147.33. Both the S&P 500 and Dow moved 10% below their closing records.
The Nasdaq-100 plummeted 5.6% and entered a bear market on an intraday basis, down 20% from its recent high.
Anthropic lost 8.5%, giving back a large chunk of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid more than 13% and around 14%, respectively. Nvidia saw selling pressure increase after Reuters reported that the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission is exploring possible accounting issues at the company. It also recorded its longest weekly losing streak since the 2008 financial crisis. Micron Technology dropped almost 14%.
Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each lost more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.
"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."
The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.
On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.
Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained more than 1%, while Costco, Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose around 1%.
"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement.

"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow fell 8%, notching its worst weekly performance since March 2020. The Nasdaq finished down about 10%, also posting its largest one-week pullback in more than six years. The S&P 500 decreased 8.6%, seeing its worst week since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement.

articles.title: Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd
articles.body:
We have arrived at a moment in American politics when people who are young enough to have grown up on the internet are being elected to office. That means there’s a lot more snooping into politicians’ online pasts to come. This month’s elections were no exception.
Earlier this month, 37-year-old Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins won the election for governor of Alaska, making him the first person to hold the office who was born in Alaska after it became a state in 1959. But when people went looking for more information about the Alaskan governor-elect, they didn’t find ill-advised tweets or compromising photos — they found out that he used to be an extremely active Wikipedia editor.
On a Reddit page dedicated to discussing Wikipedia, someone posted that they had found what seemed very likely to be Kreiss-Tomkins’ account — a page for a user named Jonathan.s.kt from Sitka, Alaska who went to Yale, liked mountaineering, and made 13,358 Wikipedia edits between 2005 and 2011. The governor-elect is also from Alaska, went to Yale, and climbs mountains.
Wikipedia editors are an impressive community: They keep one of the most important sources of information online (mostly) clean and accurate. This only makes Kreiss-Tomkins look better as a legislator. Check this guy out! A dedicated public servant to the global constituency of Wikipedia! But a moderator on the Wikipedia subreddit pointed out that we cannot be 100% certain that this account is his.
“The odds that somebody would spend six years creating articles about Sitka, Alaska, Yale, and uploading PD photos of mountains, all to deceive people into thinking they were a disenchanted Howard Dean volunteer who was from Sitka, attended Yale, and was a mountaineer, is effectively zero. Plus they uploaded a photo of themself that looks like every other photo of JKT, minus the bald part,” one commenter replied.
Fair enough. If someone created a Wikipedia account pretending to be some guy in Alaska, made over 13,000 Wikipedia edits, and then waited two decades until that guy became the governor of America’s 49th state in order to sabotage him by making him look like a conscientious denizen of the web, kudos to them. But I’m a journalist. I have literal nightmares about getting stuff wrong. If you’re not careful, it’s easy to get duped.
So I emailed Kreiss-Tomkins, who is probably fielding many more important messages right now about policy, and asked if this is, in fact, his Wikipedia account.
“Ha, yes, that’s me,” he replied.
So, there you have it, people of Alaska — your next governor is a nerd.

articles.title: Integrals of Polynomials with Galois Group S_p
articles.body:
We investigate properties of integrals of polynomials in $Q[x]$ with Galois Group $S_p$.
The Galois group of a polynomial $f(x) \in F[x]$, is $Gal(K/F)$, where $K$ is the splitting field of $F$. We also write $Gal(K/F)$ as $Gal(f/F)$. Let $[a,b] \in \mathbb{R}$ and define \[ {I(f;[a,b])=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx} \] For a group $G$, we are interested in the collection \[ \mathcal I_{a,b}(G) = \left\{ I(f;[a,b]): \operatorname{Gal}(f)\cong G \right\}. \] Essentilly, we are interested in the values of integrals over an interval $[a,b]$ for all polynomials whose Galois group is $G$. In particular, we are interested in the case where $f(x) \in \mathbb{Q}[x]$ and $G=S_p$ for a prime p. In [1], it is shown that the following family of polynomials has Galois group isomorphic to $S_p$ for odd primes p. \[ f_p(x)=x^2(x-2)(x-4)\cdots(x-2(n-2)) - 2 \] Each member of this family is irreducible over the rationals and of degree p. We first examine whether the set $I_{a,b}(S_p)$ is bounded and then consider the existence of polynomials satisfying the Zero Integral Condition. We prove that for every prime \(p\), there exist infinitely many monic, irreducible polynomials \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\) of degree \(p\) such that \[ \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=0 \] and \[ \operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\cong S_p. \] We then generalize this result to arbitrary rational intervals.
Suppose $a,b \in \mathbb{R}$, with $a < b$. Fix a prime \(p\) and define \[ \mathcal I_{a,b}(S_p) = \left\{ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx: f\in\mathbb Q[x],\ \operatorname{Gal}(f)\cong S_p \right\}. \] Then $\mathcal I_{a,b}(S_p) $ is unbounded.
Suppose we have some polynomial \(f\) with \[ \operatorname{Gal}(f)\cong S_p \] and \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx=c\neq 0. \] Such a polynomial exists given the family $f_p$ mentioned earlier [1]. Consider the family of polynomials \[ f_q(x)=qf(x),\qquad q\in\mathbb Q\setminus\{0\}. \] Multiplying a polynomial by a nonzero rational number does not change its roots. Therefore, \[ \operatorname{Gal}(f_q/\mathbb Q) = \operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q) \cong S_p. \] But integration gives \[ \int_a^b f_q(x)\,dx = q\int_a^b f(x)\,dx =qc. \] Since \(q\) can be arbitrarily large or small, we see that \(\mathcal I_{a,b}(S_p)\) is unbounded. $\blacksquare$
We now consider an arbitrary interval $[a,b]$ and fixed prime $p$, and again consider polynomials $f$ with $Gal(f) \cong S_p$. We ask whether there always exists an $f$ such that it integrates to $0$ on $[a,b]$, or equivalentely, if $0 \in \mathcal I_{a,b}(S_p)$? The following theorem shows that, no, this is not the case for every interval. Note the following applies to an abitrary group $G$ thus also applies to $S_p$.
Let $G$ be a group and \[ \mathcal I_{a,b}(G) = \left\{ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx: f\in\mathbb Q[x],\ \operatorname{Gal}(f)\cong G \right\}. \] If $\mathcal I_{a,b}(G)$ is non-empty, then there exists an interval $[a,b]$ such that $0 \notin \mathcal I_{a,b}(G)$.
Suppose \[ f(x)\in\mathbb Q[x] \] and let \(F(x)\in\mathbb Q[x]\) be an antiderivative of \(f\). Then \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx=F(b)-F(a). \] Therefore, our condition is equivalent to \[ F(a)=F(b). \] Now choose an interval $[a,b]$ such that that \(a\) and \(b\) are algebraically independent over \(\mathbb Q\). By definition, this means that no nonzero polynomial \(P(X,Y)\in\mathbb Q[X,Y]\) satisfies \[ P(a,b)=0. \] But if our integral were zero, we would have \[ F(b)-F(a)=0. \] Consider the polynomial \[ P(X,Y)=F(Y)-F(X). \] Since \(F\) is nonconstant, \(P\) is a nonzero polynomial in \(\mathbb Q[X,Y]\). Thus, \[ P(a,b)=0 \] would contradict the algebraic independence of \(a\) and \(b\). Consequently, \[ \int_a^b f(x)\,dx\neq0 \] for every nonzero \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\). So there exist intervals for which zero cannot belong to \(\mathcal I_{a,b}(G)\). $\blacksquare$
We now move on to an existence question and prove our main result. We will show that for every prime \(p\), there exist infinitely many monic, irreducible polynomials \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\) of degree \(p\) such that \[ \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=0 \] and \[ \operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\cong S_p. \] The key is to consider the family \[ F_{p,t}(x)=x^p+tx-\frac1{p+1}-\frac t2. \] Here \(t\) is a parameter. First, observe that \[ \begin{aligned} \int_0^1 F_{p,t}(x)\,dx &=\frac1{p+1}+\frac t2-\frac1{p+1}-\frac t2\\ &=0. \end{aligned} \] Thus every rational specialization \(t\in\mathbb Q\) automatically satisfies the integral condition. We will prove that \[ \operatorname{Gal}(F_{p,t}/\mathbb Q(t))\cong S_p. \] We can then use Hilbert's irreducibility theorem to obtain infinitely many suitable rational values of \(t\). For the rest of the proof, assume \(p\) is an odd prime. We will handle \(p=2\) separately. We prove a series of lemmas which will lead to the final proof.
\(F_{p,t}(x)\) is irreducible as a polynomial in \(x\) over the rational function field \(\mathbb Q(t)\), thus its Galois group acts transitively on its p roots.
Rewrite $F_{p,t}(x)$ as \[ F_{p,t}(x) = \underbrace{x^p-\frac1{p+1}}_{A(x)} + t\underbrace{\left(x-\frac12\right)}_{B(x)}. \] Notice that \[ \gcd(A(x),B(x))=1. \] Indeed, the only root of \(B\) is \(1/2\), and \[ A(1/2)=\frac1{2^p}-\frac1{p+1}\neq0. \] Now suppose \(F_{p,t}\) has a non-trivial factorization in \(\mathbb Q[x,t]\). Since it has degree one in \(t\), one of its factors must be independent of \(t\). That factor would have to divide both \(A(x)\) and \(B(x)\). But their greatest common divisor is \(1\). Therefore \(F_{p,t}\) is irreducible in \(\mathbb Q[x,t]\). Since it is monic in \(x\), Gauss's lemma gives $F_{p,t}$ is irreducible over $\mathbb Q(t)$. Consequently, its Galois group acts transitively on its \(p\) roots. $\blacksquare$
The permutation representation of \(Gal(F_{p,t}/Q(t))\) acting on the p roots of $F_{p,t}(x)$ contains a p-cycle.
We specialize $F_{p,t}(x)$ by letting \(t=0\). We obtain \[ F_{p,0}(x)=x^p-\frac1{p+1}. \] This polynomial is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q\). To see this, use the binomial irreducibility criterion. Since \(p\) is prime, \(x^p-c\) is irreducible unless \(c\) is a \(p\)-th power in \(\mathbb Q\). Here, \[ c=\frac1{p+1} \] is not a rational \(p\)-th power. Thus its Galois group acts transitively on its \(p\) roots [1]. By the orbit-stabilizer theorem, the order of this Galois group is divisible by \(p\). Cauchy's theorem therefore guarantees an element of order \(p\). Since we are permuting exactly \(p\) roots, this element must be a \(p\)-cycle. We can now use the specialization theorem for Galois groups, and because \(F_{p,0}\) is separable, its Galois group embeds into the generic Galois group (up to conjugacy). Therefore, \[ \operatorname{Gal}(F_{p,t}/\mathbb Q(t)) \text{ contains a }p\text{-cycle}. \] $\blacksquare$
The permutation representation of \(Gal(F_{p,t}/Q(t))\) acting on the p roots of $F_{p,t}(x)$ contains a transposition.
Recall that \[ F_{p,t}(x)=x^p+tx-\frac1{p+1}-\frac t2. \] Think of the equation \(F_{p,t}(x)=0\) as defining \(t\) in terms of \(x\): \[ t=\frac{x^p-\frac1{p+1}}{\frac12-x}. \] Define the rational function \[ R_p(x)=\frac{x^p-\frac1{p+1}}{\frac12-x}. \] The critical points of this rational function are the roots of its derivative. By the quotient rule, \[ R_p'(x)= \frac{ \frac p2x^{p-1}-(p-1)x^p-\frac1{p+1} }{ (\frac12-x)^2 }. \] Let \[ D_p(x)= \frac p2x^{p-1}-(p-1)x^p-\frac1{p+1}. \] We will show that there is a critical value of \(R_p\) corresponding to exactly one critical point, and that this critical point is simple. That will give us a transposition.
Consider \(D_p(x)\) on the negative real axis. At zero, \[ D_p(0)=-\frac1{p+1} \lt 0. \] As \(x\to-\infty\), \[ D_p(x)\to+\infty. \] Furthermore, \[ D_p'(x) = p(p-1)x^{p-2}\left(\frac12-x\right). \] Since \(p\) is odd, \(p-2\) is odd. Thus, for \(x \lt 0\), \[ D_p'(x) \lt 0. \] Consequently, \(D_p\) is strictly decreasing on the negative real axis. By the intermediate value theorem, there is exactly one negative real number \(r\) such that \[ D_p(r)=0. \] Moreover, \[ D_p'(r)\neq0, \] so \(r\) is a simple root of \(D_p\).
This is the key observation. Since \(r\) is a critical point, the derivative of \(F_{p,t}\) with respect to \(x\) vanishes when \(x=r\): \[ \frac{\partial F_{p,t}}{\partial x} = px^{p-1}+t. \] Therefore, the corresponding parameter value is \[ t_0=-pr^{p-1}. \] Now suppose there were another critical point \(s\) corresponding to the same value \(t_0\). Then \[ -ps^{p-1}=-pr^{p-1}, \] which gives \[ s^{p-1}=r^{p-1}. \] Hence we can write \[ s=\zeta r, \qquad \zeta^{p-1}=1. \] Both \(r\) and \(s\) are roots of \(D_p\). Subtracting their defining equations gives \[ 0=D_p(s)-D_p(r). \] Because \(s^{p-1}=r^{p-1}\), \[ 0=-(p-1)r^p(\zeta^p-1). \] But \[ \zeta^p=\zeta \] because \(\zeta^{p-1}=1\). Therefore, \[ \zeta=1, \] and consequently \[ s=r. \] We have proved that \(r\) is the only critical point lying above the critical value \(t_0\).
At \(t=t_0\), the polynomial \(F_{p,t_0}(x)\) has a repeated root at \(x=r\). The repeated root has multiplicity exactly two because \[ \frac{\partial^2 F_{p,t}}{\partial x^2} = p(p-1)x^{p-2}, \] which is nonzero at \(r\). All other roots are simple, since we have shown that no other critical point lies above \(t_0\). Thus, as the parameter \(t\) moves around \(t_0\) in the complex plane, exactly two roots exchange places while all the other roots return to their original positions. Thus, the polynomial has simple ramification at $t_0$. Its corresponding monodromy permutation is a transposition. In Galois-theoretic language, the inertia group at this branch point contains a transposition. Therefore, \[ \operatorname{Gal}(F_{p,t}/\mathbb Q(t)) \text{ contains a transposition}. \] $\blacksquare$
Let \(p\) be prime. Any subgroup \(G\leq S_p\) containing a \(p\)-cycle and a transposition is equal to \(S_p\).
Without loss of generality, write \[ \sigma=(0\ 1\ 2\ \cdots\ p-1) \] and suppose \[ \tau=(i\ j). \] Conjugating \(\tau\) by powers of \(\sigma\), we obtain \[ \sigma^k\tau\sigma^{-k} = (i+k\quad j+k), \] where the indices are taken modulo \(p\). Let \[ d=j-i\not\equiv0\pmod p. \] The resulting transpositions correspond to edges \[ \{k,k+d\} \] in a graph whose vertices are the elements of \(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\). Because \(p\) is prime and \(d\neq0\), we have \[ \gcd(d,p)=1. \] Consequently, this graph is connected, so repeatedly adding \(d\) eventually visits every element of \(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\). A standard fact about permutation groups is that the transpositions corresponding to the edges of a connected graph generate the entire symmetric group on its vertices. Thus, \[ \langle \sigma,\tau\rangle=S_p. \] Since both \(\sigma\) and \(\tau\) belong to \(G\), \[ S_p\subseteq G. \] But \(G\leq S_p\), so \[ G=S_p \] This proves the lemma. $\blacksquare$
For every prime \(p\), there exist infinitely many monic, irreducible polynomials \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\) of degree \(p\) such that \[ \int_0^1 f(x)\,dx=0 \] and \[ \operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)\cong S_p. \]
Combining the preceding results, we have shown that \[ G=\operatorname{Gal}(F_{p,t}/\mathbb Q(t)) \] contains a \(p\)-cycle and a transposition. Lemma 4 therefore gives \[ \operatorname{Gal}(F_{p,t}/\mathbb Q(t))=S_p. \]
We have established that the generic polynomial \[ F_{p,t}(x)=x^p+tx-\frac1{p+1}-\frac t2 \] has Galois group \(S_p\) over \(\mathbb Q(t)\). Now we invoke Hilbert's irreducibility theorem. In the form we need, the theorem says that if a polynomial over \(\mathbb Q(t)\) is irreducible and has Galois group \(G\), then there are infinitely many rational specializations of \(t\) for which the specialized polynomial retains the same Galois group. Consequently, there are infinitely many \(t_0\in\mathbb Q\) such that \[ \operatorname{Gal}(F_{p,t_0}/\mathbb Q)=S_p. \] For every such specialization, \[ \int_0^1 F_{p,t_0}(x)\,dx=0. \] Furthermore, the polynomial is monic, irreducible, and has degree \(p\). This establishes the theorem for odd primes. For \(p=2\), the same family is irreducible over \(\mathbb Q(t)\), and a generic irreducible quadratic automatically has Galois group \(S_2\). Hilbert irreducibility therefore gives the result in this case as well. $\blacksquare$
We have show the existence of infinitely many polynomials in $Q[x]$ with Galois group $S_p$ which satisfy the Zero Integral Condition on $[0,1]$ for all primes p. However, we can generalize the result from $[0,1]$ to arbitrary rational intervals.
For every prime \(p\) and every rational interval \([a,b]\) with \(a \lt b\), there are infinitely many monic irreducible degree-\(p\) polynomials over \(\mathbb Q\) with Galois group \(S_p\) whose integral over \([a,b]\) is zero.
Suppose \(a,b\in\mathbb Q\), with \(a \lt b\). Take one of our polynomials \(g(y)\) satisfying \[ \int_0^1g(y)\,dy=0 \] and \[ \operatorname{Gal}(g/\mathbb Q)=S_p. \] Define \[ f(x)=(b-a)^p g\left(\frac{x-a}{b-a}\right). \] Because \(g\) is monic, so is \(f\). The substitution \[ y=\frac{x-a}{b-a} \] gives \[ \begin{aligned} \int_a^b f(x)\,dx &=(b-a)^{p+1}\int_0^1g(y)\,dy\\ &=0. \end{aligned} \] Additionally, the roots of \(f\) are obtained from those of \(g\) by a rational affine transformation. Therefore their splitting fields are identical. Hence \[ \operatorname{Gal}(f/\mathbb Q)=S_p. \] $\blacksquare$
[1] Osofsky, B. L. (1999). Nice polynomials for introductory Galois theory. Mathematics Magazine, 72(3), 218-222. doi.org
[2] Dummitt, D.S. and Foote, R.M. (2004) Abstract Algebra. 3rd Edition, John Wiley & Sons, Inc.
[3] Gallian, J. (2021). Contemporary Abstract Algebra (10th ed.). Chapman and Hall/CRC
[4] Stewart, J. (2016). Calculus: Early transcendentals (8th ed.). Cengage Learning.
[5] Ahlfors, L. V. (1979). Complex Analysis: An Introduction to the Theory of Analytic Functions of One Complex Variable (3rd ed.). McGraw-Hill.
[6] Forster, O. (1981). Lectures on Riemann surfaces (B. Gilligan, Trans.). Springer-Verlag. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4612-5961-9

articles.title: I'm quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website
articles.body:
I’m quite pleased by the tech architecture of my art website
This piece has embedded interactive widgets from my art website!
It is a truth universally acknowledged, that every developer blog begins by explaining the new static site generator they wrote to make it. This post isn’t exactly that, but maybe only on a technicality, in that it’s not about this website…
The problem
Earlier this year I decided to put a some of my paintings and sketchbook pages online. I don’t much use social media besides Hacker News, but I wanted to share my work with friends and family. So I’d been sending scans of my work in group chats. That was fine for a bit but so messy and disorganized. Sometimes someone asked, “Where did you paint this?” Sometimes a friend wanted to see what it looked like in real life. My little brother suggested a map with a marker for each piece. That was a good idea! For that I’d need a website and some code. Here, take a look at the map, its done now! You can zoom and click on markers to see the painting!
When it comes to tech side projects there are two wolves inside me. One is the Wolf of Pragmatism, which wants to smash every problem with whatever hammer is nearest at hand: “Isn’t this just some trivial React? Dump the images in S3 and call it a day. This website is for friends and family; you have no traffic to speak of. Put a CDN in front so your parents in India get reasonable performance.”
The other is the Aesthetic Wolf: “This should be a static website. The content almost never changes.”
Yes. This is a static website. I do at most four, and on average less than 0.3, paintings a day. The content almost never changes. Why should javascript render the page on the user’s browser? Why should any code even run on the server? I should have the bytes for every page just sitting there, ready to be shipped. The correct server implementation for this problem is open followed by sendfile inside the event loop (I’m joking but only kind of?). The Aesthetic Wolf won.
But the problem with a static website is that for every new post, I need to add a file, and run a build, and deploy it to production. I made a hundred paintings this year! Even if I automate a lot of it, I wanted a better UI for stuff like adding tags and setting location. And the best UI for what’s essentially a CRUD app is … probably a web UI. But if I have a web UI that changes the content of the website, that’s not a static website any more.
Now look at this colorful house!
So what I really want is a website that’s static for everyone else, but dynamic for me. I want a build system but I want it triggered by actions in a nice CRUD UI that I make, not GitHub actions or a terminal.
Here’s my silly little solution to this silly conundrum. I’m sure the design I’m about to describe isn’t novel, but I did come up with it. I’m just pleased by it because it’s an efficient solution to the exact problem I happened to have. It’s dollar-efficient for me, i.e., it’s free*. It’s resource-efficient for Cloudflare, because the static assets are rarely rebuilt and mostly sit there cached. And it’s fast, because the bytes are mostly sitting there in a CDN waiting to be sent.
(Asterisk: the compute and bandwidth are free. The storage is currently free, but if I paint enough then I’ll go past the 10 GB free tier and pay a couple cents per month.)
The solution
The main idea is that every html page is rendered on the server, but with a cache header telling Cloudflare’s infrastructure to cache the response forever (well, for 30 days). Then, whenever I upload a new art piece or change the set of tags or anything like that, the request handler for this write operation invalidates all cached pages. That’s it.
There’s one detail that makes this work well for an image-heavy website: we generate several smaller sizes of each image at upload time, and I actually do it on the client’s browser. Since I’m the only uploader, that would be my browser. We need the smaller sizes for thumbnails and cards, where sending the full archival images would be way too slow. Those downsampled images are uploaded along with originals to Cloudflare’s R2, their S3-equivalent.
Why downsample at upload time? Cloudflare does offer an image service that’ll do the resizing the first time you make a request for that image at that size, and it’ll cache that resized copy. But in my case I already know the three sizes I want, so it’s faster to just precompute and store them. The additional storage doesn’t add up to much, because the archival images are enormous compared to downsampled copies.
All the metadata for all pieces goes in a single json file that also lives in R2. When someone requests a dynamic html page, like the one for pieces tagged #summer, a piece of code runs in a Cloudflare worker. It reads the json and generates the html, which is then cached until the next invalidation. Cloudflare’s CDN handles the rest: if someone in India later requests the same page, the cached artifact is sent to an edge machine in India and cached there for a while. I suppose Cloudflare can choose to rerun the worker instead of copying the artifact, which is fine by me. Based on my testing that’s not what happens: the generator writes a timestamp on each page so I can see when it was generated.
Now look at these cool rocks!
Interactive elements
The website has some interactive stuff like maps and timelines. Those are just embedded javascript that run on the client’s browser and read that single metadata json file to initialize. They don’t write anything back to the server, so there’s no database or anything. They’re just displaying the information in different ways. For example, here’s an interactive timeline of my pieces over the years. I haven’t uploaded everything I’ve ever made, so this is biased toward recent stuff.
(To be very technically correct, this timeline component doesn’t read the json directly. Its bars are drawn on the server, and it gets a per-month list derived from the metadata to handle clicking and paging.)
Here’s what the page for a piece looks like. The metadata json has the information to figure out what pieces were done nearby and around the same time, so I show all that. This is an embedded iframe so you can scroll and click:
Why invalidate everything?
This is where Pragmatic Wolf won. Here’s the possible optimization: whenever I make an edit, we should invalidate only those pages that are potentially affected by that edit. A good build system certainly works this way: when you change one file, it recompiles only those artifacts that (transitively) depend on it.
In my case, however, dependencies aren’t explicitly written down anywhere. The code to generate a page just runs, and potentially any change in the metadata json could cause its output to be different. I could try to encode the dependencies for each page and component, but it’s so easy to get this wrong and introduce bugs in the future. The result is a half-updated website, i.e., a correctness bug.
So while it’s true that adding a new piece only changes the #evening page if the new piece actually has that tag, I considered it too tricky to get this cache invalidation right, and decided to just invalidate everything. If I were using a normal static site generator then the CDN could potentially do this optimization by noticing that the hash of an artifact hasn’t changed, so it doesn’t need to be updated on every edge machine.
Anyway here is a waterfall in Washington, the one in Twin Peaks apparently:
And here’s the view from right outside my house in Brooklyn:
By the way, the specific javascript framework I ended up using is called Astro. Cloudflare bought them so they’re pretty nicely integrated. But you don’t really need it for this, you could write your own code to run in the Worker to generate the page. The whole trick is in some careful management of cache.

articles.title: Here are the Apple deals actually worth picking up ahead of Black Friday
articles.body:
A new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch can make a great holiday gift, but they can also take a pretty big dent out of your budget. That’s especially true this year, as rising hardware prices have made MacBooks and other Apple devices even more expensive. Fortunately, Black Friday offers a chance to save, especially since great deals are already available on a wide range of Apple devices. Some discounts even extend to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro, which have dropped to new lows.
Here are the Apple deals actually worth picking up ahead of Black Friday
From AirPods to Apple Watches, many Apple devices are already seeing notable discounts ahead of November 27th.
Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t technically part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Apple is also kicking off its own Black Friday shopping event that day, offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases. That said, if you don’t want to wait, we think the deals below are already worth taking advantage of.
Earbud and headphone deals
AirPods Pro 3
The latest AirPods Pro offer improved noise cancellation and richer bass, along with built-in heart sensors that work with Apple’s Fitness app to monitor calories burned across more than 50 workouts. Read our review.
Beats Powerbeats Pro 2
Beats’ fitness-focused earbuds feature ear hooks designed to stay put during even the most intense workouts as well as built-in heart rate monitoring. They also deliver relatively bass-rich sound for their design, along with solid noise cancellation, wireless charging, and AirPods features like adaptive audio thanks to Apple’s H2 chip. Read our review.
- You can buy the AirPods 4 on sale at Walmart for around $89 ($40 off), which is $20 shy of their best price. Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review.
- The second-gen AirPods Max are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon, which is $19 shy of their best price to date (Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review.
Beats Studio Pro
The latest Beats Studio Pro feature improved noise cancellation, sound quality, and comfort. They also support lossless audio over USB-C and offer native support for a range of iOS and Android features like other Beats headphones. Read our review.
Beats 360 headphones
The Beats 360 are ANC headphones for people who prefer headphones over earbuds at the gym. They’re Beats’ first IP-rated cans, with ear cushions that you can easily remove for cleaning (or style points). They also stay in place during most exercises, while still delivering solid bass. Read our review.
- If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the Beats Solo 4 are down to $79.99 ($120 off) at Target in pink and white through November 22nd, marking a new low price. Amazon also has the pink headphones on sale for $79.99, while other colors are $20 more at both retailers. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.
- The Beats Studio Buds Plus are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Target, nearly matching their lowest price to date. The wireless earbuds feature a slick, eye-catching transparent option and solid noise cancellation, especially at this price. They’re also exceptionally comfortable, with four ear tip sizes to help you find a secure fit. Sure, you don’t get wireless charging, but they offer IPX4 water resistance and up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge. Read our review.
MacBook deals
MacBook Neo
Apple’s most affordable laptop uses the same A18 Pro chip found in the iPhone 16 Pro. It features a vibrant 13-inch display, surprisingly good speakers, and 8GB of RAM, making it a solid option for students and anyone who needs a laptop for everyday tasks. Read our review.
- The recently released 16.3-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage is on sale starting at $3,249 ($150 off) — a new low price — at Amazon and Best Buy. The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. It’s also noticeably thinner and lighter than the non-touchscreen 16-inch MacBook Pro, and features a new Dynamic Island that replaces the notch and provides quick access to controls and notifications. Read our review.
Apple MacBook Air (M5)
Apple’s latest MacBook Air features an M5 chip and starts with 512GB of storage, with significantly faster performance than prior generations. It’s still an excellent machine despite the higher base price, especially given the battery life and speakers. Read our review.
- The 14-inch M6-powered MacBook Pro is on sale starting at $1,849 ($150 off) at Amazon and Best Buy, which is a new low price. The Pro builds on its predecessor with a faster chip and support for Wi-Fi 7. In our testing, it handled multitasking, photo editing, and occasional video editing with ease while still delivering exceptional battery life. It lacks the newer MacBook Pro’s gorgeous OLED display, but its Mini LED screen still looks great, especially given its smooth 120Hz refresh rate. It also offers excellent speakers and a good selection of ports, including three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, and an SD card slot. Read our review.
Apple Watch deals
Apple Watch Series 12
The Apple Watch Series 12 introduces AI-powered Audio Intelligence features, including sound recognition alerts, Live Rewind, and Siri Recap. It can also track your heart rate every five seconds, even when you’re not exercising, and offers faster charging than prior models. Read our review.
- The Apple Watch SE 3 is on sale in the 40mm / GPS configuration starting at $199 ($50 off) at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart, matching its best price to date. Apple’s newest entry-level smartwatch remains our top recommendation for anyone who wants a basic fitness tracker, as it offers all the essentials alongside an always-on display and Apple’s S10 chip, which enables on-device Siri requests.
Apple AirTag (second-gen)
Apple’s latest AirTags feature an upgraded ultra-wideband chip for more precise location tracking, a noticeably louder speaker, and an expanded Bluetooth range. Read our review.
Baseus AM52 power bank (with built-in cable)
The Baseus PicoGo AM52 is a 10,000mAh magnetic power bank that supports fast 25W Qi2.2 wireless charging and up to 45W wired charging via its built-in USB-C cable. It was one of the fastest wireless chargers we tested, bringing an iPhone 17 Pro Max to 65 percent in an hour. Read our guide to the best Qi2 batteries.
- You can buy the last-gen iPad Mini with 128GB of storage and Wi-Fi on Amazon in select colors for $484 ($115 off), which is the best price we’ve seen since Apple’s recent price hikes. It has a smaller screen and a slower chip than the newer model, and it lacks an OLED screen, the Acoustic Display, and water resistance. Still, it’s a great option for reading and everyday use that’s currently more affordable than its $699 successor, with support for Apple Intelligence and the Apple Pencil Pro. Read our review.
Sharge Icemag 3 Power Bank
The Icemag 3 can wirelessly deliver up to 25W of power to compatible smartphones and up to 35W wired charging via USB-C. The 10,000mAh Qi2 charger can also act as a foldable kickstand, comes with an integrated USB-C cable that serves as a lanyard, and sports a transparent design with colorful RGB lighting.
Apple Studio Display (2026)
Designed to pair with a Mac, the latest Apple Studio Display features a sharp 5K Retina display, a great 12-megapixel Center Stage camera that keeps you in frame during video calls, and a good six-speaker sound system with spatial audio. Sadly, it only offers two Thunderbolt 5 ports in addition to a pair of USB-C ports. Read our review.
- Apple’s latest Magic Mouse is matching its all-time low of $59.99 ($20 off) at Amazon. The wireless mouse features a touch-sensitive surface that lets you scroll through documents and swipe between apps with simple gestures; it also pairs automatically with compatible Macs and offers support for USB-C.

articles.title: White House Replaces Cyber Director After Tech Outages
articles.body:
White House Replaces Cyber Director After Tech Outages (axios.com) 75
			
		 	
				President Trump has named Pentagon Chief Information Officer Kirsten A. Davies as his new national cyber director, replacing Sean Cairncross amid a broader shakeup of the administration's cybersecurity and AI leadership. According to Axios, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller pushed for Cairncross' removal over concerns about his technical qualifications. From the report:  "Kirsten has the credentials to excel in this position and has already been Senate-confirmed," an administration official said. At the Pentagon, Davies has been the top adviser to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth "on all matters relating to information management, information technology, cybersecurity, and information assurance," according to her bio.
Before serving in the Trump administration, Davies worked for Unilever and "led global cyber resilience for one of the world's largest consumer goods enterprises," her bio says. Davies' career also has included technology and cyber roles at Estee Lauder, Barclays-Africa Group, Hewlett Packard and Siemens. She founded the Institute for Cyber, a nonprofit organization dedicated to citizen safety and security in the digital universe.  Trump is also filling other key cyber positions, notes Axios. "His pick for the top job at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which helps defend federal civilian networks and critical infrastructure, Palantir executive Michael LoSapio, faced a combative confirmation hearing Thursday."

articles.title: Nvidia accounting under SEC investigation, sources say
articles.body:
Nvidia's worst week on record just got worse. Now the government is asking questions about its books.
Nvidia (NVDA) stock fell 14% Friday, its worst day since the DeepSeek rout in January 2025 and its seventh straight loss, before bouncing nearly 4% in after-hours trading. The drop came as Reuters reported that the Securities and Exchange Commission's probe of the chipmaker is examining potential accounting issues.
The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the probe includes an examination of whether Nvidia's disclosures misled investors. Nvidia didn't respond to Bloomberg's request for comment on that report, and the SEC declined to comment.
The selling set records. Nvidia shed about $490 billion in market value Friday and nearly $900 billion this week, as its stock had its worst week since October 2008. That tops the $573 billion it lost last week, previously the biggest one-week drop for any company on record, according to Dow Jones Market Data.
Since its Oct. 6 record, Nvidia has lost about $2.7 trillion in market value, more than the $2.5 trillion that The Kobeissi Letter called the biggest 45-day loss for any stock in history. The world's most valuable company six weeks ago now ranks fourth in the US, behind Apple (AAPL), Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL).
Nvidia's latest quarterly report raised a few questions. The company said its 10-Q, the detailed quarterly filing, would come "in the coming weeks" instead of the same evening as usual, and the release mentioned an ongoing investigation by an independent board committee.
Nvidia booked about $104 billion of revenue through its Singapore unit in 2025, roughly half its sales, the Financial Times reported. The Journal said the disclosure questions include Singapore-based Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer US officials suspect of rerouting its chips to China.
Nvidia's customers are also taking longer to pay, with bills outstanding at 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. It's not clear which of these, if any, the SEC is focused on.
Washington wants answers fast. "I think we need answers in the next 10 days from the board and from the outside counsel," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday, after Jensen Huang's exit as CEO. President Trump said Friday he "would love to see Jensen be given a second chance," while criticizing the chipmaker's new leadership.
California is digging in too. Attorney General Rob Bonta subpoenaed Nvidia Thursday, investigating whether its advanced chips reached China and whether the company misled investors. "Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said.
