articles.title: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
articles.body:
Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.
GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.
Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.
In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.
Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.
“We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.
In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.
Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.
Apple did not respond to a request for comment.
India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

articles.title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
articles.body:
President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.
Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.
“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”
Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”
Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.
Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:
Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.
We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.
So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

articles.title: California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China
articles.body:
California Issues Subpoena to Nvidia Over Chip Sales to China 27
			
		 	
				California Attorney General Rob Bonta has issued subpoenas to Nvidia and former CEO Jensen Huang regarding reports that they misled investors about advanced AI chips potentially reaching China. "The conduct of Nvidia and its former CEO raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors," Bonta said in a press release. "My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information -- and if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law." The probe follows Huang's resignation amid allegations involving a suspected Chinese spy and comes as the SEC reportedly conducts a similar investigation. The Hill reports:  Bonta's office said the information obtained through the subpoenas will help it to determine if Nvidia, which is based in Santa Clara, Calif., violated state law through its alleged actions. "Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta continued.
[...] Following the Huang scandal, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents Thursday showing the U.S. authorized the sale of nearly 900,000 Nvidia and AMD AI chips to Defense Department-designated Chinese military companies. An Nvidia spokesperson previously told The Hill, "The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes." "Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," the spokesperson added.

articles.title: Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space
articles.body:
Mercury-Bound X-Ray Telescope Delivers First Images After Eight Years In Space (phys.org) 4
			
		 	
				A British-built X-ray telescope aboard the European-Japanese BepiColombo spacecraft has captured its first astronomical images after eight years in space and roughly 6.2 billion miles of travel. Phys.org reports:  A team led by the University of Leicester has been making calibration measurements with the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS), one of the instruments on the two-spacecraft BepiColombo mission to Mercury, which begins its orbital insertion tomorrow (Nov. 21) in preparation for the final stage of arrival at our solar system's smallest planet. After an eight-year journey, it is vital that the team checks how MIXS is performing. Although they have been monitoring the instrument during its trip, it was only in September, following the separation of the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) from the joined science orbiters, Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO) or Mio, that MIXS could finally see into space for the first time and calibration measurements could be made before the orbit insertion sequence begins.
The Crab Nebula is 6,500 light-years away and a well-characterized astrophysical source of X-ray light. By observing it, the team can work out the performance characteristics of MIXS in space and compare these with calibration measurements made with the same instrument in the laboratory in 2015. These observations provide MIXS's first view of an astronomical X-ray source. The main observation sequence consisted of 55 spacecraft slews, with 39 hours of observations during Sept. 11-12. Measuring how much the Crab Nebula's image is spread across MIXS's detector helps the scientists measure MIXS's angular resolution, or how sharply it will be able to distinguish features on Mercury's surface. They found this to be slightly better than when it was last measured in the lab in 2015. 
"During our calibration observations we have determined that MIXS is generally performing fantastically well in space! We have no effects in our images that are associated with 'stray light' (optical photons getting in when they should not). We continue to see effects of galactic cosmic rays as we did during cruise, but we understand these and can filter them out," said Professor Emma Bunch, Principal Investigator (PI) for the MIXS instrument and Director of the Institute for Space at the University of Leicester.
"We see some self-fluorescence which appears when the sun is illuminating the optic, but this won't affect our dayside observations of Mercury's surface. And the detector has suffered no radiation damage after eight years in space. We see some effects in the instrument that we are still studying and expect to undertake some optimization procedures during the Mercury commissioning phase to fine-tune MIXS in preparation for the science phase."

articles.title: Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis
articles.body:
Anthropic Mathematician Claims to Prove Riemann Hypothesis (scientificamerican.com) 49
			
		 	
				Slashdot has been covering the Riemann Hypothesis for years.
2000: Prove The Riemann Hypothesis And Make.Money.Fast 
2002: More on Riemann Hypothesis 
2008: Claimed Proof of Riemann Hypothesis 
2008: Prominent Mathematicians Rebuke Recent Riemann Hypothesis Proof 
Add a new headline to the list...
2026:  Using AI, mathematician claims to have solved one of math's great mysteries 
joshuark shares a report from Scientific American: Levent Alpoge, a mathematician at Anthropic, has claimed to have solved the Riemann Hypothesis with the help of Anthropic's AI model Claude, but the proof is not yet independently verified and remains under scrutiny. [An AI-generated solution of the 167-year-old problem, long considered far out of reach to human mathematicians, would cap off the technology's year-long conquest of math in spectacular fashion.] The Riemann hypothesis was first proposed in 1859 by the mathematician Bernhard Riemann. It claims that the locations of the prime numbers along the number line, which appear random at first blush, are actually determined by an intricate, meaningful order.
[...] Alpoge posted his Claude proof coded in the programming language Lean, which verifies the mathematical correctness of each argument. Issues can arise in Lean, but it shouldn't take long for experts to verify whether the hypothesis is properly coded, and if the proof is correct. If that happens, it will cap off a year in which AI's mathematical capabilities ascended from unreliable college student to a superhuman force, leaving no part of the discipline undisrupted. [...]  Alpoge's statement is elegiac -- recognizing the sense of grief many mathematicians are feeling -- but also optimistic. "It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light," he wrote, "but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater." [...]
The Riemann result, if correct, will echo far beyond mathematics. It doesn't have any immediate real-world applications -- it won't upend global banking or make the internet run faster. But after a year of watching LLMs surpass one math benchmark after another, there is no more staggering achievement it could possibly reach. A machine may have just solved a problem that the smartest people on the planet all agreed they were nowhere close to figuring out. As MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland once put it to me: "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."
"If the proof is correct and understood, this completes a dictionary between different branches of math where the connections were only partial," says Hector Pasten, a mathematician at the Pontifical Catholic University of Chile. "Something like a Rosetta Stone."
"If true, even from a first high level scan of the summary of the proposed argument, it is very plausible to me that the new ideas in the proof will open up brand new avenues of thinking in number theory and have an immense impact beside the obviously extremely influential result in itself," added mathematician Carlo Pagano, a professor at Concordia University and a visiting researcher at Google DeepMind.
In a separate article from Scientific American, independent mathematicians say the AI-assisted proof is almost certainly valid. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland said the chance of anything being wrong was "approximately zero" after independently compiling and checking the code. However, researchers are still conducting final checks to ensure the proof accurately represents the original hypothesis and does not exploit any loopholes in Lean's verification system.
But did a human beat the AI?  The Washington Post reports:
Just hours after AlpÃgeâ(TM)s claim circulated on social media, Ravi Vakil, president of the American Mathematical Society and a professor at Stanford University, said in a hurried statement that mathematician Alessandro Masullo had a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis without AI several months earlier. The draft, which runs some 940 pages, is in need of significant revisions, Masullo said in a statement, and was not ready for publication. Online observers quickly noted that it contained omissions and apparent errors.
But in the introduction to the draft, he published a striking flag.
âoeIf any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this,â he wrote. âoeWe are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.â

articles.title: Anthropic Shares Tank After Huge IPO As the Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gains
articles.body:
Anthropic Shares Tank After Huge IPO As the Nasdaq Erases 2026 Gains 33
			
		 	
				U.S. stocks extended their sell-off Friday as Anthropic shares plunged more than 11% on their second day of trading, despite the AI company's record-setting IPO a day earlier. The Nasdaq fell more than 3%, wiping out its gains for 2026, while the S&P 500 dropped nearly 2% and joined the Dow in correction territory, down at least 10% from recent highs. articles.title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
articles.body:
YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg. Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.
YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
The potential settlement would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, Bloomberg reports.
The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court. The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California, judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.
Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge’s request for comment.
In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction.

articles.title: Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
articles.body:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.
Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.
Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website, Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday.
The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.
A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:
I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August, but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”
Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules, a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”
In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture, a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.
OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.
OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.
Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

articles.title: My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
articles.body:
My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%
Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!
My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.
I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.
But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦
The setup#
- MacBook Pro M3 Pro
- 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable
- UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display
- UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post
What I thought was interesting#
Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.
I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.
So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.
The driver and flow control#
The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.
Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…
I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.
But the upload was always fine#
Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!
Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:
So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.
Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!
When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.
Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.
As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.
Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.
OK, well, what now?#
I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.
The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…
So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!
With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:
Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:
$ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])"
# old adapter (RTL8156B)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3
# new adapter (RTL8157)
packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7
# bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8
I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.
Final thoughts#
I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?
See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

articles.title: The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
articles.body:
The stochastic parrots have apparently proved the Riemann Hypothesis
“… it is very probable that all roots are real. Of course one would wish for a rigorous proof here; I have for the time being, after some fleeting vain attempts, provisionally put aside the search for this, as it appears dispensable for the immediate objective of my investigation.” –Bernhard Riemann, 1859
[Update: According to “Poe’s Law,” there is no irony or sarcasm on the Internet so obvious that it won’t fly over countless people’s heads. In line with that, lots of people on social media are now saying variants of “how dare Scott Aaronson call LLMs ‘stochastic parrots,’ that demeaning and trivializing term from 2021? Doesn’t he understand that these so-called ‘stochastic parrots’ just proved the Riemann Hypothesis?” ROFL.]
I’m in California to visit Oratomic and then Inkhaven. I woke up this morning to the news that Levent Alpöge says that he’s gotten Anthropic models to prove the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, producing 17.4 million (!!) lines of Lean code.
At a dinner last night, someone asked me “so, how much longer until an AI proves the Riemann Hypothesis? Still several more years?” I replied, don’t be sure of such things anymore. After all, AI has already proved that the nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function are at most 3/8 away from the critical line (Quanta just published its article on that breakthrough yesterday!), and that already carries most of the implications for number theory that a full proof of RH would have. So who the hell knows what else is possible, and how quickly?
For those tuning in from home, the Riemann Hypothesis says (in its easiest-to-understand version) that the number of prime numbers from 1 to n is very close to what it would be if each integer x>1 had an independent 1/ln(x) probability of being prime, up to a standard statistical error term that never exceeds Õ(√n). While we’ve known since 1896 that the number of primes from 1 to n is asymptotic to n/ln(n) (that’s the famous Prime Number Theorem), you could’ve imagined the deviations being much larger.
David Hilbert famously said, “If I were to awaken after having slept for a thousand years, my first question would be: Has the Riemann Hypothesis been proven?” Meanwhile G. H. Hardy, on a ship that he feared might sink, sent his colleagues a telegram claiming to have proven RH, so that if the worst came to pass, at least the world might believe that a proof sank with him.
Many will of course question whether the proof announced today will stand. They’ll point out that, despite how heavily the world is now “lean-ing” on it, the Lean formal verification system still has issues, from kernel bugs (which have, in the past, allowed proofs of 0=1) to uncertain soundness of the underlying type theory. In my view, these issues can and should urgently be fixed! Until they are, a sufficiently motivated AI could almost certainly exploit them to prove a false statement!
All the same, I see zero indications that that’s happening right now. I note that, so far, not one of the AI results with Lean certificates has needed to be retracted (while several without Lean certificates have needed to be). So I’m not 100% sure, but my bet is that the proof will stand.
Mathematicians of course won’t be satisfied with 17 million lines of Lean. They’ll be satisfied when, and only when, they’re able to explain and distill and reconstruct the ideas for themselves. And that will probably take years, since human mathematicians move only at biological speeds. And while they’re working on it, how many more such wonders will there be, in this age of wonders and terrors?
My 9-year-old son, informed that RH was proved, replied that he’s not even surprised at this point. Maybe you need to have come of age in the human math era to be surprised by such things.
The P=?NP problem now moves firmly into place as the Final Boss of the Math We’ve Cared About, the position I always thought it should occupy. But for how much longer? For how much longer will anything last that we currently take for granted?
It was only a couple days ago that my wife and I had the following conversation:
Dana: I turned off the irrigation, yet somehow water in our house is still leaking. We need to…
Me: Look, a lot of the smartest people I know now think that recursive self-improvement and the end of the entire known world are coming in 12-18 months. This leak…
Dana: We should still fix the leak.

articles.title: Astra 6.2 and Sol 6.2 flop at Simple Bench
articles.body:
We introduce SimpleBench, a multiple-choice text benchmark for LLMs where individuals
                            with
                            unspecialized (high school) knowledge outperform SOTA models. SimpleBench includes over 200
                            questions covering spatio-temporal reasoning, social intelligence, and what we call
                            linguistic adversarial robustness (or trick questions). For the vast majority of text-based
                            benchmarks LLMs outperform a non-specialized human, and increasingly, exceed expert human
                            performance. However, on SimpleBench, a non-specialized human baseline is 83.7%, based on
                            our small sample of nine participants, outperforming every tested LLM, including
                            today's top model, Claude Fable, which scored 81.9%. While we expect model performance to improve over time, the
                            results of SimpleBench confirm that the memorized knowledge, and approximate reasoning
                            retrieval, utilized by frontier LLMs is not always enough to answer basic questions just
                            yet. 
For a deeper dive into our results and our methods, check out the full technical report here.
Use all of these models on the Simple Bench app - LMcouncil.ai

articles.title: Twice Baked Potatoes
articles.body:
I thought I loved loaded baked potatoes until I tried Twice Baked Potatoes. Two words…Next Level! Who knew a deconstructed loaded baked potato, mixed perfectly with all your favorite toppings, then restuffed into crispy potato skins, would taste so good? Yes, it’s an extra step, but it’s sooo worth it! Beth and I made these potatoes three times, and each time we debated on who would get to take the leftovers home. Listen, I’m just saying if you’ve ever been hesitant on whether the extra step to make “twice” baked potatoes was worth it…trust us, it’s worth it!! And at just $0.70 per potato half, I’ll happily make a whole tray any day!
All recipes are rigorously tested in our Nashville Test Kitchen to ensure they are easy, affordable, and delicious.
“This was my first time making twice baked potatoes and they turned out great! I don’t cook very often but this recipe was easy to follow, and as a bonus, there weren’t many dishes to clean.”
mark
All the Good Stuff Goes Inside
Unlike regular baked potatoes, twice baked potatoes are indeed baked twice in the oven. They’re first baked whole until the insides are fluffy and tender. The creamy potato flesh is then scooped out and mixed with all your favorite mix-ins like butter, sour cream, bacon, and cheese. (But hey, no pressure. Feel free to use whatever toppings you have on hand. You can also switch things up and use one of the combinations listed in our traditional baked potatoes blog post!)
Now comes my favorite part. I pile the filling back into the skins and save some cheddar for the top, so there’s cheese stirred into the mash and a melty layer over it. Picture a loaded baked potato, except each bite has the perfect amount of toppings. It’s actually genius and I’m kinda upset that I wasn’t making these years ago! Make sure to also try our twice baked potato casserole next if you love this flavor combo!
Recipe Success Tips
- Russet potatoes are the best choice. After making this recipe three times, I’m sticking with russets! Their thick skins make sturdy shells that hold up to the second bake, even when they’re piled high with filling. The starchy insides also bake up fluffy and mash easily with the butter and sour cream. I recommend choosing potatoes that are a similar size so they finish baking at about the same time.
- Oil and season the skins before baking. I use my hands or a brush to spread a thin layer of olive oil over each dry potato, then finish with a little salt. Getting oil on the whole potato before the first bake is my secret to crispy twice baked potatoes!
- Check the center and leave a little potato behind. The first bake is done when a fork slides easily into the center of the largest potato. Once the potatoes are cool enough to handle, slice each one in half, and start scooping from the middle with a spoon and work toward the edges. Leave about ¼ inch of potato along the sides and bottom so the shells stay sturdy when you fill them.
- Mash just until fluffy. I find the potato flesh is easiest to mash while it’s still warm. Stop once the filling looks light and fluffy, especially if you’re using a hand mixer. Too much mixing can make the potatoes gummy.
Variations to Try!
I went with a classic bacon and cheddar filling for these potatoes, but you can play around with what you’ve got. A little leftover meat, a handful of veggies, or the last of a block of cheese can all save you a trip to the store!
- Make it spicy: Stir a spoonful of Buffalo sauce into the filling, then taste before adding more. If you’re serving kids who hate spice, I’d set some filling aside before adding the sauce. That way, you get a few halves with a little heat and tang, and the rest stay mild.
- Swap the bacon for another protein: Fold leftover cooked shredded chicken into the mash where you’d normally add the bacon. Diced baked ham or cooked chorizo would work here, too. Chop any long strands or larger pieces so the meat mixes evenly through the filling and is easy to scoop into the shells.
- Add some greens: Wilt a handful of fresh spinach in a skillet, then squeeze out any excess liquid, chop it, and fold it into the filling. Frozen spinach works, too. I’d thaw it first and squeeze it well so it doesn’t water down the mash. If you’ve got broccoli to use up, steam a few florets until tender, drain them well, and chop them small before stirring them in (similar to our broccoli cheddar stuffed baked potatoes).
- Change up the cheese: Use whatever cheddar you already have in your fridge! Mild cheddar keeps the flavor mellow, medium gives you a little more cheesy flavor, and sharp cheddar really stands out alongside the smoky bacon. Other good melting cheeses work here, too. Monterey Jack is mild and creamy, mozzarella gives you a stretchy topping, and pepper jack adds a little heat.
How to Make Twice Baked Potatoes Step-by-Step Photos
Gather all of your ingredients: Preheat the oven to 400°F (200°C or 180°C fan) so it can come up to temperature while you prep the potatoes. Line a sheet pan with parchment paper.
Prick the potatoes: Wash and dry 4 russet potatoes well (if they aren’t dry, they won’t crisp up!) Prick each one several times with a fork so steam can escape as the potatoes bake.
Brush with olive oil: Set the potatoes on the lined sheet pan and drizzle them with 1 Tbsp olive oil. Use a silicone brush or your hands to spread the oil all the way around each potato. An even coat helps the skins crisp up extra good.
Season and bake: Now evenly sprinkle ½ tsp salt over the potatoes, turning them as you go so the skins are seasoned all over. Bake for 50-60 minutes, depending on their size.
Cook the bacon until crisp: While the potatoes are in the oven, chop 4 oz. bacon and cook it in a skillet over medium heat for about 10-15 minutes. Once the pieces are browned and crisp at the edges, transfer them to a paper towel-lined plate to soak up the excess grease.
Test the largest potato: After about 50 minutes, push a fork toward the center of the biggest potato. It should slide in easily. If the middle still feels firm, give the potatoes a little longer in the oven.
Scoop out the potato flesh: Once the potatoes are cool enough to handle, slice them in half lengthwise and use a spoon to scoop out the flesh. If they’re still a little warm, I like to hold each half steady with a clean kitchen towel as I scoop. Leave about a ¼-inch rim of potato around the edges so the skins hold their shape when you fill them.
Add the butter, dairy, and seasonings: Transfer the warm potato flesh to a large bowl with 4 Tbsp butter, ½ cup sour cream, and ¼ cup milk. Add the remaining ½ tsp salt and ¼ tsp freshly cracked black pepper. The warmth from the potatoes helps the butter melt into the mash.
Mash just until fluffy: Use a potato masher or hand mixer to break up the larger lumps. Stop once the mash looks light and fluffy, since too much mixing can make it gummy.
Slice the green onions: Thinly slice 3 green onions so they’re easy to scatter through the filling and over the tops. Set half aside for serving.
Make the filling: Add the cooked bacon, ½ cup shredded cheddar, and half the sliced green onions to the mash. Fold gently with a spoon or spatula until you can see little bits of bacon and green onion throughout.
Fill the potato skins: Spoon about ⅓ cup of filling into each half. It’s okay if the mash is mounded a little above the rim. I spoon it in fairly loosely to keep the filling fluffy.
Top with cheddar: Finally, divide the remaining ¾ cup shredded cheddar among the eight halves, scattering it from end to end so each one gets an even layer of cheese.
Bake the potatoes again: Return the filled potatoes to the 400°F oven for about 20 minutes. Start checking after about 10 minutes, since ovens vary. Look for the shreds to melt together across the top and use a thermometer to check that the center of the filling has reached 165°F.
Finish with green onions: Scatter the reserved green onions over the hot potatoes just before serving. They add a little fresh crunch to the soft and cheesy filling. Serve and enjoy!
What to Serve with Twice Baked Potatoes
I love bringing a tray of twice baked potatoes to a tailgate or potluck because everyone can grab a half. Four potatoes make eight side servings in this recipe, so it’s easy to figure out how many you’ll need. Hosting Christmas or Thanksgiving? You can stuff the potatoes the day before and save the second bake for just before dinner. I’d slide them into the oven as soon as the Thanksgiving turkey comes out to rest.
For a filling family dinner on a budget, I like to pair these with oven roasted chicken legs because the lemon pepper seasoning is so, so good with the cheesy potatoes. Smothered pork chops are another option I love because the chops and onion gravy cook in one skillet while the potatoes finish in the oven. You can make dinner out of the potatoes themselves, too. I serve two halves per person with a crisp simple side salad and a tangy vinaigrette to cut through the richness.
Storage & Reheating
Store leftover twice baked potatoes in an airtight container in the fridge for 3-4 days. Refrigerate them within 2 hours of cooking to keep things food safe!
Make Ahead
You can bake the potatoes, make the filling, and stuff the skins up to 24 hours ahead. Keep the stuffed potatoes in an airtight container in the fridge until you’re ready for the second bake. I like to take them out while the oven preheats to take the chill off. They may need a few extra minutes in the oven to heat through.
Freezing
- Freeze before the second bake: Assemble the potatoes and top them with cheddar, then freeze them on a sheet pan until firm, about 2 hours. Wrap each frozen half in foil and transfer it to a freezer-safe airtight container or bag. Use within 2-3 months and follow either oven method below to finish baking them.
- Freeze fully baked leftovers: Once they’ve cooled completely, place them in a freezer-safe bag. You can also wrap each half in foil before bagging it if you want to pull out one at a time (as shown below). Freeze for about 3 months.
Reheating
- From the fridge: Warm fully baked leftovers in a 350°F oven or in the microwave until the center reaches 165°F.
- Straight from the freezer: Preheat the oven to 375°F and loosely wrap each potato half in foil to keep it from drying out and protect the cheese from overbrowning. Bake for 20-25 minutes with the foil on, then unwrap and bake for another 20-25 minutes, until the cheese is melted and the center reaches 165°F.
- Thaw in the fridge first: Thaw the potatoes overnight, then bake them on a parchment-lined baking sheet at 350°F for 20-25 minutes, until the tops are golden and the centers reach 165°F.
- Microwave fully baked leftovers: Remove any foil, place a potato half on a microwave-safe plate, and cover it with a slightly damp paper towel. Microwave on high for about 4-5 minutes from frozen or 2-3 minutes if thawed. Check as you go and heat in 30-second to 1-minute intervals as needed until the center reaches 165°F. If you’d like to crisp up the skin, finish it in a toaster oven or regular oven.
Love Loaded Potatoes? Try These Recipes Next:
- On a cold night, all I want is a bowl of Loaded Potato Soup with tangy sour cream and plenty of crispy bacon and cheddar on top.
- These Loaded Smashed Potatoes have golden, crispy edges seasoned with everything bagel seasoning, plus melted cheddar and a dollop of cool sour cream.
- When I want to make loaded potatoes for a crowd, I’ll serve this Twice Baked Potato Casserole so everyone can scoop up some creamy mash with melted cheddar and crispy bacon themselves!
- Tuck leftover turkey and stuffing into crispy Thanksgiving Potato Skins with melted cheese and a spoonful of sweet-tart cranberry sauce on top.
More Russet Potato Recipes
Our Twice Baked Potatoes recipe was originally published 10/2/23. It was retested, reworked, and republished to be better than ever 11/21/26.

articles.title: GrapheneOS claims Google is now waging war against it, could lock Pixel bootload
articles.body:
Affiliate links on Android Authority may earn us a commission. Learn more.
GrapheneOS claims Google is now waging war against it, could lock Pixel bootloader
Nov 20, 2026 — 2:25 AM ET
- The GrapheneOS team has claimed that Google was trying to harm the project and wipe it out.
- Google was allegedly contacting Android OEMs to ask whether they were working with GrapheneOS, and was purportedly threatening these brands.
- The team also suggested that Google could start locking the bootloader on Pixels and taking other actions to make Android forks unviable.
GrapheneOS is the leading Android fork if you want a secure and private smartphone experience. Pixels were the only officially supported platform, but the team is also working with Motorola to launch a Motorola Signature 27 phone with GrapheneOS. However, the developers of this software have now made some interesting claims against Google.
The GrapheneOS team claimed on X that Google was contacting Android OEMs to ask whether them whether they were working with the GrapheneOS project. Furthermore, the team asserts that Google was threatening these brands by citing Google Mobile Services licensing terms.
The group also suggested that Google might eventually institute a variety of measures to thwart GrapheneOS and other Android forks:
We expect Google will begin bootloader locking Pixels, continue heavily pushing the illegal Play Integrity API and trying to make forks of AOSP non-viable. Many of their actions are clear violation of US criminal law. US antitrust law even includes prison time for individuals.
GrapheneOS leadership even said they wanted to talk to US attorney-general Todd Blanche and others in a bid to stop “Google’s escalating anti-competitive behavior.” In saying so, the team also praised Google’s engineers for directly working with the project.
“There are a lot of engineers at Google who support what we’re building and have directly worked with us,” it explained. “People there have repeatedly helped us and even explicitly added support for GrapheneOS to Google software including supporting Vanadium for Play services FIDO2 and passkeys.”
Unfortunately, the team says Google’s business division was the problem rather than its engineers:
Google’s business side is actively trying to wipe out alternatives. Google Mobile Services licensing has many illegal terms aimed at preventing competition. That isn’t enough for them. They’re very directly trying to harm GrapheneOS in multiple ways and outright wipe it out.
Either way, you won’t need to buy a Pixel phone if you’d like to use GrapheneOS. The project formed a partnership with Motorola last year, and the Signature 27 will be available as a GrapheneOS variant. Nevertheless, it would be very concerning if Google were pressuring OEMs to stop working with GrapheneOS. This apparent pressure would also come years after Google lost court battles over its agreements with OEMs. These previous agreements included terms restricting manufacturers when it came to shipping devices with Android forks.
We’ve contacted Google and Motorola for comment regarding these GrapheneOS claims. We’ll update our article as soon as the companies issue a response to us.

articles.title: Lean Verification of the Riemann Hypothesis - Joint statement by...
articles.body:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.
On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.
We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.
Our rationale is outlined below.
The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.
- The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory.
- Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures.
- 
The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis.
- 
The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.
Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.
We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

articles.title: RCE in Gnupg
articles.body:
[Announce] GnuPG Security Advisory for GPGME (T8557,CVE-2026-129975)
Werner Koch 
    wk at gnupg.org
       
Fri Nov 20 19:01:51 CET 2026
    
    
Hello!
We are pleased to announce the availability of a new GPGME release:
version 2.3.1.  This version fixes a *critical security bug* found in
all prior versions.  We also release a new Gpg4win versions and and
GnuPG Desktop and GnuPG VS-Desktop versions which all make use of GPGME.
Description
===========
By using an OpenPGP key containing a crafted very long user id it is
possible to trigger a double free.  This double free can be used
exfiltrate data from applications by sending for example signed data.
Exploiting this bug to mount an Remote Code Execution attack (RCE) can't
be ruled out.  Thus an immediate update is highly suggested.
Our internal ID is T8557 (https://static.dev.gnupg.org/T8557)
The CVE-id is CVE-2026-129975.
This vulnerability was discovered by Johan Carlsson and we were informed
by GitLab on 2026-11-12.  Initially we set 2026-11-25 for a coordinated
disclosure; due to the new Ruby2Shell bug GitLab had to update earlier
and thus we also disclosed the GPGME bug on 2026-11-20.
The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the
status lines and key listings from gpg.  Initially a buffer of 1024
bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required.  When
reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but
it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the
function.  Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or
other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to
the freed memory.  Eventually the context is released and the memory
freed a second time.  Due to other allocations in between the common
double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered.
Impact
======
All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared
libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected.  Examples of software
using GPGME are
 - Gpg4win
 - GnuPG Desktop
 - GnuPG VS-Desktop
 - Most mail clients
 - Many XMPP clients
 - Samba
 - Flatpack
Solution
========
Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1.  If you need a
DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version.
For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME
2.3.1.
If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME
version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to
very old versions.
There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.
Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19)
================================================
         [compared to version 2.2.0]
 * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM.
   Add mappings for algos used bei backends.   [rMa85fa49236]
 * Fix a double free in the status line read code.
   [T8557,CVE-2026-129975]
 * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release:
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 GPGME_PK_DLTHM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLKEM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLDSA                NEW.
 Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427
Getting the Software
====================
Please follow the instructions found at <https://gnupg.org/download/> or
read on:
The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature
are available here:
 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k)
 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig
A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is
attached.   Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.
Debian Packages
===============
We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants.
See https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/ or use the menu to switch
to other distros/releases.
Windows Installer
=================
A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer,
including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF
reader has also been released.  Head over to https://gpg4win.org/
Checking the Integrity
======================
See https://gnupg.org/download/integrity_check.html
The checksum for gpgme is:
1134a407b50204ee6fb9efaa6e1451c2460e543e  gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2
*Thank you all*
   Your GnuPG hackers
p.s.
This is an announcement only mailing list.  Please send replies only to
the gnupg-users at gnupg.org mailing list.
* List of Release Signing Keys:
  To guarantee that a downloaded version has not been tampered by
  malicious entities we provide signature files for all tarballs and
  binary versions.  The keys are also signed by the long term keys of
  their respective owners.  Current releases are signed by one or more
  of these five keys:
    ed25519 2020-08-24 [SC] [expires: 2030-06-30]
    6DAA 6E64 A76D 2840 571B  4902 5288 97B8 2640 3ADA
    Werner Koch (dist signing 2020)
    ed25519 2021-05-19 [SC] [expires: 2027-04-04]
    AC8E 115B F73E 2D8D 47FA  9908 E98E 9B2D 19C6 C8BD
    Niibe Yutaka (GnuPG Release Key)
    rsa3072 2025-05-09 [SC] [expires: 2033-03-03]
    3B76 1AE4 E63B F351 9CE7  D63B ECB6 64CB E133 2EEF
    Alexander Kulbartsch (GnuPG Release Key)
    ed25519 2026-07-20 [SC] [expires: 2036-06-30]
    D02A E491 73BD AD56 E4F8  8223 707E 56D3 DEF4 115C
    Ingo Klöcker (Release Signing Key 2026)
    brainpoolP256r1 2021-10-15 [SC] [expires: 2029-12-31]
    02F3 8DFF 731F F97C B039  A1DA 549E 695E 905B A208
    GnuPG.com (Release Signing Key 2021)
    brainpoolP384r1 2026-02-23 [SC] [expires: 2034-02-23]
    1493 269D E61F 124A A69A  316E 3ADF 34EB DBB2 00A4
    GnuPG.com (Release Signing Key 2026)
  The keys are available at https://gnupg.org/signature_key.html and in
  any recently released GnuPG tarball in the file g10/distsigkey.gpg .
  Note that this mail has been signed by a different key.
* Debian Package Signing Key:
  The new Debian style packages are signed using this key:
    ed25519 2025-07-08 [SC] [expires: 2035-07-14]
    3209 7B71 9B37 45D6 E61D DA1B 85C4 5AE3 E1A2 B355

  See the package website (https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg) for a list
  of supported distributions and a download link for the key.

nothing to hide is no different from saying you don't care about free
speech because you have nothing to say.                - Edward Snowden

The root cause for this bug are two GPGME internal functions to read the
status lines and key listings from gpg.  Initially a buffer of 1024
bytes is allocated which is reallocated if more space is required.  When
reallocating the pointer to the new buffer is used by the function but
it is only assigned back to the context object at the end of the
function.  Thus if the function returns early due to an read error or
other events the context is not updated and keeps the stale pointer to
the freed memory.  Eventually the context is released and the memory
freed a second time.  Due to other allocations in between the common
double free checks of memory allocators may not be triggered.
Impact
======
All software using a GPGME version prior to 2.3.0 either as shared
libary, DLL, or statically linked is affected.  Examples of software
using GPGME are
 - Gpg4win
 - GnuPG Desktop
 - GnuPG VS-Desktop
 - Most mail clients
 - Many XMPP clients
 - Samba
 - Flatpack
Solution
========
Please update your GPGME shared library to version 2.3.1.  If you need a
DLL you may take it from from the updated Gpg4win version.
For statically linked binaries remmeber to build them against GPGME
2.3.1.
If for some reasons GPGME can't be updated, you may patch your GPGME
version using the attached patch which likley applies cleanly even to
very old versions.
There is no need to udpate GPGMEPP or GPGMEQT.
Noteworthy changes in version 2.3.1 (2026-11-19)
================================================
         [compared to version 2.2.0]
 * New constants GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM.
   Add mappings for algos used bei backends.   [rMa85fa49236]
 * Fix a double free in the status line read code.
   [T8557,CVE-2026-129975]
 * Interface changes relative to the 2.2.0 release:
 ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
 GPGME_PK_DLTHM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLKEM                NEW.
 GPGME_PK_MLDSA                NEW.
 Release-info: https://dev.gnupg.org/T8427
Getting the Software
====================
Please follow the instructions found at <https://gnupg.org/download/> or
read on:
The GPGME source code compressed using BZIP2 and its OpenPGP signature
are available here:
 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2 (1393k)
 https://gnupg.org/ftp/gcrypt/gpgme/gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2.sig
A sufficient patch to solve the security bug for older versions is
attached.   Note that version 2.3.0 was never publicly available.
Debian Packages
===============
We also provide Debian style packages for a couple of Debian variants.
See https://repos.gnupg.org/deb/gnupg/trixie/ or use the menu to switch
to other distros/releases.
Windows Installer
=================
A new version of Gpg4win (5.1.2), our full featured Windows installer,
including the fixed version of GPGME, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF
reader has also been released.  Head over to https://gpg4win.org/
Checking the Integrity
======================
See https://gnupg.org/download/integrity_check.html
The checksum for gpgme is:
1134a407b50204ee6fb9efaa6e1451c2460e543e  gpgme-2.3.1.tar.bz2
*Thank you all*
   Your GnuPG hackers

articles.title: ClawDOS – An AI coding agent for DOS
articles.body:
An AI coding agent for DOS. It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. A (real) human’s note: Backstory: The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. Old, meet new. New, meet old: I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent? I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type CLAWDOS at the C:\> prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. HARNESS.EXE is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS. Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API. One message: “Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.” ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running. The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand. ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a WG.EXE under 10 KB. Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor: ▶ Watch the WarGames demo on YouTube Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in C:\MEMORY, finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA. That Run call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB: And this is what Claude made of it: Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do. Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s PLAY language. A chat screen built for the CGA. Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy. Eighteen tools. Claude works on the machine through these: A development kit on the disk. Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in external/. All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one. Memories and skills. Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories: Safe mode. On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks Allow ...? (y/n) first. F3 turns it off. Conversations that last. Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too. Any model, mid-conversation. /model lists the providers in CLAWDOS.CFG and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works. Easy on a slow link. The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on. A flight recorder. CLAWDOS.LOG has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads. api anthropic claude-opus-5-5 round=1 ttft=2750 total=4015 up=165 len=1784 stop=tool_use in=2 out=221 cr=5543 cw=739 th=cont relaunch: program 61.5 s, CLAWDOS away 82.3 s flowchart LR subgraph DOS["IBM PC XT (8088, 640K, CGA)"] direction TB subgraph APP["HARNESS.EXE"] direction TB UI["Chat screen"] LOOP["Agent loop
Messages API requests, SSE and JSON,
history on disk"] TOOLS["Tools
files, search, DOS programs, screenshots,
memory and ports, speaker"] end NET["mTCP + packet driver"] APP <--> NET end TUNNEL["TLS tunnel
copies bytes"] API["Claude Messages API"] NET <-->|"plain HTTP"| TUNNEL TUNNEL <-->|"HTTPS"| API docs/API.md has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back. You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is python. python3 scripts/setup-tools.py # fetch the compilers, FreeDOS, mTCP and the emulators echo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... > .env python3 scripts/build.py # build/CLAWDOS.IMG, a bootable disk python3 tunnel/tunnel.py # the TLS tunnel, on port 8443 python3 scripts/run86box.py # boot an IBM PC XT At the C:\> prompt, type CLAWDOS. No key? python3 tunnel/mockapi.py plays the API offline: type CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023 and send !help. On a real PC: build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443), copy CLAWDOS.IMG to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type CLAWDOS. Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG). /model, /chats, /memories, /new and /quit work from the input box. CLAWDOS -m "..." sends a message from the command line and -c NAME reopens a chat. ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see LICENSE. HARNESS.EXE links mTCP, which is GPLv3. The FreeDOS boot sector in src/boot/freedos is vendored unmodified under its own GPLv2-or-later license (its COPYING). Disk images you build hold other people’s software (FreeDOS, mTCP, and Turbo C from your own floppies): don’t redistribute an image with Turbo C on it. ClawDOS stands on mTCP, FreeDOS, Open Watcom, the PicoMEM, 86Box and DOSBox-X.
