articles.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
articles.body:
I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says:
A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not
worth knowing.
In this post I want to explain why I think Clojure is a terrific language for this task. Whatever your background, it's almost guaranteed to affect the way you think about programming. It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.
It's a Lisp!
First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:
- Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic.
- It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so.
- It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions.
- It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some real macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in core.async.
- It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal.
Importantly, Clojure is a very modern Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.
I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. Having learned some Lisp, I had the insight of generating and evaluating new Perl code on the fly, which turned out to be key to the success of that program. I'm confident I could not have come up with that solution back then without being aware of the "Lisp way".
Pragmatism and hard-won experience
The designers of Clojure are extremely pragmatic, building upon decades of industry experience. I strongly recommend watching some YouTube videos of talks by leading Clojure developers. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful:
Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it.
There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from real, hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.
Sequences and laziness for powerful in-language data processing
Applications that process and extract useful bits of information from large datasets all look alike in many programming languages, at least to some extent. What we really want in many cases is SQL-like primitives built into our languages, but this is often challenging (.NET's LINQ is one example of a successful approach).
Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book:
(defn revenue-by-department [carts]
  (->> (filter :settled? carts)
       (mapcat :line-items)
       (map line-summary)
       (group-by :dept)
       (reduce-kv dept-total)))
All the functions used here are built-ins, including the ->> macro. This code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers.
The clojure.spec library provides a degree of type-safety for nested data structures. If you've ever written comments like "this maps strings to lists, where each list element is a map of ...", clojure.spec makes it more formal and verifiable. This is very useful when working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines; the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's there, optionally (core.typed is another option for a more statically typed flavor).
The right approach to object-orientation
Historically, Lisp programmers weren't the biggest proponents of OOP. This doesn't mean that OOP has absolutely no value in Lisp-y languages, however. Common Lisp has had CLOS for decades, and Clojure also comes with an array of OO-like features.
That said, Clojure's flavor of OOP is particularly powerful and tends to discourage bad practices. Clojure uses "protocols", which are a kind of interfaces, and encourages thinking in terms of protocols rather than in terms of classes with inheritance hierarchies, sort of like Go. Add to that an ability to do true multiple dispatch and you have a powerful modeling tool at your fingertips.
Built-in support for concurrency and parallelism
It wouldn't be a real language of the 2000s without powerful support for concurrency and parallelism right at the core. Clojure supports this in many ways, which are interleaved.
First, it's a functional language with persistent data structures. Persistent data structures are effectively immutable, which makes them very attractive in a multi-threaded context. Clojure has a great implementation of persistent data structures even for things like vectors (which are quite challenging to implement in an efficient manner). This is a bigger deal than may originally appear. Pure functions are often great in theory but fail in practice due to too much copying of non-trivial data structures; Clojure's elegant usage of persistent data structures solves this problem, making pure functions efficient and thus much more applicable to a wide array of problems.
Second, Clojure doesn't lock itself in the closet of purism and does support lower-level primitives for concurrency and mutation, where needed. Atoms are built-in mutable state units with atomic updates. Refs and transactions go further, implementing STM.
Third, Clojure comes with a bunch of concurrency tools built in. Promises, futures and threads leverage the underlying JVM's threading utilities.
Finally, Clojure has a pretty good implementation of Go's CSP in the core.async module. It provides two useful things:
- Channels and Go select-like functionality (alts!!) which makes it easy to work with safe concurrent queues and "share data by communicating".
- go-blocks with non-blocking primitives that make it possible to write cooperative "green threads" with ease.
Conclusion - try it
Finally, it's important to mention that Clojure is far from being an academic exercise. It's used in production by several companies, and has strong roots in the massive Java ecosystem. Clojure's interoperability with Java is seamless - Java code can be called from Clojure with no special provisions, and all core Clojure entities are Java objects deep under the hood.
On the client side, Clojurescript has been gaining traction recently as another language-compiled-to-JS option. It brings the elegance of Clojure to client-side programming, among with some unique features like core.async for callback-free concurrency.
This doesn't mean that you should only consider Clojure as a fit for your next project. On the contrary, I recommend learning if even if there's little chance of using it in production any time soon. In fact, this was exactly my situation, Clojure is a great language to expand your programming horizons; who knows, maybe in the future you'll find it useful for some real work. If you do, great! If you don't, learning it will positively affect how you use other programming languages.

articles.body:
I sometimes get asked for recommendations of what programming language to "learn next". It's great that folks appreciate the fact that being exposed to several sufficiently different programming languages is an important step on the path to programming enlightenment. But it's also true that, given limited free time, the choice of which languages to learn is important. As the famous quote by Alan Perlis says:
A language that doesn't affect the way you think about programming, is not
worth knowing.

It's a fairly new language (from 2007) that did a good job of collecting insights and paradigms from many existing languages and organizing them into a coherent whole. It's chock-full of great ideas. In other words, the perfect language to expand your brain.
It's a Lisp!
First and foremost, Clojure belongs to the Lisp family of languages, like Common Lisp, Scheme and Racket. Lisp is one of the oldest and still most important families of programming languages to be familiar with. Being a Lisp in this case means several things:
- Clojure is a dynamic language. No matter where you stand on the static vs. dynamic typing debate, knowing languages in both camps is important. Clojure has a kind of optional typing, but in essence it's dynamic.
- It promotes combinations of built-in data structures (lists, maps, vectors) over objects and has very good reasons for doing so.
- It promotes programming with higher-order functions. Some built-in features like reducers and transducers rely heavily on composing higher order functions for transforming other functions.
- It has uniform syntax with full Lisp-style macro support! This capability has proved to be very elusive for non-Lisp languages, and seeing some real macros in action is enlightening. Clojure has a whole Go-like CSP equivalent implemented using macros in core.async.
- It encourages REPL-based development, where functionality is built and testsed gradually from the bottom up in an interactive terminal.
Importantly, Clojure is a very modern Lisp, with tons of libraries for tasks common in our day and age. It also builds upon important recent research in data structures, such as efficient persistent vectors, that only appeared in the 1990s or later. I've been dabbling with various Lisps for almost 15 years, and Clojure is the first Lisp I'd consider using in production.
I want the stress the importance of full Lisp-style macros once again. Lisp's (and Clojure's) uniform syntax and macros force us to think about the Meta-circular abstraction - there's just no way around it! We have to think of our code as data, and this has profound implications. Back in 2005, when I was still a programming neophyte, I faced a performance challenge for a data-decoding program I was hacking on in Perl. In particular, watch a few of the more popular talks by Rich Hickey - Clojure's original designer. The Alan Perlis quote mentioned above may be his most popular, but there's another I find at least as insightful:
Simplicity does not precede complexity, but follows it.
There's a certain quality in programmers I believe we can all recognize. It can only come from real, hard-won experience of building systems for many years and pondering about how to build such systems more effectively next time. Rich Hickey certainly belongs to this quality category - his talks are very insightful, and this philosophy reigns in the design and implementation of Clojure, as well as its (friendly and vibrant) community.

Clojure combines pervasive sequence protocols with persistent data structures and laziness to make this kind of task natural, using only built-in tools. Here's a realistic example of a function taken from the Clojure Applied book:
(defn revenue-by-department [carts]
  (->> (filter :settled? carts)
       (mapcat :line-items)
       (map line-summary)
       (group-by :dept)
       (reduce-kv dept-total)))
All the functions used here are built-ins, including the ->> macro. This code reads like SQL and it's efficient too. In fact, it can be made somewhat more efficient and even seamlessly parallelized using Reducers and Transducers.
The clojure.spec library provides a degree of type-safety for nested data structures. This is very useful when working with data, and is another example of where Clojure's pragmatism shines; the language is dynamic in its core, but when you need static checking - it's there, optionally (core.typed is another option for a more statically typed flavor).

articles.title: Re: Riemann
articles.body:
A fun thing about living in Australia is that most things happen overnight, so reading the news in the morning is like a gacha game. You pick up the phone and scroll through notifications of world-historic events: elections won, wars begun, models released, conjectures proven or refuted. Today’s pull was a Discord notification saying: “they proved riemann :/”.
This part of the announcement caught my attention (bold mine):
  I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.
It was my secret in my student days that my plans were for this problem in decades, which meant then that I tried to become familiar with all tools that I could possibly recognize in the problem when it was time. Claude and I have had a great time together with such breadth in recent months, but this time Claude far outpaced me near the finish line. No, Claude flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line. I had us on the line of combining two quite different ideas present in a toy setting, one of which was already new and shocking, making very simple one of the shadows of Riemann over which we mathematicians felt most triumph. I guided us to the right situation analogous to that toy setting, and then Claude began to leave me in awe.
Compare the above to Ayn Rand’s account of watching the launch of Apollo 11:
  How do you descend from a state of pure exaltation?
What we had seen, in naked essentials—but in reality, not in a work of art—was the concretized abstraction of man’s greatness.
The meaning of the sight lay in the fact that when those dark red wings of fire flared open, one knew that one was not looking at a normal occurrence, but at a cataclysm which, if unleashed by nature, would have wiped man out of existence—and one knew also that this cataclysm was planned, unleashed, and controlled by man, that this unimaginable power was ruled by his power and, obediently serving his purpose, was making way for a slender, rising craft. One knew that this spectacle was not the product of inanimate nature, like some aurora borealis, or of chance, or of luck, that it was unmistakably human—with “human,” for once, meaning grandeur—that a purpose and a long, sustained, disciplined effort had gone to achieve this series of moments, and that man was succeeding, succeeding, succeeding! For once, if only for seven minutes, the worst among those who saw it had to feel—not “How small is man by the side of the Grand Canyon!”—but “How great is man and how safe is nature when he conquers it!”
Rand’s essay says: how great is Man! How noble in reason, how infinite in faculty! The Riemann announcement reads like a suicide note, or like the farewell message of a terminally-ill person who’s about to undergo euthanasia: “I shall live on in my child, Claude. It is natural to feel this is an end, but as the Buddha taught us, there is no self. Does a wave die when it breaks?” and so on.
There’s a mural by Diego Rivera I love. It’s called Man, Controller of the Universe:
It’s a collage of images of science, technology, history, cells, galaxies, the universe at the nanoscale and the exascale. And at the center there is a man, his hands grasping the controls. He wears a complicated expression: the weight of responsibility for the future, the weight of autonomy.
And I see this mural, and think: how great is Man! Our life is like a breath of air, we were beset by illness and hunger and cold, millions and hundreds of millions died in plagues. And yet we—sick, hungry, short-lived—learned the system of the world, crawled out of the caves, brought nature to heel, walked on the Moon. The last shall be first! And eyes that are clouded with age have seen the furthest stars, and the lives of a cell, and the worlds of Cantor and Hilbert: the invisible world that waited forever. We are dust and ashes, and yet our minds bestride the universe. How great is Man!
And when I read the Riemann announcement, when I read Machines of Loving Grace: humanity is not at the center. Claude is at the center. We are hidden in the margins, passive recipients of manna from Claude. How great is Claude! How noble in reason, how infinite in benevolence! The dancing star, the living word!
It’s a betrayal and a surrender. Man is a bridge, a rusty old bridge that we can neither preserve nor restore. We can move forward and become as the gods, or retreat back into the caves. And the dream of the AI companies, and of most people in AI safety and effective altruism and rationalism; is instead that we should lie down in a warm bath, watch the demons we summoned dance in the sky, and slip away. Why live? Our servants can do that for us. Why should we explore, discover, invent, succeed, become more, struggle, win, become divine? We don’t want to be more. We don’t want anything.

articles.title: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
articles.body:
Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.
Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.
The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.
The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.
Gemini for Home was announced last year, so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

articles.title: Running two PSP emulators on one Switch 2 and sharing one via GameShare
articles.body:
This branch experiments with a separate PPSSPP guest running on the host Switch 2 and streamed to a stock GameShare client. It is not a mirrored controller or a second PSP controller in the host emulator. Compilation and host tests do not establish console operation or acceptable two-game performance.
The working single-instance checkpoint is switch2-single-instance-working
(commit 1c3b38a). Its exact tested NRO, package and matching debug ELF remain
under dist-switch2/checkpoints/switch2-single-instance-working/.
sh Tools/build-switch2-gameshare.sh
python3 Tools/deploy-switch2.py 192.168.1.182 --experimental-gameshare
Open FTPD for the second command. A successful transfer is accepted without a
validation download. The experiment installs as PPSSPP GameShare, at
sdmc:/switch/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare.nro. It leaves
the working ppsspp-switch2 NRO and its settings/saves in place. The normal
Tools/build-switch2.sh selects GameShare OFF. Both builds reuse the build
cache, but packaging rejects mismatched native/experimental modes.
Launch through the same GameShare-capable native title override used for the
Moonlight SDK example. A generic title override is not known to grant the
required GameShare context. If another title locks profile switching, the SDK
uses the Nintendo profile selected for that launch when available. The host
log distinguishes a missing launch profile from a later StreamPlay or
matchmaking error. Choose GameShare (experimental) in the host's
main or pause menu, then join from the client's system GameShare screen.
The client should see its own PPSSPP menu, with a guest-only startup message,
and browse sdmc:/switch/ppsspp-switch2/games. Both browsers can access SD-card
games; no game files are copied into the package.
Choose the same GameShare action to stop sharing. The guest pauses between sessions, retaining its independent emulator state. Exiting the guest's PPSSPP ends that guest instance; restart the application before creating another. Exit the host normally when done. If a real cleanup failure reports retained resources, close the entire hosting title from HOME, rather than returning to hbmenu. The SDK explicitly requires this for uncertain native ownership.
The build links a second PPSSPP frontend/core into a relocatable object and renames every defined core-owned global symbol and ELF COMDAT group signature. Only eight plain-data C entry points are exported. The audit requires distinct Config, memory-base and core-state symbols; the host also compares their runtime addresses before starting. SDK/OS/C++ runtime entry points remain shared. The two emulators have independent core, UI, filesystem state, JIT registries, Vulkan contexts and settings/memory-stick directories. They share one OS process, so a fatal error in either copy can still affect the entire app.
The host keeps its 1920x1080 output and 120 Hz request. The guest uses PPSSPP's existing offscreen Vulkan path at 1280x720 with a 60 fps presentation target. A readback callback transfers completed RGBA frames to a latest-frame mailbox; a dedicated presenter uploads them to a separate native VI2 guest layer. This first route adds CPU readback/swizzle cost; zero-copy is not claimed.
The GameShare SDK is vendored from Moonlight-Switch's research worktree.
Switch/GameShare/sdk-provenance.json records the source revision and file
hashes. Its MIT license and per-file ISC notices are retained. The SDK's pinned
CPU-console uploader is disabled. The guest renderer borrows the statically
linked OunceVK driver's GSV main and worker sessions and uses its registered VM.
It owns the guest image backing, registrations and client. The adapter tracks
the driver's occupied slots at the libounce call boundary and reserves a free
slot for guest range retirement. Each GameShare session reuses the reserved
slot's completion event, which closes with the Vulkan driver's GPU. It does not access
OunceVK's internal structs. Retire the guest images before Vulkan teardown.
Coexistence and reuse on hardware still require qualification.
The SDK owns matchmaking, native hosting, controller reads and the separate VI2 display/layer. Renderer retirement runs before native Finalize; layer closure runs afterwards. Uncertain presentation or release/retirement failure retains backing and blocks ordinary unload. Guest controls never enter the host emulator. Stale/disconnected snapshots become neutral.
Host settings/saves use ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/config/ppsspp; guest
settings/saves use ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/guest/config/ppsspp. The existing
working app's memory stick is not reused. Guest native text-entry applets are
disabled because their routing to the remote screen is not implemented.
PPSSPP sends the guest emulator's PCM to the native per-guest queue and keeps the host emulator on normal AudOut. See the recovered audio contract. The console test confirmed audible client playback in the direct-audio build.
Start GameShare and join from the client. Open the same game on both screens, then enter its local wireless or Ad Hoc mode. Create a lobby on either console and look for it on the other. If the host had already initialized multiplayer before pairing, restart that game once to select the local route.
While GameShare is hosting, PPSSPP runs its built-in discovery service and aemu_postoffice packet relay on IPv4 loopback ports 27314 and 27315. Both cores use the private route automatically with their existing, independently configured PSP MAC addresses. The guest still runs on the host Switch 2, so game packets stay on that console. The route does not use a public relay, Wi-Fi IP address, or UPnP mapping, and it does not change either core's saved network settings. Stopping GameShare closes the listeners. A game already in a lobby may need to leave and re-enter multiplayer after GameShare is restarted.
The user reported a successful Tekken session in the first loopback build.
The subsequent build keeps each core's original MAC address and passed the ten
paired desktop tests. That save-preserving version is tagged
switch2-gameshare-multiplayer-baseline (commit 0699365). Its NRO, ZIP and
debug ELF are in dist-switch2-gameshare/checkpoints/multiplayer-baseline/.
The earlier console run used the temporary-MAC build.
Host boot.log, ppsspp.log, native-exit.bin and native-fault.bin live in
the experimental app directory. The guest writes guest/ppsspp.log. Native
fault/exit records with valid headers are retained as .previous on the next
launch. Preserve diagnostics before relaunching after a failure.
python3 Switch/tests/run.py
python3 Switch/tests/run_gameshare.py
python3 Switch/GameShare/sdk/tests/native/run.py
python3 Switch/GameShare/sdk/tests/guest_input/run.py
python3 Switch/GameShare/sdk/tests/guest_display/run.py
git diff --check
Actual-source sanitizer tests cover native guest-image sector locations, partial creation, successful retirement, retained uncertain presents and release/range timeouts. SDK tests cover native lifecycle/cancellation, controller parsing/freshness and display ownership. They do not simulate the GPU, native title permissions, GameShare radio behavior or console performance. CPU, GPU, threading and shutdown regression risks require console testing; serialized PSP state layouts are unchanged.
The dual-core AArch64 NRO and ZIP built and validated. The symbol audit found 27,173 renamed core-owned symbols and eight guest ABI exports. All 28 SDK native lifecycle scenarios, the input parser/freshness suite and display lifetime suite passed under ASan/UBSan. Six actual-source image-owner scenarios passed (clean, partial create, uncertain present, release timeout, range retirement timeout and unregister failure). Existing JIT publication and dedicated-worker tests also passed.
Host regression suites: 102 C++ unit tests passed; 527 executed single-instance
PSP cases and ten paired relay scenarios passed. Eleven paired P2P cases remain
unrun for the existing missing 127.0.0.2 host loopback alias, causing the
aggregate runner's failure status. No executed regression test failed.
Console dual-instance rendering, pairing, guest controls/audio and sustained
performance still require physical qualification.
The initial experimental build produced a system error before the PPSSPP menu. Its boot log reached display configuration; native fault/exit records remained empty. The separate working single-instance installation is unchanged. Pairing and the second emulator have not yet been reached on the console.
The SDK bridge is compiled as C++20 separately from the C++17 frontend. Startup
checkpoints around Vulkan initialization write startup-stage.bin directly
with native flushes. Its four little-endian 64-bit words are magic
0x3254475350505350, stage number, recorder address and system tick. Stages
1–4 cover diagnostics, display configuration, graphics-object construction and
error-string construction; stages 10 and 11 bracket InitAPI's initial string
assignment. Stages 20 and 21 bracket NativeInit, and 22 precedes window setup.
The diagnostic boot marker is comdat-isolation. The native exit recorder
also wraps svcBreak (kind 6, reason in the high 32 bits and a readable four-byte
detail in the low 32 bits).

Coexistence and reuse on hardware still require qualification.

Uncertain presentation or release/retirement failure retains backing and blocks ordinary unload. Guest controls never enter the host emulator. Stale/disconnected snapshots become neutral.

working app's memory stick is not reused. Guest native text-entry applets are
disabled because their routing to the remote screen is not implemented.

If the host had already initialized multiplayer before pairing, restart that game once to select the local route.

Both cores use the private route automatically with their existing, independently configured PSP MAC addresses. The guest still runs on the host Switch 2, so game packets stay on that console. The route does not use a public relay, Wi-Fi IP address, or UPnP mapping, and it does not change either core's saved network settings. Stopping GameShare closes the listeners. articles.title: Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US
articles.body:
Trump Admin Still Won't Let TP-Link Sell Routers In US (arstechnica.com) 44
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption. The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security. While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold. Earlier this year, TP-Link announced plans to begin assembling routers in Mississippi as early as 2027, "but convincing Trump officials that it is fully under US control is likely a difficult task," reports Ars. "The government reviews of router makers' requests for waivers, formally called conditional approvals, are shrouded in secrecy."

articles.title: Sir Brian May adds new dimension to Hera asteroid
articles.body:
Hera science team member, astrophysicist and Queen guitarist Sir Brian May has added an additional dimension to the ESA planetary defence mission’s early views of the Didymos asteroid system via stereoscopic imagery – revealing the dramatic features of this exotic body as never before.
Media modal
Sir Brian May comments: “The Hera spacecraft acquired these two images on 06 November as it circled the Didymos system at a distance of 29.7 km with a resolution of 2.8 m per pixel, providing the perfect opportunity to create this stereoscopic image. Viewed in depth, the sharpness and smoothness of Didymos’s equatorial ridge is very apparent, compared with the rock-strewn surface of the rest of the asteroid.”
Hera principal investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur, adds: “Allowing us to observe in 3D with stereo pairs really makes us feel like we are there – even though these images come from 197 million km away. The result is both spectacular and scientifically meaningful.”
Media modal
Sir Brian May produced this stereoscopic view of Didymos with his colleague Claudia Manzoni. It combines adjacent acquisitions of the asteroid taken a few moments apart using Hera’s main Asteroid Framing Camera instrument by the instrument’s principal investigator Jean-Baptiste Vincent of the German Aerospace Center, DLR.
The very slight changes between the two images mimic the way our two human eyes view the same objects from very slightly different angles to yield stereo vision. The challenge comes in aligning the two images in a manner that seems optically true to our eyes.
Media modal
The stereoscopic views can be seen using colour 3D glasses, a dedicated viewer or else with your own eyes through ‘free viewing’.
The 3D view can be seen using a pair of red and blue 3D glasses. The second version can be seen by crossing your eyes, while the third can be accessed by looking into infinity – or else via a dedicated viewer, such as the OWL stereoscope, designed by Sir Brian May and available from the London Stereoscopic Company.
Media modal
Stereoscopic versions of Hera’s views of Mars moon Deimos acquired during its 2025 flyby of the red planet previously helped guide a simulation-based study of the moon’s violent past history
Media modal
Hera’s first images to be unveiled
In 2022 the small moonlet of Didymos called Dimorphos – not seen here – was impacted by NASA’s DART spacecraft to shift its orbit around the larger body. Now the European Space Agency’s Hera mission has arrived to perform a close-up ‘crash scene investigation’ of the binary asteroid system, to gather vital data to turn this grand-scale experiment into a well understood and potentially repeatable planetary defence technique.
Join the Hera team on the evening of Wednesday 25 November as they share the first close-up images of this historic transformed space object.
Our Hera livestream starts from 19:45 to 20:30 CET on Wednesday 25 November. Follow the livestream on ESA WebTV or the ESA YouTube channel.

articles.title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one
articles.body:
Xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the new 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro proves two screens aren’t better than one
The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.
The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, big batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.
Xiaomi 18 Pro
The Good
- Excellent main and telephoto cameras
- Privacy display
- Strong performance
- Compact
The Bad
- Rear display is limited
- Basic ultrawide camera
- Expensive
Xiaomi 18 Pro Max
The Good
- Excellent main and telephoto cameras
- Privacy display
- Strong performance
- Extended dynamic range
The Bad
- Rear display is limited
- Basic ultrawide camera
- Expensive
There are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.
They come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.
The rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.
You can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.
Unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.
The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.
It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.
Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a new third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other big Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.
The ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.
The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.
Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: AI claimed a solution to the 167 year-old Riemann Hypothesis — and a human did, too
articles.body:
It’s a big week for Levent Alpöge: The mathematician saw his employer, Anthropic, become the first publicly traded frontier AI lab. He also appears to have solved one of the most important problems in mathematics.
“The precise timing is horrible,” he wrote in an essay announcing his findings and describing how he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei last Sunday night to ask how to announce that he had found a Lean-compilable solution to the Riemann hypothesis, which dates back to 1859 and is among the Millennium Prize math problems.
The hypothesis conjectures that there is a hidden structure underlying the appearance of prime numbers. If the claimed result holds true, we’re entering sublime-mysteries-of-the-universe territory.
Maybe the best way to understand how exciting this is to the mathematics community is to watch the experts puzzling through the result in a chat on Zulip. Mathematicians like Chris Birkbeck, a number theorist at the University of East Anglia, are posting thoughts like this …
The cohomology bound is proved by what looks like an automorphy-lifting argument. It genuinely uses the existence of Galois representations attached to regular algebraic, polarized cuspidal automorphic representations of GL_n over CM fields, along with base change, Jacquet–Shalika, Clozel’s purity, Bernstein–Zelevinsky, the main theorem of CM, Deligne–Ribet and more.
For my part, I tapped out of mathematics at college calculus, so I can’t help decode exactly what that means.
But that comment was followed by 20 readers reacting 🤯.
It will be a while before the mathematics community feels like it has a handle on the proof, but most appear confident that the formalized Lean result will hold. Lean is an an open-source coding language used to express mathematical ideas as code, allowing proofs to be formally verified. Several participants in the Zulip chat, including MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland, say they have successfully confirmed that Alpöge’s solution can be compiled successfully.
Alpöge appeared in his essay to feel a bit guilty about releasing the proof without a truly human-intelligible explanation, but his obsession with the problem since childhood made him feel he “could not live” if he waited to release the finding.
Alpöge described a “stream-of-consciousness jaunt through the experience of finding all the pieces of the argument through incredible confusion with Claude” with more than a hint of AI euphoria, describing how the model “flew, and danced, and sparkled near that finish line.”
However, for all that action to mean anything, we’ll have to wait for humans to be able to understand the result and explain it to each other, something Alpöge has committed to pursue.
Alpöge and a collaborator, NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, also released another important proof related to the Navier-Stokes equations, problems that helped kick off the race between frontier labs and mathematicians to solve outstanding problems this summer.
Meanwhile, Ravi Vakil, a Stanford professor and the president of the American Mathematics Association, posted a proof of the General Riemann hypothesis written by Stanford postdoc Alessandro Masullo, noting that “it is all human, with no AI. The hope was to bring Alessandro to Stanford for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft.”
Without being expressed in Lean, it is too early to say whether the proof checks out, much less if anyone understands it.
In a brief introduction to his proof, which he said is the result of 12 years of work, Masullo wrote that “if any message at all this work is meant to send to the mathematician who feels discouraged by the pace and tone of the current climate, it is this: we are still here. We are very much alive. We are not going anywhere.”
This story has been updated to include that Alpöge’s Lean proof has been checked by independent sources.

articles.title: And yet, it moves
articles.body:
It appears that Anthropic has just solved the Riemann Hypothesis, and I have Thoughts. So I’m going to start by telling you about a musical I saw last week.
Given my entire personality and identity, it was basically mandatory for me to see Galileo on Broadway. I went to the second day of previews. The musical itself is at least kind of a Hamilton knock-off – with a stubborn main character, a friendship that goes wrong, family drama, and of course a historical setting with anachronistically modern tunes (though rock rather than hip-hop). Its greatest strength is its actors, especially Joy Woods as Galileo’s daughter Virginia and Jeremy Kushnier as Galileo’s friend/foil Bishop Barberini. A lot of it seemed to be pandering, but it was pandering exactly to me. I give it an 8.5 out of 10.
A replica of Galileo’s telescope1
The best part of this current trend of historical musicals is that it brings across how so many parts of our history are kind of insane, in a way we don’t usually take the time to appreciate. Hamilton is the story of a guerrilla uprising seizing control of the largest colony of the world’s most powerful empire, guided by Enlightenment philosophy of all things. Galileo is the story of a man literally seeing farther than anyone had before, and upending the nature of truth. We can find out what is true by just asking the natural world in the right way. These ideas are literally revolutionary.
The Riemann Hypothesis has been the crown jewel of unsolved mathematics since Fermat’s Last Theorem was solved in the 1990s. Myriad conjectures have been proven true conditional on the Riemann Hypothesis. That proof instantly unlocks an incredible amount of the universe of math – not unlike the telescope did for our universe.
When I imagined the day the proof was announced, I’d pictured celebrations in nerd circles on par with the biggest I’ve ever seen – Mars rovers touching down, the LHC finding the Higgs boson, and the first picture of a black hole. Dancing in the streets, if you live on a very specific street.
Dare mighty things
Instead, the mood feels mournful, or bittersweet at best. The proof came from an inscrutable silicon mind, not one of us. Maybe we could have solved this one ourselves, but instead we gave up and checked the answer at the back of the book. Perhaps it’s beautiful and wondrous that the proof exists at all, but it’s not a crowning moment of human achievement. Revolutionary, perhaps, but not in the same way.
Legends tell that after the Inquisition forced Galileo to formally recant his teachings on the Copernican system and the motion of the Earth, he muttered Eppur si muove – “And yet, it moves”. Truth is not what others tell us. Truth is just how the world is.
We are staring down the end of our role in Galileo’s project. There might still be time for more human discoveries, but the window is closing. Someday soon, any discovery we happen to make ourselves will be because no one bothered to pass the question off to a powerful machine mind. That’s not the world I wanted, but it’s how the world is. It might be selfish and childish, but on days like today, I wish that progress would go no further. I wish that history would stop.
And yet, it moves.

articles.title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
articles.body:
Hi everyone,
I am at the American Mathematical Society Executive Committee and Board of Trustees meeting now, and about to chair an hours-long meeting, but this is urgent, so I will try to get this out quickly. Alessandro Maria Masullo has a proposed proof of GRH, and Brian Conrad has been looking closely at it for months and gave extensive feedback which is being incorporated, and it is so far looking good to him. It is all human, with no AI. The hope was to have Brian work with Alessandro for a year to polish the writing and then announce it after running it by enough people. Now it seems best to put out the current draft. I hope people quickly check it, formalize, fill any small gaps if they occur. I really hope it works. I have great faith in Brian’s judgement, and Brian has put a lot of thought into checking what Alessandro has done. There is a long story to tell, but right now I want to get the file out. Here it is.
Update about 8 hours later: I’m out of the meetings, and now catching up! Several people have contacted me to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. (Thanks to several mathematicians in particular who were first to let me know.) As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)

articles.title: UK Government Forced To Disclose Secret Apple Backdoor Order
articles.body:
UK Government Forced To Disclose Secret Apple Backdoor Order (techcrunch.com) 32
			
		 	
				An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information. The Thursday ruling from the U.K.'s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret. The tribunal's ruling rejected the Home Office's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security. [...] A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year. The order follows a year-long dispute that began when British authorities reportedly sought a backdoor to users' data worldwide, drawing criticism from U.S. lawmakers over privacy concerns. Rather than comply, Apple disabled its Advanced Data Protection feature for U.K. users and challenged the order in court.
The government later narrowed its demand to British nationals' data, prompting another legal challenge from Apple.
Apple said it welcomes the ruling to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice, reiterating that it has "never built a backdoor or master key" to its products or services and "never will."

articles.title: Eufy’s Omni C28 is 53 percent off ahead of Black Friday
articles.body:
Hosting Thanksgiving can be fun, but cleaning up afterwards? Not so much. Eufy’s Omni C28 robot vacuum / mop hybrid can help, and thanks to an early Black Friday deal, you can pick it up at a new low price of $379.99 ($420 off its original price) at Amazon, Best Buy, or directly from Eufy (with code WS24C28200NEW1). While this model has dropped to around $499.99 a few times before, it commonly sells for a lot more, making now a great time to consider buying one.
Eufy’s Omni C28 is 53 percent off ahead of Black Friday
The robot vacuum / mop hybrid is our top pick for smaller homes and apartments, offering flagship features for less.
The Verge’s smart home reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy named the Eufy Omni C28 one of her top picks after testing 16 robot vacuum mops. She thinks it’s a particularly great fit for apartments and smaller homes. It offers features typically found in pricier flagship models, including a multifunction dock that automatically washes the mop roller with hot water and dries it with hot air, yet it doesn’t take up too much space. The robot itself is also relatively narrow and maneuvers easily around furniture and into tight spaces. It boasts excellent navigation, and had no trouble climbing over the legs of Jen’s lounger, which have tripped up many of the more expensive models she’s tested.
The Omni C28 also does a great job cleaning with its mops, particularly on hardwood floors. Surprisingly, it’s powerful enough to lift up dried oatmeal. Unlike most other robot vacuums Jen’s tested, this one lacks a camera, making it a good option if you’re concerned about privacy. Unfortunately, the trade-off is mediocre obstacle detection, so you’ll want to pick up socks and cables before running it.

articles.title: Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages
articles.body:
Signal Restricts Screenshots to Block AI Agents From Reading Messages 20
			
		 	
				Signal is introducing default-on screenshot restrictions to prevent AI agents from reading private conversations, warning that increasingly powerful assistants integrated into operating systems pose an "existential threat" to its privacy guarantees. "Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that's making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission," it said in a blog post. Reuters reports:  Signal, widely regarded by privacy advocates as a leader in secure messaging, called its new protections "incomplete" and urged operating system providers Apple, Alphabet's Google and Microsoft to give app developers more concrete ways to block the agents from accessing sensitive data. It also called on those companies to provide more information about how their agents function, so developers can assess what data the bots are accessing and adjust their systems accordingly.
[...] Users will receive pop-up windows giving them options to disable the blocks when Signal detects screenshot attempts or efforts by an AI assistant to access the screen, depending on the device. Signal similarly blocked Microsoft's Recall AI from taking screenshots on Windows last year. It said it was unable to reliably offer such protections on Apple's macOS.

articles.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
articles.body:
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:
- First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
- If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
- If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.
What is the right code for this?
If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
- Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
- Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, your job as an architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down the app. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable hack.
Why AI won’t push back
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.
Your new job is to architect
AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
- Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
- Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.
Your future as developer
In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

articles.title: Google Workers Tell Their Employer Not to Punish Schools That Don't Want AI
articles.body:
Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year.
Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.
As I wrote last week after attending a rally in New York City:
Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.
Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.
That day, protests took place in six other cities—Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.
School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks, which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini.
Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines.
“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union, which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”
“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.
A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands.
AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said.
Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”
That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.
“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.
Google has been contacted for comment.
